1.titre: What Excel is for: workbooks, sheets, cells and the ribbon
1.html:
Why it matters

On a placement, at business school or in your first job, Excel is everywhere: budgets, sales tracking, schedules, customer lists, marks. Lots of people have used it for years without really knowing how it is organised, and they waste time. Today we lay the foundations: the vocabulary and the layout of the screen. Everything else in the course builds on this.

This course uses Excel 365 in English. Function names are in English (SUM, AVERAGE...) and arguments are separated by a comma. On a Mac, the interface is very similar; in Google Sheets, the logic is the same, with a few differences we will point out along the way.

So what is Excel?

Excel is a spreadsheet: a program that stores data in a grid and performs calculations on it. Its great strength: when you change a figure, every calculation that depends on it updates by itself.

Excel does three things: store data, calculate, and present results.

The basic vocabulary

  • Workbook: the Excel file itself (for example budget-2026.xlsx). A workbook contains one or more sheets.
  • Sheet (or worksheet): a tab at the bottom of the screen. A new workbook opens with one sheet called Sheet1.
  • Column: identified by a letter (A, B, C... up to XFD, which is 16,384 columns).
  • Row: identified by a number (from 1 to 1,048,576).
  • Cell: the box where a column and a row meet. It has an address: column then row, for example B3.
  • Range: a group of adjacent cells, written with a colon: B2:B5 means "from B2 to B5".

The layout of the screen

  • The ribbon, at the top: the commands, arranged in tabs (File, Home, Insert, Formulas, Data, Review, View...). The Home tab holds what you use most: font, alignment, number formats.
  • The Name Box, on the left below the ribbon: it shows the address of the selected cell. You can type D200 there and press Enter to jump straight to it.
  • The formula bar, to the right of the Name Box: it shows the real contents of the cell. If the cell displays 1,230 but contains a calculation, this is where you see the calculation.
  • The sheet tabs, at the bottom left, and the status bar at the very bottom: when you select several numbers, it shows their average, count and sum straight away.

Example: a placement budget

Nina (fictional) is doing a six-month placement in Lille. She records her monthly budget in a sheet:

AB
1ItemAmount (€)
2Placement allowance650
3Rent420
4Groceries150
5Transport30
6Left over=B2-B3-B4-B5 displays 50

In B6, Nina doesn't type 50: she types a formula that starts with an equals sign. Excel calculates 650 − 420 − 150 − 30 = 50. If her rent drops to €400, she only changes B3, and B6 immediately shows 70. That is the whole point of Excel. We will learn to write formulas in detail in module 2.

What you see and what is stored

Click on B6: the cell displays 50, but the formula bar shows =B2-B3-B4-B5. Make this a habit: the cell shows a result, the formula bar shows the contents. It is the first thing to check when a figure looks odd.

Good habits from day one

  1. One piece of information per cell: write 650 in a cell and "€" in the column heading, not "650 € allowance" in a single box.
  2. Headings in row 1: every column has a clear header.
  3. No blank rows in the middle of your data: Excel uses them to guess where your table ends.
  4. Calculate with formulas, never with a calculator: a figure typed by hand doesn't update.

Exercise

  1. What is the address of the cell in the 4th column and the 7th row?
  2. How many cells does the range A2:C5 contain?
  3. In Nina's budget, groceries go up to €180. What do you need to change, and what does B6 display?
  4. Your colleague typed "1200 euros" in a cell of the budget. Why is that a bad idea?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. The 4th column is D: the address is D7.
  2. 3 columns (A, B, C) × 4 rows (2 to 5) = 12 cells.
  3. You only change B4 (180). B6 displays 650 − 420 − 180 − 30 = 20.
  4. With the word "euros", Excel treats the cell as text: you can't calculate with it. You should type 1200 and put the unit in the column heading (or use a currency format, lesson 3).

Key takeaways

  • A workbook contains sheets, made up of cells identified by column then row (B3).
  • A range is written with a colon: B2:B5.
  • The ribbon groups the commands; the formula bar shows a cell's real contents.
  • A formula starts with = and recalculates by itself.
  • One piece of information per cell, headings in row 1, no blank rows.

Next lesson: entering and editing data, text, numbers, dates and the fill handle.

2.html:
Why it matters

An Excel table is only as good as its data. If a date is entered wrongly or a number is taken for text, every calculation behind it will be wrong, often without any error message. Today you learn to enter data cleanly, correct it quickly, and let Excel fill in series for you.

Entering data in a cell

  • Click on a cell and type. Confirm with Enter (you move down one cell) or Tab (you move right).
  • Esc cancels what you are typing.
  • To edit without retyping everything: double-click in the cell, or press F2, or click in the formula bar.
  • To clear the contents: select and press Delete.

The three main types of data

TypeExample enteredDefault alignment
TextMarseilleLeft
Number1250.5Right
Date15/09/2026Right (it's a hidden number)

Alignment is a valuable clue: if a number lines up on the left when you haven't changed anything, Excel has probably taken it for text. It won't be included in calculations.

The classic traps

  • The decimal separator: in UK English Excel, you type 12.5, not 12,5. With a comma, Excel may see text, or even read it as a thousands separator.
  • Spaces and units: "€12" typed with the symbol often works, but "12 euros" becomes text. Type the number on its own.
  • Dates: type 15/09/2026. Excel recognises it and stores it as a number (the number of days since 1 January 1900), which will let you calculate durations in module 4.
  • Leading zeros: a code like 01234 loses its zero, because Excel sees the number 1234. To keep it, type an apostrophe in front: '01234. The cell becomes text, which is what you want for a code.

Tip: Ctrl+; inserts today's date in the cell.

The fill handle

Select a cell: a small square appears at the bottom right of the selection. That is the fill handle. Drag it down or to the right, and Excel extends the contents.

You selectYou drag across 3 more cells
MondayTuesday, Wednesday, Thursday
JanuaryFebruary, March, April
Week 1Week 2, Week 3, Week 4
01/10/202602/10/2026, 03/10/2026, 04/10/2026
5 (on its own)5, 5, 5 (a simple copy)
5 and 10 (both)15, 20, 25 (Excel continues the step of 5)

Remember the rule: with a single number, Excel copies; with two numbers selected, it continues the series. After dragging, a small "Auto Fill Options" button appears: it lets you choose between copying the cells and filling a series.

Two time-saving moves

  • Double-click the handle: Excel fills down to the end of the data in the neighbouring column. Ideal for a formula over 500 rows.
  • Ctrl+D: copies the contents of the top cell into the selected cells below.

Example: tracking sales on a placement

Hugo (fictional), an intern in a shop, tracks the week's sales. He types "Monday" in A2, drags the handle down to A6, enters his figures, then writes a formula in D2 and double-clicks the handle to copy it down:

ABCD
1DayItemsAverage price (€)Revenue (€)
2Monday1225=B2*C2 → 300
3Tuesday830=B3*C3 → 240
4Wednesday1522=B4*C4 → 330
5Thursday1027=B5*C5 → 270
6Friday2024=B6*C6 → 480

Hugo only wrote the formula once: when it was copied, Excel automatically adjusted the row number (B3*C3, then B4*C4...). We will see why in the lesson on references (module 2).

Changing the structure

  • Insert a row: right-click the row number, then Insert. Same for a column with its letter.
  • Delete a row or column: right-click, then Delete. Careful: clearing the contents (Delete key) is not deleting the row.
  • Undo a mistake: Ctrl+Z. Redo: Ctrl+Y.

Exercise

  1. You type 2026 in A1 and drag the handle down to A4. What does A4 contain? And if you had typed 2026 in A1 and 2027 in A2 before dragging both down to A4?
  2. In Hugo's table, what is the total revenue for the week?
  3. A colleague entered 1250,5 in a cell and the number is displayed on the left. What happened?
  4. You need to enter the area code 07. How do you keep the zero?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. With a single cell, Excel copies: A4 contains 2026. With 2026 and 2027 selected, it continues the series: A3 = 2028 and A4 = 2029.
  2. 300 + 240 + 330 + 270 + 480 = €1,620.
  3. They used a comma instead of a decimal point: UK English Excel took it as text (aligned left). You need to type 1250.5.
  4. Type '07: the apostrophe forces text and the zero stays visible.

Key takeaways

  • Enter confirms and moves down, Tab confirms and moves right, F2 edits, Esc cancels.
  • Text on the left, numbers and dates on the right: a number on the left is suspicious.
  • Decimal point in English Excel: 12.5. Dates in the format 15/09/2026.
  • Fill handle: a single number is copied, two numbers create a series; days and months extend by themselves.
  • Double-click the handle or use Ctrl+D to fill down quickly.

Next lesson: formatting cleanly, number formats, alignment, borders and column width.

3.html:
Why it matters

A table that is correct but unreadable won't get read. On a placement, your manager will also judge your work on its presentation: aligned amounts, clear percentages, visible headings. Good news: a few settings are enough. And there is one golden rule to understand before anything else.

Formatting changes what is displayed, never the stored value.

Number formats

You will find them on the Home tab, Number group, or in the Format Cells dialog box (shortcut Ctrl+1, Number tab).

FormatStored valueDisplay
General1234.51234.5
Number, 2 decimal places, thousands separator1234.51,234.50
Currency (€)1234.5€1,234.50
Percentage, 0 decimal places0.15516%
Percentage, 1 decimal place0.15515.5%
Short Date4628015/09/2026

Two points to understand properly:

  • A percentage is a decimal number: 15.5% is stored as 0.155. If you apply the Percentage format to a cell containing 15.5, it will display 1550%. Instead, type 15.5% directly: Excel stores 0.155 and displays it as a percentage.
  • Hidden decimals still exist: 0.155 displayed as "16%" is still 0.155 in calculations. To really round a value, you will need a function (ROUND, in module 2).

The Accounting format looks like Currency, but lines the € symbol up at the edge of the cell and shows a dash for zeros: handy in financial tables.

Alignment, font, borders

  • Alignment: keep numbers on the right (the digits line up by units, which is easier to read). Centre column headings instead.
  • Wrap Text (Home, Alignment group): a long heading is displayed over several lines in its cell.
  • Font: put headers in bold, and the total row too. Avoid more than two colours.
  • Borders: a line under the headers and above the total is often enough. A full grid makes things look heavy.

Merging: best avoided

"Merge & Center" combines several cells into one. It's tempting for a title, but it gets in the way of sorting, copy-pasting and selecting columns. Use Center Across Selection instead: Ctrl+1, Alignment tab, Horizontal, "Center Across Selection". Same look, none of the drawbacks.

Column width and row height

  • If a cell displays ########, it's not an error: the column is too narrow for the number or date.
  • Double-click the right border of the column letter: the width adjusts to the longest content.
  • You can select several columns and double-click one border to adjust them all at once.

Example: a presentable budget

Léo (fictional) is preparing the budget for a student society event. Before formatting, his cells show 1200, 0.25 and 300. After formatting:

ABC
1ItemAmountShare of total
2Venue€1,200.00=B2/B5 → 50.0%
3Catering€900.00=B3/B5 → 37.5%
4Publicity€300.00=B4/B5 → 12.5%
5Total=B2+B3+B4 → €2,400.00=C2+C3+C4 → 100.0%

Column B: Currency format, 2 decimal places. Column C: Percentage format, 1 decimal place. 1,200 / 2,400 = 0.5, displayed as 50.0%. The values haven't changed, only the display is clearer.

Copying formatting

The Format Painter brush (Home tab, on the left) copies the format of one cell to another, without touching the contents. One click for a single use, a double-click to use it several times (Esc to stop).

Exercise

  1. A cell contains 0.075. What does it display in Percentage format with 1 decimal place? With 0 decimal places?
  2. In Léo's budget, catering goes up to €1,100. What is the new total, and what share does the venue represent (1 decimal place)?
  3. A column of dates displays ########: what do you do?
  4. Your classmate types 20 in a cell then applies the Percentage format. What do they get, and what should they have done?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. With 1 decimal place: 7.5%. With 0 decimal places: 8% (rounded display, the value is still 0.075).
  2. Total: 1,200 + 1,100 + 300 = €2,600. Venue share: 1,200 / 2,600 ≈ 0.4615, displayed as 46.2%.
  3. The column is too narrow: double-click the right border of the column letter to adjust it.
  4. They get 2000%, because 20 × 100. They should have typed 20% directly (stored as 0.2) or typed 0.2 and then applied the format.

Key takeaways

  • Formatting changes the display, not the value.
  • Ctrl+1 opens Format Cells. Useful formats: Number, Currency, Accounting, Percentage, Date.
  • A percentage is stored as a decimal: 15.5% = 0.155. Type 15.5% directly.
  • Numbers on the right, headings in bold, light borders. Avoid merging: use "Center Across Selection".
  • ######## = column too narrow: double-click the border.

Next lesson: the keyboard shortcuts that save you hours.

4.titre: The keyboard shortcuts that save you hours
4.html:
Why it matters

Watch someone who is really at ease in Excel: they barely touch the mouse. It's not magic, it's a short list of shortcuts learnt one at a time. On a 5,000-row file, scrolling to the end of the data with the mouse wheel takes a minute; with the keyboard, a fraction of a second. No need to learn them all today: pick three or four and use them this week.

On a Mac, most of the shortcuts below exist with the Cmd key instead of Ctrl, but not all of them: if in doubt, hover over the button in the ribbon and the tooltip shows the shortcut.

The essentials

ShortcutAction
Ctrl+C / Ctrl+X / Ctrl+VCopy / cut / paste
Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+YUndo / redo
Ctrl+SSave
Ctrl+FFind
Ctrl+HFind and replace
Ctrl+1Format Cells
F2Edit the active cell

Moving around fast

ShortcutAction
Ctrl+arrowJumps to the edge of the data block in the direction of the arrow
Ctrl+HomeGoes back to A1
Ctrl+EndGoes to the last used cell in the sheet
Ctrl+Page Down / Ctrl+Page UpMoves to the next / previous sheet
F5Go To an address (for example B500)

Ctrl+Down arrow stops at the last filled cell before a blank. If there is an empty cell in the middle of your column, it stops just before it: that's also a quick way to spot gaps in your data.

Selecting fast

ShortcutAction
Shift+arrowExtends the selection by one cell
Ctrl+Shift+arrowExtends the selection to the edge of the block
Ctrl+ASelects the data block (press again: the whole sheet)
Ctrl+SpaceSelects the entire column
Shift+SpaceSelects the entire row

Entering and calculating faster

ShortcutAction
Ctrl+DFills the top cell down (lesson 2)
Ctrl+;Inserts today's date
Alt+=AutoSum: inserts =SUM(...) over the neighbouring range
Ctrl+EnterEnters the same input into all the selected cells
Alt+EnterLine break inside a cell
F4Repeats the last action (and, in a formula, adds $ signs: module 2)

The Alt key: the whole ribbon from the keyboard

Press Alt once and let go: letters appear on the ribbon tabs, then on each button. You can type the letters one after another to reach any command without the mouse. No need to memorise them: they are shown on screen.

Example: total sales in three seconds

Sofia (fictional), a marketing intern, receives the monthly sales for a product:

AB
1MonthSales (€)
2January4,200
3February3,850
4March5,100
5April4,650
6Total=SUM(B2:B5) → 17,800

Her method: click on B2, Ctrl+Down arrow to reach B5, Down arrow to move to B6, then Alt+=: Excel suggests =SUM(B2:B5). Enter, and the total appears: 4,200 + 3,850 + 5,100 + 4,650 = 17,800. Always check the suggested range before confirming: if there's a blank in the column, Excel may stop too early.

Exercise

  1. You are in A1 of a file with 3,000 rows of sales in column B. Which shortcuts select all the sales, from B2 to the last row?
  2. You want to write "Chase up" in 40 non-adjacent cells at once. How do you do it?
  3. In Sofia's table, May (€3,900) is added in row 6 and the total moves down to B7. Which formula and what result?
  4. Ctrl+Down arrow from B2 stops at B57 even though the list goes down to B300. What does that tell you?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Click on B2 (or Right arrow then Down arrow), then Ctrl+Shift+Down arrow: the selection extends to the last sale (as long as there's no empty cell in the middle).
  2. Select the cells while holding Ctrl, type the text, then confirm with Ctrl+Enter.
  3. =SUM(B2:B6) → 17,800 + 3,900 = 21,700.
  4. There is very probably an empty cell in B58: a gap in the data, worth checking.

Key takeaways

  • The must-haves: Ctrl+C, X, V, Z, Y, S, F, H and Ctrl+1.
  • Ctrl+arrow to jump to the edge of the data, Ctrl+Shift+arrow to select up to the edge.
  • Alt+= for an AutoSum, Ctrl+Enter to fill several cells in one go.
  • Alt on its own shows the ribbon letters.
  • Learn three shortcuts a week, not thirty at once.

Next lesson: organising your workbook, sheets, freezing panes, printing and saving as xlsx, csv or pdf.

5.titre: Organising your workbook: sheets, panes, printing, formats
5.html:
Why it matters

A good workbook makes sense without its author. On a placement, your file will be opened by your supervisor, printed for a meeting, sent to a client or imported into another program. Today we look at how to organise it, make it readable on screen and on paper, and save it in the right format.

Managing sheets

  • Add a sheet: the + button to the right of the tabs, or Shift+F11.
  • Rename: double-click the tab. A short, clear name: "Data", "Calculations", "Summary" rather than "Sheet3".
  • Move: drag the tab. Copy: drag it while holding Ctrl.
  • Colour or delete: right-click the tab. Careful, deleting a sheet can't be undone with Ctrl+Z.

A layout that works almost every time:

SheetContents
Read meWhat the file is for, who made it, date last updated
DataThe raw data, one row per item, no calculations
CalculationsThe intermediate formulas
SummaryThe results to show

Freezing panes

When you scroll down a long list, the column headings disappear and you no longer know what you're reading. The fix: View tab, Freeze Panes.

  • Freeze Top Row: row 1 stays visible.
  • Freeze First Column: column A stays visible.
  • Freeze Panes: everything above and to the left of the selected cell stays fixed. Select B2 to freeze both row 1 and column A.

Example: tracking a class's marks

Inès (fictional), her year's student rep, collects marks out of 20. Row 1 and column A are frozen (select B2, then Freeze Panes):

ABCD
1StudentMarketingFinanceAverage
2Adam1411=(B2+C2)/2 → 12.5
3Bérénice1615=(B3+C3)/2 → 15.5
4Chloé913=(B4+C4)/2 → 11

Even at row 120 or column Z, Inès can see the student's name and the subject name. The brackets in the formula are essential: we'll see why in module 2.

Printing without wasting paper

  1. Ctrl+P opens the print preview: always check how many pages are planned.
  2. In the settings, choose Fit Sheet on One Page, or "Fit All Columns on One Page" for a long table.
  3. Choose Landscape orientation for a wide table.
  4. To print only part of it: select it, then Page Layout tab, Print Area, Set Print Area.
  5. To repeat the heading row on every page: Page Layout tab, Print Titles, then "Rows to repeat at top".

Saving in the right format

Ctrl+S saves; F12 opens "Save As" so you can choose a format. If your file is on OneDrive or SharePoint, AutoSave (top left) saves continuously.

FormatWhat it keepsWhen to use it
.xlsxEverything: sheets, formulas, formattingThe normal working format
.xlsmEverything, plus macrosOnly if the file contains macros
.csvThe values of the active sheet only, as textExchanging data with another program
.pdfA fixed image that can't be editedSending a document to read or print

The CSV trap

A CSV is a plain text file: one line per row of the table, values separated by a delimiter. In UK English Excel, that delimiter is a comma (hence the name, comma-separated values). When you save as CSV, you lose the other sheets, the formulas (only the results remain) and all the formatting. Excel warns you: always keep your .xlsx version alongside. Inès's table as a CSV gives, for example:

  • Student,Marketing,Finance,Average
  • Adam,14,11,12.5

In Google Sheets, the equivalent is under File, Download (xlsx, csv, pdf...).

Exercise

  1. You want row 1 and columns A and B to stay visible. Which cell do you select before clicking Freeze Panes?
  2. In Inès's table, Dimitri has 12 in marketing and 17 in finance. What is his average?
  3. Your workbook has three sheets and formulas. You save it only as .csv and close it. What do you lose?
  4. Your supervisor wants a document to read on their phone, with no risk of it being changed. Which format do you choose?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. C2: everything above (row 1) and to the left (columns A and B) stays frozen.
  2. (12 + 17) / 2 = 14.5.
  3. You lose the other two sheets, the formulas (only the results remain) and the formatting. You should have kept an .xlsx version.
  4. PDF: it looks the same everywhere and isn't easy to edit.

Key takeaways

  • Well-named sheets: Data, Calculations, Summary, and why not a "Read me".
  • Freeze Panes keeps visible what is above and to the left of the chosen cell.
  • Before printing: Ctrl+P, preview, fit to one page, repeated titles.
  • .xlsx for working, .csv for exchanging data (one sheet, values only), .pdf for sharing.

Next module: basic formulas, operators, SUM, AVERAGE, references and percentages.

6.titre: Writing a formula: operators, precedence, common mistakes
6.html:
Why it matters

In module 1, you saw that a formula recalculates by itself. Today, you learn to write formulas yourself, without slipping up. Most beginner mistakes don't come from Excel but from a misunderstood order of calculation: one forgotten bracket, and a 30% margin becomes a 300% margin.

The rules for writing formulas

  1. A formula always starts with =. Without it, Excel displays the text as it is.
  2. It can contain numbers (=12*3), references to other cells (=B2*C2) and functions (=SUM(B2:B5), next lesson).
  3. Always prefer references to hard-coded numbers: if B2 changes, the result follows.
  4. To enter a reference without typing it: after the =, click on the cell you want.

The operators

OperatorRoleExampleResult
+Addition=7+310
-Subtraction=7-34
*Multiplication=7*321
/Division=7/23.5
^Power=2^38
&Joins two pieces of text="Ms "&"Durand"Ms Durand

Comparisons (=, <, >, <=, >=, <>) return TRUE or FALSE: =B2>100 displays TRUE if B2 is over 100. They'll come in very handy in module 3.

The order of calculation

Excel follows the maths rules of precedence:

1. Brackets, 2. powers, 3. multiplication and division, 4. addition and subtraction. At equal precedence, left to right.

FormulaCalculation Excel performsResult
=2+3*43 × 4 first, then + 214
=(2+3)*42 + 3 first, then × 420
=10/2*5Left to right: 10 / 2 = 5, then × 525
=2*3^23^2 = 9 first, then × 218
=-2^2An Excel quirk: the minus sign applies before the power, (−2)^24

The last case is surprising: in maths, −2^2 equals −4. In Excel, =-2^2 gives 4. If you want −4, write =-(2^2). Above all, remember the practical rule: when in doubt, add brackets. They cost nothing.

Example: a placement quote

Clara (fictional), an intern at a small business, is preparing a quote. VAT is 20%:

AB
1Unit price excl. VAT (€)80
2Quantity15
3VAT rate20%
4Total excl. VAT (€)=B1*B2 → 1,200
5VAT (€)=B4*B3 → 240
6Total incl. VAT (€)=B4*(1+B3) → 1,440

In B6, the brackets are essential. Without them, =B4*1+B3 calculates 1,200 × 1 + 0.2 = 1,200.2: a wrong result, with no error message at all. It's the most dangerous trap, because Excel doesn't warn you.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the =: the cell displays B1*B2 as text.
  • A number stored as text (lesson 2 of module 1): it's ignored or causes an error.
  • Typing a result in by hand instead of a formula: it no longer updates.
  • Dividing by an empty cell: Excel displays #DIV/0!. We'll cover all the errors in lesson 10.
  • A reference that goes round in circles: if B4 contains =B4+1, Excel flags a circular reference. A formula must never depend on itself.

To see all the formulas in a sheet rather than their results: Formulas tab, Show Formulas. Click again to return to the normal view.

Exercise

  1. Work these out by hand, then check in Excel: =5+10/5, =(5+10)/5, =3*2^2, =20-4-6.
  2. In Clara's quote, the quantity goes up to 25. What do the total excl. VAT and the total incl. VAT become?
  3. A colleague writes =B4*1.2 for the total incl. VAT. The result is correct today. Why is it still a worse formula than =B4*(1+B3)?
  4. Which formula calculates the average of 12, 15 and 18 without a function? Which trap should you avoid?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =5+10/5 → 10 / 5 = 2, then + 5 = 7. =(5+10)/5 → 15 / 5 = 3. =3*2^2 → 2^2 = 4, then × 3 = 12. =20-4-6 → left to right, 16 − 6 = 10.
  2. Total excl. VAT: 80 × 25 = €2,000. Total incl. VAT: 2,000 × 1.2 = €2,400.
  3. The 20% rate is hard-coded in the formula. If it changes (or for a product at 5.5%), you'll have to edit every formula instead of a single cell B3.
  4. =(12+15+18)/3 → 45 / 3 = 15. Without brackets, =12+15+18/3 gives 12 + 15 + 6 = 33, which is wrong.

Key takeaways

  • A formula starts with = and should use references, not hard-coded numbers.
  • Operators: + - * / ^ and & for text.
  • Precedence: brackets, powers, multiplication and division, addition and subtraction, then left to right.
  • A forgotten bracket gives a wrong result with no error message: when in doubt, add brackets.
  • Formulas tab, Show Formulas, to review a whole sheet.

Next lesson: the basic functions, SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT and COUNTA.

7.titre: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT, COUNTA
7.html:
Why it matters

Adding up 300 cells with + signs is slow and risky. Functions do the job in one line. The six functions in this lesson are the most used in Excel: with them, you can already answer "how much in total?", "how much on average?", "what's the best and the worst?" and "how many rows?".

How a function is written

=NAME(argument1,argument2,...)

  • The name of the function, in English in English Excel.
  • Brackets, containing the arguments: often a range, such as B2:B7.
  • Arguments are separated by a comma: =SUM(B2:B7,D2:D7). Google Sheets in English uses the comma too; in some European language versions you'll see a semicolon instead (and local names: SOMME, MOYENNE...).

When you type =SU, Excel suggests a list of functions: choose with the arrow keys and confirm with Tab. A tooltip then reminds you which arguments are expected.

The six functions

FunctionWhat it returns
SUMThe total of the numbers
AVERAGEThe average of the numbers (sum divided by how many there are)
MINThe smallest number
MAXThe largest number
COUNTThe number of cells that contain a number
COUNTAThe number of non-empty cells (numbers, text, dates...)

Example: mid-term exam marks

Yanis (fictional), a tutorial assistant, collects the marks out of 20 for six students. One student doesn't have a mark yet (empty cell), one was absent ("abs"):

AB
1StudentMark
2Alice12
3Bastien15
4Camille(empty)
5Dylan8
6Emmaabs
7Farid17
FormulaResultExplanation
=SUM(B2:B7)5212 + 15 + 8 + 17; text and blanks are ignored
=COUNT(B2:B7)4Four cells contain a number
=COUNTA(B2:B7)5Five non-empty cells, counting "abs"
=AVERAGE(B2:B7)1352 / 4: only numbers count
=MIN(B2:B7)8The lowest mark
=MAX(B2:B7)17The highest mark

The average trap

AVERAGE ignores empty cells and text, but it counts zeros. If Yanis replaces "abs" with 0, the sum stays at 52 but there are 5 marks: the average drops to 52 / 5 = 10.4. It's neither right nor wrong: it's a decision. Does an absent student count as zero or are they simply not marked? Choose deliberately, and write it down in a note.

COUNT or COUNTA?

  • To count amounts, marks, quantities: COUNT.
  • To count filled rows (customer names, order references): COUNTA.
  • The difference between the two often reveals a problem: here, COUNTA − COUNT = 1, so there's a non-numeric value ("abs") in a column of marks.

Several ranges, several arguments

Functions accept several arguments: =SUM(B2:B7,D2:D7) adds up two columns, =MAX(B2:B7,10) returns the larger of the best mark and 10. You can also select non-adjacent ranges with the mouse by holding Ctrl while you write the formula.

A reminder from module 1: Alt+= inserts an AutoSum, and the status bar shows the average, count and sum as soon as you select cells. Handy for checking a result at a glance.

Exercise

  1. A week's sales are €320, €410, €0, €380 and €290 (in B2:B6). What do SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX return?
  2. In Yanis's table, Camille finally gets 11. What do SUM, COUNT, COUNTA and AVERAGE become?
  3. A column of 200 orders contains references (text). Which function counts them?
  4. Write the formula that gives the gap between the best and the worst mark in B2:B7.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. SUM: 320 + 410 + 0 + 380 + 290 = €1,400. AVERAGE: 1,400 / 5 = €280 (the 0 counts). MIN: 0. MAX: 410.
  2. SUM: 52 + 11 = 63. COUNT: 5. COUNTA: 6. AVERAGE: 63 / 5 = 12.6.
  3. =COUNTA(...): COUNT would ignore the text and return 0.
  4. =MAX(B2:B7)-MIN(B2:B7) → in the example, 17 − 8 = 9.

Key takeaways

  • A function is written =NAME(arguments), with arguments separated by ,.
  • SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX ignore text and empty cells.
  • AVERAGE counts zeros: a 0 and an empty cell don't give the same average.
  • COUNT counts numbers, COUNTA counts non-empty cells.

Next lesson: relative, absolute ($) and mixed references, so you can copy formulas without breaking anything.

8.html:
Why it matters

You saw in module 1 that a formula copied down adapts by itself: =B2*C2 becomes =B3*C3. That's brilliant... until the day you want part of the formula not to move. That's where the $ symbol comes in. This lesson is one of the most important in the course: it saves you from dozens of silent errors.

Relative reference: it moves

By default, a reference like B2 is relative. Excel doesn't remember "cell B2" but "the cell located in such a position relative to me". If you copy the formula one row down, the reference moves down one row; one column to the right, it shifts one column.

Absolute reference: it stays fixed

With $ signs, the reference is absolute: $B$1 always refers to B1, wherever you copy the formula. The $ in front of the letter locks the column, the $ in front of the number locks the row.

Written asTypeWhen copied downWhen copied right
B1RelativeB2, B3...C1, D1...
$B$1Absolutestays $B$1stays $B$1
B$1Mixed (row locked)stays B$1C$1, D$1...
$B1Mixed (column locked)$B2, $B3...stays $B1

The F4 key

No need to type the $ signs: in a formula, put the cursor on a reference and press F4. Each press cycles through: B1 → $B$1 → B$1 → $B1 → B1. On some laptops, you need to press Fn+F4. On a Mac, the shortcut is Cmd+T.

Example: a commission rate

Thomas (fictional), on a sales placement, calculates the sales team's commission. The rate (5%) is in a single cell, B1:

ABC
1Commission rate5%
2SalespersonSales (€)Commission (€)
3Amel12,000=B3*$B$1 → 600
4Bruno8,500=B4*$B$1 → 425
5Cyril15,200=B5*$B$1 → 760

Thomas wrote =B3*$B$1 in C3 then copied it down. B3 is relative: it becomes B4 then B5. $B$1 is absolute: it stays on the rate.

What happens without the $

If Thomas had written =B3*B1, copying it would have given =B4*B2 in C4: B2 contains the text "Sales (€)", hence the #VALUE! error. And in C5, =B5*B3 = 15,200 × 12,000 = 182,400,000: an absurd result, with no error message. Hence the rule:

When a formula uses a parameter cell (rate, price, total), lock it with $ before copying.

Another advantage: if the rate goes up to 6%, Thomas only changes B1, and all the commissions recalculate (€720, €510 and €912).

Mixed references: a price table

Mixed references are used when you copy a formula in both directions. Example: a printing price grid, quantity × unit price depending on the format:

ABC
1Quantity, unit price€0.10€0.25
2100=$A2*B$1 → 10=$A2*C$1 → 25
3500=$A3*B$1 → 50=$A3*C$1 → 125
41,000=$A4*B$1 → 100=$A4*C$1 → 250

A single formula, written in B2 and copied everywhere: $A2 locks column A (the quantities) but lets the row move down; B$1 locks row 1 (the prices) but lets the column move across.

A tip: share of the total

Calculating each row's share of a total is the most common case: =B3/$B$6, with the total locked. It's exactly the mistake people make most often on placements: forgetting the $ on the total, and getting #DIV/0! from the second row onwards.

Exercise

  1. In D5, you write =B5*$F$2, then copy it to D6 and to E5. What formulas do you get?
  2. In Thomas's table, add Diane with €9,800 of sales in row 6. What formula is in C6 after copying, and what commission?
  3. What formula should you write in B2 of the price grid so you can copy it everywhere? What does it give in C4 if C1 is €0.30?
  4. The sales of 4 shops are in B2:B5 and their total in B6 (€50,000). Shop 1 sold €12,500. Which formula in C2, to copy down to C5, gives each one's share? What result in C2?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. In D6: =B6*$F$2. In E5: =C5*$F$2. The relative part moves, the absolute part stays.
  2. =B6*$B$1 → 9,800 × 5% = €490.
  3. =$A2*B$1. In C4: =$A4*C$1 → 1,000 × 0.30 = €300.
  4. =B2/$B$6 → 12,500 / 50,000 = 0.25, which is 25% in Percentage format.

Key takeaways

  • Relative (B1): moves when copied. Absolute ($B$1): never moves.
  • Mixed: B$1 locks the row, $B1 locks the column.
  • F4 cycles through the four forms.
  • Always lock a parameter cell (rate, price, total) before copying.
  • Copying without $ can give an absurd result with no error message: check the second row.

Next lesson: percentages, changes and rounding with ROUND, ROUNDUP and ROUNDDOWN.

9.html:
Why it matters

"Sales grew by 12%", "the margin is 35%", "80% of the budget is spent": in business, almost every comment on figures goes through percentages. There are three calculations to master, one classic mistake to avoid, and three rounding functions to present clean results.

Reminder: a percentage is a number

As seen in module 1, 12% is stored as 0.12. To calculate 12% of 2,500, you write =2500*12% or, better, =B2*C2 with C2 in Percentage format. The result is 300.

The three calculations to know

QuestionFormulaExample
What share of B does A represent?=A/B300 out of 1,200 → 25%
What is the change from old to new?=(new-old)/oldfrom 12,500 to 14,000 → 12%
What does a value become after a t% increase?=value*(1+t)2,000 + 3% → 2,060

For a decrease, you write =value*(1-t): €80 with a 25% discount gives 80 × 0.75 = €60. The formula =new/old-1 gives the same change as =(new-old)/old.

Example: a shop's revenue

Lucie (fictional), on a work-study programme in a cosmetics shop, compares two years:

ABCD
1Department2025 (€)2026 (€)Change
2Skincare12,50014,000=(C2-B2)/B2 → 12.0%
3Make-up8,0007,200=(C3-B3)/B3 → −10.0%
4Fragrances4,5005,400=(C4-B4)/B4 → 20.0%
5Total=SUM(B2:B4) → 25,000=SUM(C2:C4) → 26,600=(C5-B5)/B5 → 6.4%

Check: (14,000 − 12,500) / 12,500 = 1,500 / 12,500 = 0.12. And for the total: 1,600 / 25,000 = 0.064. Notice that the overall change (6.4%) is not the average of the three changes: (12 − 10 + 20) / 3 = 7.3%. Always recalculate the change from the totals.

The trap: up then down

A €100 price rises by 20%, then falls by 20%. Back to €100? No: 100 × 1.2 = 120, then 120 × 0.8 = €96. Successive percentages multiply, they don't add up.

Points or per cent?

If a margin goes from 30% to 33%, it gains 3 percentage points, but it grows by 3 / 30 = 10%. In a meeting, say "points" for a difference between two percentages: it's a very common mix-up.

Rounding for real: ROUND, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN

Cell formatting only hides decimals. When you need a genuinely rounded value (a price, an invoice, a number of boxes), use a function.

=ROUND(number,num_digits), and likewise ROUNDUP (always up) and ROUNDDOWN (always down).

FormulaResultComment
=ROUND(3.14159,2)3.14To the nearest, 2 decimal places
=ROUND(2.5,0)3A 5 rounds up (away from zero)
=ROUNDUP(12.01,0)13Always up
=ROUNDDOWN(12.99,0)12Always down
=ROUND(1234.5,-2)1200A negative number of digits rounds to the hundreds

Which one to choose?

  • ROUND: to present an amount (an invoice to the cent: =ROUND(B2*1.2,2)).
  • ROUNDUP: when you need "enough" of something. 130 guests, tables of 12: =ROUNDUP(130/12,0) gives 11 tables (130 / 12 ≈ 10.83; with 10 tables, you'd be short of seats).
  • ROUNDDOWN: when you can only count whole units. With a €500 budget and tickets at €45, =ROUNDDOWN(500/45,0) gives 11 tickets (500 / 45 ≈ 11.1).

Exercise

  1. Lina's rent goes from €650 to €676. Which formula and what change?
  2. A product at €45 excl. VAT goes up by 8%. What is the new price, rounded to the cent with a function?
  3. A pass rate goes from 60% to 66%. Express the change in points, then as a percentage.
  4. For a seminar of 47 people, a minibus has 9 seats. How many minibuses should you book? Write the formula.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =(676-650)/650 → 26 / 650 = 0.04, which is +4%.
  2. =ROUND(45*(1+8%),2) → 45 × 1.08 = €48.60.
  3. +6 points; as a percentage, 6 / 60 = +10%.
  4. =ROUNDUP(47/9,0) → 47 / 9 ≈ 5.22, so 6 minibuses.

Key takeaways

  • Share: =A/B. Change: =(new-old)/old. Increase of t: =value*(1+t).
  • Successive percentages multiply: +20% then −20% makes −4%.
  • A difference between two percentages is expressed in points.
  • ROUND to the nearest, ROUNDUP upwards, ROUNDDOWN downwards; formatting only hides.

Next lesson: reading and fixing the errors #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, #REF!, #N/A and #NAME?.

10.html:
Why it matters

A message like #VALUE! looks scary, but it's actually good news: Excel is telling you there's a problem, and often which one. The truly dangerous errors are the ones that don't show up (a forgotten bracket, a missing $). Today, you learn to read each error code, find its cause and fix it.

The five main errors

ErrorWhat it meansExample
#DIV/0!Division by zero or by an empty cell=B2/C2 with C2 empty
#VALUE!Wrong data type: text where a number is expected=B2*C2 with C2 = "abs"
#REF!Invalid reference: the target cell has been deleted=B2+#REF! after deleting column C
#N/AValue not available: a lookup found nothingAn XLOOKUP that can't find the customer (module 5)
#NAME?Excel doesn't recognise a name in the formula=SUMM(B2:B5) or =AVERAG(B2:B5)

And two displays that are not formula errors: ######## (column too narrow, seen in module 1) and the small green triangle in the corner of a cell, which flags a doubt (for example a number stored as text).

Causes and fixes

#DIV/0!

Often an empty cell that will be filled in later, or a reference that slipped when copied because a $ was missing (lesson 8). Check the divisor. In module 3 we'll learn to display a clean message instead with IF and IFERROR.

#VALUE!

A cell contains text: "abs", "12 euros", a number with a comma instead of a decimal point, or an invisible space. Functions like SUM ignore text, but the operators + - * / return #VALUE!. Fix the source data.

#REF!

You deleted a row, a column or a sheet used by a formula, or copied a formula to an area where the reference falls off the sheet. The simplest fix: Ctrl+Z straight away. Otherwise, rewrite the lost reference.

#N/A

It almost always comes from a lookup function that can't find the value it's looking for (typo, extra space). You'll mostly meet it in module 5.

#NAME?

A typo in a function name, a function name from another language version (=SOMME(...) in English Excel), or text written without quotation marks: =B2&euros instead of =B2&" euros". Tip: type function names in lower case. If Excel recognises them, it switches them to capitals when you confirm; if they stay in lower case, there's a typo.

Example: a placement dashboard full of errors

Jade (fictional) takes over her predecessor's file. She spots the errors and fixes them one by one:

ABCD
1Sales repSales (€)MeetingsSales per meeting
2Hélène6,00020=B2/C2 → 300
3Igor4,500(empty)=B3/C3 → #DIV/0!
4Jules3,600twelve=B4/C4 → #VALUE!
5Total=SUM(B2:B4) → 14,100=SUM(C2:C4) → 20=AVERAG(D2:D4) → #NAME?

Fixes: Igor had 15 meetings, so Jade enters 15 in C3 (D3 = 4,500 / 15 = 300). She replaces "twelve" with 12 in C4 (D4 = 3,600 / 12 = 300). She corrects the function: =AVERAGE(D2:D4) → 300. The meetings total becomes 20 + 15 + 12 = 47. Note: before the fixes, =SUM(C2:C4) showed 20 with no error, even though data was missing. No error doesn't prove the result is right.

Tools for investigating

  • Click on the cell and read the formula bar: that's the first reflex.
  • F2: the formula's references are shown in colour, with matching coloured boxes around the target cells.
  • Formulas tab, Formula Auditing group: Trace Precedents draws arrows to the cells used; Evaluate Formula shows the calculation step by step; Error Checking goes through the errors.
  • An error spreads: if D3 shows #DIV/0!, any formula that uses D3 (an average, a total) will also show an error. Always trace back to the first cell in error.

Exercise

  1. Which error do you get with =SUMM(B2:B5) (an extra M)? And with ="Total: "+B5?
  2. You delete column C while D2 contains =B2/C2. What happens?
  3. In Jade's corrected table, Kenza is added in row 5 with €5,000 and 0 meetings (she's just started). What's displayed in D5, and why isn't it a data entry mistake?
  4. The average at the bottom of a column shows #VALUE!, but the average formula is written correctly. What do you check?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =SUMM(B2:B5) → #NAME? (unknown function). ="Total: "+B5 → #VALUE!: + expects numbers; to join text, you use &.
  2. D2 becomes =B2/#REF! and shows #REF!. Ctrl+Z immediately to undo the deletion.
  3. #DIV/0!: 5,000 / 0. The data is true (0 meetings); it's the calculation that doesn't make sense yet. We'll learn to display a clean message with IF in module 3.
  4. The error probably comes from a cell in the column that is itself in error: the error spreads. Trace back to the first cell in error with Trace Precedents.

Key takeaways

  • #DIV/0!: division by zero or by an empty cell.
  • #VALUE!: text where a number is needed.
  • #REF!: a target cell has been deleted (Ctrl+Z!).
  • #N/A: a lookup found nothing. #NAME?: a misspelt function name or text without quotation marks.
  • Errors spread: trace back to the first one. And a result without an error isn't necessarily right.

Next module: logic, with the IF function, AND, OR, COUNTIF, SUMIF and IFERROR.

11.html:
Why it matters

Until now, your formulas always calculated the same thing, whatever the situation. But in real life, we often reason with conditions: if the student gets at least 10, they pass; if the sales rep beats their target, they get a bonus; if an expense goes over budget, we want to see it straight away. The IF function lets Excel make a decision for you. It's probably the most used function after SUM.

The structure of IF

IF takes three arguments, separated by commas:

=IF(test, value if true, value if false)

  • The test: a comparison that answers TRUE or FALSE, for example B2>=10.
  • The value if true: what Excel displays when the test is met.
  • The value if false: what Excel displays otherwise.

To write the test, you have six comparison operators:

OperatorMeaningExample
=equal toC2="Yes"
<>not equal toC2<>"Yes"
>strictly greater thanB2>1000
<strictly less thanB2<0
>=greater than or equal toB2>=10
<=less than or equal toB2<=B3

Example: mid-term exam results

A lecturer enters her students' marks in column B. In C2, she writes =IF(B2>=10,"Pass","Fail"), then copies the formula down with the fill handle.

ABC
1StudentMarkResult
2Léa14Pass
3Hugo8Fail
4Inès10Pass
5Tom9.5Fail

Look at Inès: with exactly 10, she passes, because the test is >=. With >10, she would have failed. Choosing between > and >= is one of the most common sources of error: always reread your brief ("at least 10" means >=10).

IF can return a calculation

The values if true and if false don't have to be text. They can be numbers, references or calculations. Example: a company pays a bonus of 5% of sales to reps who reach at least €20,000 in sales, and nothing to the others. In C2: =IF(B2>=20000,B2*5%,0).

ABC
1Sales repSalesBonus
2Nadia€25,000€1,250
3Paul€18,000€0
4Sami€20,000€1,000

Nadia: 25,000 × 5% = €1,250. Paul doesn't reach the threshold: €0. Sami is right on the threshold: 20,000 × 5% = €1,000.

Good practice: put the threshold (20,000) and the rate (5%) in separate cells, for example F1 and F2, and write =IF(B2>=$F$1,B2*$F$2,0). The day the rule changes, you change a single cell. This is where the absolute references from module 2 come back.

The classic traps

  • Forgetting the quotation marks around text: =IF(B2>=10,Pass,Fail) returns #NAME?, because Excel thinks Pass is the name of a function or range. Text always goes between straight quotation marks.
  • Putting quotation marks around a number: "0" is text, not the number zero. It can't be added up properly. Write 0.
  • Comparing text: C2="yes" is also true if the cell contains "Yes" or "YES", because IF isn't case-sensitive. But an extra space after "Yes" makes the test fail.
  • Leaving a cell blank: to display "nothing", use two quotation marks side by side: =IF(B2>=10,"Pass","").

In Google Sheets, IF is written and works in exactly the same way.

Exercise

Here is Camille's monthly budget tracker, with the planned budget in B and actual spending in C.

ABCD
1ItemBudgetActualStatus
2Groceries€300€340
3Going out€150€120
4Transport€60€60
  1. Write a formula in D2 that displays "Over" if actual is greater than budget, and "OK" otherwise. What does it give on the three rows?
  2. Write a formula in E2 that displays the amount of the overspend (actual minus budget) if there is one, and 0 otherwise. What results do you get?
  3. Hugo writes =IF(C2>B2,Over,OK). What result does he get, and why?
  4. A school awards a grant to students whose average is at least 15. Write the formula for an average in B2, displaying "Grant" or nothing at all.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =IF(C2>B2,"Over","OK"). Groceries: 340 > 300, so Over. Going out: 120 is not greater than 150, so OK. Transport: 60 is not strictly greater than 60, so OK.
  2. =IF(C2>B2,C2-B2,0). Groceries: 340 − 300 = €40. Going out: €0. Transport: €0.
  3. He gets #NAME?: without quotation marks, Excel looks for names called Over and OK, which don't exist. He needs to write "Over" and "OK".
  4. =IF(B2>=15,"Grant",""). "At least 15" translates to >=, and "" displays an empty cell.

Key takeaways

  • =IF(test,value if true,value if false): Excel chooses between two results.
  • The test uses =, <>, >, <, >=, <=. "At least" means >=.
  • Text goes in quotation marks, numbers without; "" displays an empty cell.
  • Results can be calculations: =IF(B2>=20000,B2*5%,0).
  • Put thresholds and rates in separate cells, with absolute references.

Next lesson: combining several conditions with AND, OR, NOT, and choosing between more than two results with nested IFs and IFS.

12.titre: AND, OR, NOT and nested IFs / IFS
12.html:
Why it matters

Yesterday, your test only looked at one thing. But real rules often combine several: a candidate is shortlisted for the placement if they have an average of at least 12 and a good level of English; a mark should give one grade out of five, not just "pass" or "fail". Today, you learn to combine conditions and to choose between more than two results.

AND, OR, NOT

These three functions return TRUE or FALSE. You almost always put them inside the test of an IF.

FunctionReturns TRUE when…Example
AND(cond1,cond2,…)all the conditions are trueAND(B2>=12,C2="Yes")
OR(cond1,cond2,…)at least one condition is trueOR(B2>=16,C2="Yes")
NOT(cond)the condition is falseNOT(C2="Yes")

Example: shortlisting candidates for a placement

A company shortlists candidates who have an average of at least 12 and a validated English level. In D2: =IF(AND(B2>=12,C2="Yes"),"Interview","Reject"). In E2, another, more flexible rule: an average of at least 12 or validated English is enough: =IF(OR(B2>=12,C2="Yes"),"Interview","Reject").

ABCD (AND rule)E (OR rule)
1CandidateAverageEnglishANDOR
2Yanis13YesInterviewInterview
3Sarah15NoRejectInterview
4Lucas11YesRejectInterview
5Emma10NoRejectReject

With AND, a single failed condition is enough to reject. With OR, a single condition met is enough to accept. NOT reverses a test: =IF(NOT(C2="Yes"),"English course advised","") picks out Sarah and Emma. Here, C2<>"Yes" would do the same thing, more simply.

More than two results: nested IFs

An IF only chooses between two values. To get more, you put a second IF in place of the first one's value if false, and so on. Example with grade bands:

AverageGrade
16 or moreExcellent
from 14 to under 16Very good
from 12 to under 14Good
from 10 to under 12Pass
under 10Fail

=IF(B2>=16,"Excellent",IF(B2>=14,"Very good",IF(B2>=12,"Good",IF(B2>=10,"Pass","Fail"))))

Excel reads the tests in order and stops at the first one that's true. With 14.5: the >=16 test is false, the >=14 test is true, so "Very good". No need to write AND(B2>=14,B2<16): if you reach the second test, the mark is already below 16.

The order trap: if you start with IF(B2>=10,"Pass",…), every mark from 10 upwards, even 18, stops at the first test. Always arrange your thresholds from largest to smallest (or smallest to largest with <).

Count your brackets carefully: you need one closing bracket per open IF, here four at the end. Excel colours matching pairs of brackets as you type to help you.

More readable: IFS

Since Excel 2019 (and in Excel 365), the IFS function avoids the pile-up of brackets. It takes "test, result" pairs:

=IFS(B2>=16,"Excellent",B2>=14,"Very good",B2>=12,"Good",B2>=10,"Pass",TRUE,"Fail")

  • It also stops at the first true test: order matters just as much.
  • It has no "value if false": if no test is true, it returns #N/A. Hence the final pair TRUE,"Fail", a test that's always true and acts as an "otherwise".
  • It doesn't exist in Excel 2016 and earlier: if you share your file with someone on an old version, stick with nested IFs. Google Sheets offers it too.
ABC
1PupilAverageGrade
2Jade17.2Excellent
3Noé14.5Very good
4Lina12Good
5Adam9.8Fail

Exercise

  1. A shop offers free delivery if the basket is over €50 (strictly) or if the customer is a subscriber ("Yes" in C2). Basket in B2. Write the formula that displays "Free" or "€4.90". What does it give for a €50 basket from a non-subscriber?
  2. A sales rep gets a bonus if their sales (B2) reach at least €20,000 and their customer satisfaction rate (C2) is at least 80%. Write the formula that displays the €500 bonus or 0. What does Paul get, with €24,000 in sales and 75% satisfaction?
  3. Write with nested IFs: under €1,000 in sales, "Low"; from €1,000 to under €5,000, "Medium"; €5,000 and over, "High". Then do the same with IFS.
  4. Ilan writes =IF(B2>=10,"Pass",IF(B2>=12,"Good","Fail")). What does his formula give for 13? Why?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =IF(OR(B2>50,C2="Yes"),"Free","€4.90"). For €50 and not a subscriber: 50 > 50 is false and C2 isn't "Yes", so €4.90.
  2. =IF(AND(B2>=20000,C2>=80%),500,0). Paul meets the first condition but not the second (75% < 80%): he gets €0.
  3. =IF(B2>=5000,"High",IF(B2>=1000,"Medium","Low")). With IFS: =IFS(B2>=5000,"High",B2>=1000,"Medium",TRUE,"Low").
  4. It displays Pass: 13 >= 10 is true, Excel stops at the first test and never looks at the 12 threshold. You need to test the highest threshold first.

Key takeaways

  • AND: all conditions true. OR: at least one. NOT: reverses a test.
  • You put them in the test of an IF: =IF(AND(B2>=12,C2="Yes"),…,…).
  • For more than two results, you nest IFs in the value if false.
  • Excel stops at the first true test: arrange your thresholds from largest to smallest.
  • IFS (Excel 2019 and 365) is more readable; end with TRUE,"…" to avoid #N/A.

Next lesson: counting, adding up and averaging with conditions using COUNTIF, SUMIF and AVERAGEIF.

13.html:
Why it matters

Your manager sends you the month's sales list and asks: "How many sales in the North region? For what amount?" You could add a column of IFs and sum it, but there's a much faster way. The COUNTIF, SUMIF and AVERAGEIF functions do an IF and a calculation in a single formula, across a whole range. They're everyday tools, on placements and in business alike.

The data for this lesson

ABC
1SalespersonRegionAmount
2AliceNorth€1,200
3BrunoSouth€800
4AliceSouth€1,500
5ChloéNorth€600
6BrunoNorth€900

In total: 5 sales worth €5,000.

COUNTIF: counting with a condition

=COUNTIF(range, criteria) counts the cells in the range that meet the criteria.

=COUNTIF(B2:B6,"North") returns 3: Alice, Chloé and Bruno made sales in the North.

SUMIF: adding up with a condition

=SUMIF(criteria range, criteria, sum range)

You test one column and add up another. =SUMIF(B2:B6,"North",C2:C6) looks at the Region column and adds up the amounts on the "North" rows: 1,200 + 600 + 900 = €2,700. Likewise, =SUMIF(A2:A6,"Alice",C2:C6) gives 1,200 + 1,500 = €2,700 for Alice.

If the criteria range and the sum range are the same, you can leave out the third argument: =SUMIF(C2:C6,">=900") adds up the amounts of at least €900: 1,200 + 1,500 + 900 = €3,600.

AVERAGEIF: average with a condition

Same structure as SUMIF: =AVERAGEIF(B2:B6,"North",C2:C6) gives 2,700 / 3 = €900, the average amount of a sale in the North. If no row matches, AVERAGEIF returns #DIV/0! (there's nothing to divide).

Writing the criteria

CriteriaMeaningExample and result
"North"equal to North (not case-sensitive)=COUNTIF(B2:B6,"North"): 3
">1000"strictly more than 1,000=COUNTIF(C2:C6,">1000"): 2
"<>North"not equal to North=COUNTIF(B2:B6,"<>North"): 2
"B*"starts with B (* stands for any characters)=COUNTIF(A2:A6,"B*"): 2
">"&F1more than the value in F1if F1 is 850: =COUNTIF(C2:C6,">"&F1): 3

Remember the writing rules: criteria with an operator go in quotation marks (">1000"). To compare with a cell, you join the operator and the cell with &: ">"&F1. Writing ">F1" would look for the text "F1", which doesn't work. The wildcard ? stands for a single character, * for any number.

Pro tip: rather than typing "North" in the formula, write North in F2 and use =SUMIF($B$2:$B$6,F2,$C$2:$C$6). With South in F3, you just copy down to get a little summary table by region.

FG (count)H (total)
2North3€2,700
3South2€2,300

Check: 2,700 + 2,300 = €5,000, the grand total. This simple check avoids plenty of mistakes.

Exercise

Here are Théo's spending over one week as a student.

AB
1CategoryAmount
2Groceries€45
3Going out€25
4Groceries€18
5Transport€12
6Going out€40
7Groceries€27
  1. Write the formula that counts the number of purchases in the "Groceries" category. Result?
  2. Write the formula for the total spent on groceries, then the one for the average amount of a grocery purchase.
  3. How many purchases are strictly over €20? Write the formula.
  4. Léna writes =SUMIF(B2:B7,">D1") to add up the amounts greater than the value in D1. Why does she get 0? Correct it.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =COUNTIF(A2:A7,"Groceries"): 3.
  2. =SUMIF(A2:A7,"Groceries",B2:B7): 45 + 18 + 27 = €90. =AVERAGEIF(A2:A7,"Groceries",B2:B7): 90 / 3 = €30.
  3. =COUNTIF(B2:B7,">20"): 45, 25, 40 and 27, so 4.
  4. Inside quotation marks, D1 is read as text: Excel looks for amounts "greater than the text D1", and finds none. She needs to write =SUMIF(B2:B7,">"&D1).

Key takeaways

  • COUNTIF(range,criteria) counts, SUMIF(range,criteria,sum_range) adds up, AVERAGEIF averages.
  • You test one column and calculate on another of the same size.
  • Criteria with an operator go in quotation marks: ">1000"; with a cell: ">"&F1.
  • Wildcards: * for several characters, ? for a single one.
  • Always check that your subtotals add back up to the total.

Next lesson: several criteria at once with COUNTIFS and SUMIFS.

14.html:
Why it matters

Yesterday, you could answer "how much on groceries?". But the next question soon arrives: "how much on groceries, in January, paid by card?". To combine several criteria, Excel offers the "S" versions (plural, for several criteria): COUNTIFS, SUMIFS and AVERAGEIFS. They've existed since Excel 2007: you'll find them everywhere.

The data for this lesson

Camille's spending record over two months:

ABCD
1MonthCategoryPaymentAmount
2JanGroceriesCard€85
3JanGoing outCash€40
4JanGroceriesCard€62
5FebGroceriesCash€30
6FebGoing outCard€55
7FebGroceriesCard€70

Total: €342.

COUNTIFS

=COUNTIFS(range1, criteria1, range2, criteria2, …)

A row is only counted if all the criteria are met (it's an AND). =COUNTIFS(B2:B7,"Groceries",C2:C7,"Card") returns 3: rows 2, 4 and 7.

SUMIFS: watch the order

=SUMIFS(sum range, range1, criteria1, range2, criteria2, …)

Here's trap number 1: in SUMIF, the sum range comes at the end; in SUMIFS, it comes at the start. It makes sense (you don't know how many criteria will follow), but people often get it wrong.

  • January groceries: =SUMIFS(D2:D7,A2:A7,"Jan",B2:B7,"Groceries") = 85 + 62 = €147.
  • Groceries paid by card: =SUMIFS(D2:D7,B2:B7,"Groceries",C2:C7,"Card") = 85 + 62 + 70 = €217.
  • With a single criterion, SUMIFS works too: =SUMIFS(D2:D7,B2:B7,"Going out") = 40 + 55 = €95.

AVERAGEIFS follows the same structure as SUMIFS: =AVERAGEIFS(D2:D7,B2:B7,"Groceries",C2:C7,"Card") = 217 / 3 ≈ €72.33.

A range of values

You can use the same range twice to set lower and upper bounds. Spending between €50 and €80 (inclusive):

=SUMIFS(D2:D7,D2:D7,">=50",D2:D7,"<=80") = 62 + 55 + 70 = €187.

This is very useful for dates: "between 1 and 31 March" is written with two criteria on the date column. We'll cover dates in detail in module 4.

What if I want an OR?

The IFS functions can only do ANDs. For "Groceries or Going out", the simplest way is to add two formulas together:

=SUMIF(B2:B7,"Groceries",D2:D7)+SUMIF(B2:B7,"Going out",D2:D7) = 247 + 95 = €342.

Be careful not to count the same row twice: here, an expense can't be both Groceries and Going out, so the addition is correct.

Common mistakes

  • Ranges of different sizes: =SUMIFS(D2:D7,B2:B6,"Groceries") returns #VALUE!. All the ranges must have the same number of rows.
  • Argument order reversed out of SUMIF habit.
  • Hidden spaces: "Groceries" followed by a space isn't equal to "Groceries". If a total looks too low, that's often why.
  • Relative ranges copied: in a summary table, lock the ranges with $ signs.

A summary table

With the categories in F2:F3, the months in G1:H1 and =SUMIFS($D$2:$D$7,$B$2:$B$7,$F2,$A$2:$A$7,G$1) in G2, copied right and down:

FG (Jan)H (Feb)
2Groceries€147€100
3Going out€40€55

Check: 147 + 100 + 40 + 55 = €342. Here are the mixed references from module 2 again: $F2 locks the column, G$1 locks the row.

Exercise

Sales at a small business (A: salesperson, B: product, C: amount), rows 2 to 7: Alice, Software, €2,000; Bruno, Training, €1,200; Alice, Training, €800; Alice, Software, €1,500; Bruno, Software, €3,000; Chloé, Training, €600.

  1. How many Software sales did Alice make? Write the formula.
  2. What is the total amount of Alice's Software sales? Write the formula.
  3. What is the total of sales between €1,000 and €2,000 inclusive?
  4. Malik writes =SUMIFS(A2:A7,"Alice",C2:C7). What will happen? Correct it.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =COUNTIFS(A2:A7,"Alice",B2:B7,"Software"): 2 (rows 2 and 5).
  2. =SUMIFS(C2:C7,A2:A7,"Alice",B2:B7,"Software"): 2,000 + 1,500 = €3,500.
  3. =SUMIFS(C2:C7,C2:C7,">=1000",C2:C7,"<=2000"): 2,000 + 1,200 + 1,500 = €4,700.
  4. He wrote the arguments in SUMIF order. But in SUMIFS, the second argument must be a criteria range: with "Alice" in that position, the formula doesn't work and Excel shows an error message. Correct version: =SUMIFS(C2:C7,A2:A7,"Alice"), which is 2,000 + 800 + 1,500 = €4,300.

Key takeaways

  • COUNTIFS, SUMIFS, AVERAGEIFS: several criteria, all required (AND).
  • In SUMIFS and AVERAGEIFS, the sum range comes first.
  • All the ranges are the same size, otherwise #VALUE!.
  • A range of values: two criteria on the same range (">=50" and "<=80").
  • For an OR, add two SUMIFs together.

Next lesson: IFERROR and robust formulas that don't collapse at the first surprise.

15.html:
Why it matters

A table sent to your manager with #DIV/0! everywhere makes a bad impression, even if your calculations are right. In module 2, you learnt to read and fix these errors. Today, you learn to anticipate them: plan what the formula should display when a piece of data is missing. But be careful: hiding an error isn't fixing it. The whole art is knowing when to do it.

The IFERROR function

=IFERROR(value, value if error)

Excel calculates the first argument. If there's no error, it displays the normal result. If there's an error (#DIV/0!, #VALUE!, #N/A, #REF!, #NAME?…), it displays the fallback value.

Example: target achievement rate

The Lille shop has just opened: its target hasn't been entered yet. In D2, the simple formula =B2/C2 gives an error for Lille. With =IFERROR(B2/C2,"n/a"):

ABCD with B2/C2D with IFERROR
1ShopRevenueTargetRateRate
2Lyon€12,000€10,000120%120%
3Lille€9,000(empty)#DIV/0!n/a
4Nantes€7,500€10,00075%75%

An empty cell counts as 0 in a calculation: 9,000 / 0 is impossible, hence #DIV/0!. With IFERROR, the table stays readable, and "n/a" (not available) explains the situation.

What should the fallback value be?

Fallback valueWhen to use itRisk
"" (empty)Table for presenting, row not filled in yetYou can no longer see that something is missing
"n/a" or a messageClearly flagging missing dataText in a column of numbers
0When the absence really is zeroDistorts averages and can mislead the reader

An example of the risk with 0: if you write =IFERROR(B2/C2,0), Lille displays 0%. The average of the three rates becomes (120 + 0 + 75) / 3 = 65%, whereas the average of the two known rates is (120 + 75) / 2 = 97.5%. With "" or text, AVERAGE ignores the cell and correctly gives 97.5%.

The danger: hiding real errors

IFERROR catches all errors, including those that reveal a real problem. If you write =IFERROR(B2/C22,"") by mistake, or if a column has been deleted (#REF!), IFERROR will quietly display an empty cell, and nobody will see the bug.

The pro rule: build and check your formula without IFERROR first. Add IFERROR only at the end, for an error case you've identified and accept.

More targeted alternatives

  • Test the cause with IF: =IF(C2=0,"n/a",B2/C2). You only handle the "empty or zero target" case. Any other error (a typo in the formula) stays visible. It's often the best choice for divisions.
  • IFNA (Excel 2013 onwards, Excel 365): =IFNA(value,value if #N/A) only reacts to the #N/A error, typical of a lookup that finds nothing. You'll use it in module 5 with the lookup functions.
  • Test for an empty cell: =IF(B2="","",B2*1.2) displays nothing until the row is filled in, which avoids showing 0s on empty rows.

Summary on the same case

Formula (revenue €9,000, target empty)Result
=B3/C3#DIV/0!
=IFERROR(B3/C3,"n/a")n/a
=IF(C3=0,"n/a",B3/C3)n/a
=IFERROR(B3/C3,0)0 (misleading)

With the two formulas that give "n/a", the result is the same here. The difference shows up the day the formula contains another error: the IF version lets you see it, the IFERROR version hides it. IFERROR also exists in Google Sheets under the same name.

Exercise

  1. You calculate the average price per item with =B2/C2 (B: revenue, C: number of items). Some rows have 0 items. Write a version with IFERROR that displays an empty cell, then a version with IF that only handles the "0 items" case.
  2. Three achievement rates: 110%, an error, 90%. What average do you get if the error is replaced with 0? And if it's replaced with ""?
  3. Sofia wrote =IFERROR(SUM(B2:B10)/C1,"") and sees an empty cell. She discovers that column C was deleted by mistake. Which error was hidden, and what's the lesson?
  4. True or false: =IFNA(B2/C2,0) turns a #DIV/0! into 0.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =IFERROR(B2/C2,""). Targeted version: =IF(C2=0,"",B2/C2).
  2. With 0: (110 + 0 + 90) / 3 ≈ 66.7%. With "", AVERAGE ignores the cell: (110 + 90) / 2 = 100%.
  3. A #REF! error: the reference to the deleted column no longer exists. IFERROR hid it. Lesson: check the formula without IFERROR first, and prefer a targeted test when possible.
  4. False: IFNA only handles #N/A. The #DIV/0! is still displayed.

Key takeaways

  • =IFERROR(value,value if error) replaces any error with a fallback value.
  • Choose the fallback value carefully: "" or a message rather than 0, which distorts averages.
  • IFERROR can hide real bugs (#REF!, typos): check without it first.
  • Prefer a targeted test when you know the cause: =IF(C2=0,"n/a",B2/C2).
  • IFNA (Excel 2013 onwards) only handles #N/A.

Next step: the module recap, to tie all these logical functions together.

16.titre: Text functions: LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LEN, UPPER, TRIM
16.html:
Why it matters

A large share of the data you'll receive on a placement isn't numbers but text: customer names, product codes, order references, addresses. And that text rarely arrives clean: random capitals, extra spaces, several pieces of information squashed into one cell. Text functions let you extract and clean this data in seconds, instead of retyping everything by hand.

Extracting part of the text

Let's take order references built like this: country code, hyphen, year, hyphen, number. For example FR-2025-0153, which is 12 characters.

FunctionRoleFormula (A2 = FR-2025-0153)Result
LEFT(text,num)the first num characters=LEFT(A2,2)FR
RIGHT(text,num)the last num characters=RIGHT(A2,4)0153
MID(text,start,num)num characters starting at position start=MID(A2,4,4)2025
LEN(text)the number of characters=LEN(A2)12

For MID, count the positions: F is 1, R is 2, the hyphen is 3, and the year starts at position 4. You take 4 characters: 2025.

Careful: these functions always return text. The result "2025" looks like a number, but it's text (it aligns left). To turn it into a real number, use =VALUE(MID(A2,4,4)): you get the number 2025, which you can compare or add up. For the number 0153, VALUE gives 153 (the leading zero disappears).

A space counts as a character: =LEN("Jean Dupont") returns 11 (4 letters, 1 space, 6 letters). LEN is often used to check an entry, for example that a postcode really has 5 characters.

Finding a position with FIND

When the length varies, you can't count by hand. =FIND(" ",A2) returns the position of the first space. To extract the first name from "Marie Curie": =LEFT(A2,FIND(" ",A2)-1). The space is at position 6, so you take 5 characters: Marie. If the text you're looking for doesn't exist, FIND returns #VALUE!.

Changing the case

FunctionFormulaResult
UPPER=UPPER("dupont")DUPONT
LOWER=LOWER("Paris")paris
PROPER=PROPER("jean DUPONT")Jean Dupont

PROPER puts a capital at the start of each word and the rest in lower case. Handy for tidying up a list of names typed any old how.

Removing extra spaces

TRIM removes spaces at the start and end, and reduces multiple spaces between words to a single one. =TRIM(" Marie Curie ") returns "Marie Curie".

Why does this matter so much? Because one invisible space is enough to make a comparison fail: "North" followed by a space isn't equal to "North", and your SUMIF from module 3 will ignore it without warning.

Example: cleaning a list of interns

In B2: =PROPER(TRIM(A2)). The functions nest: you remove the spaces first, then fix the case. In C2: =LEN(A2), in D2: =LEN(B2).

A (raw entry)B (cleaned)CD
1NameProper nameChars beforeChars after
2"  léa MARTIN"Léa Martin1210
3"hugo  petit"Hugo Petit1110

Row 2: the entry has two spaces at the start, making 12 characters; 10 remain. Row 3: two spaces between the words, 11 characters; 10 remain. Comparing LEN before and after is a good way to spot hidden spaces.

These functions exist with the same names in Google Sheets.

Exercise

  1. A2 contains the product code CHA-BLEU-XL. Write the formulas to get "CHA", "XL" and "BLEU". What does =LEN(A2) return?
  2. A3 contains "  sophie BERNARD " (two spaces before, one after). Write a formula that returns "Sophie Bernard". How many characters before and after?
  3. A4 contains the French postcode 75011 entered as text. Write the formula that extracts the département number (the first two digits) as a number.
  4. A5 contains "Durand Paul". Write the formula that extracts the surname using FIND.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =LEFT(A2,3): CHA. =RIGHT(A2,2): XL. =MID(A2,5,4): BLEU (C, H, A, hyphen, then B at position 5). =LEN(A2): 11.
  2. =PROPER(TRIM(A3)). Before: 2 + 6 + 1 + 7 + 1 = 17 characters. After: "Sophie Bernard", 14 characters.
  3. =VALUE(LEFT(A4,2)) returns the number 75.
  4. =LEFT(A5,FIND(" ",A5)-1): the space is at position 7, you take 6 characters, Durand.

Key takeaways

  • LEFT, RIGHT, MID extract; LEN counts characters (spaces included).
  • The result is text: VALUE turns it into a number.
  • FIND gives the position of a character when the length varies.
  • UPPER, LOWER, PROPER standardise the case.
  • TRIM removes extra spaces, a frequent cause of failed comparisons.

Next lesson: joining and splitting text with CONCAT, &, TEXTJOIN, the Text to Columns tool and Flash Fill.

17.titre: Joining and splitting: CONCAT, &, TEXTJOIN, Text to Columns, Flash Fill
17.html:
Why it matters

Yesterday, you extracted pieces of text. Today, we do the opposite and go faster: joining several cells into one (creating email addresses, labels, IDs) and splitting one column into several (separating first name and surname). You'll also see two formula-free tools that save a huge amount of time.

Joining with &

The & symbol sticks pieces of text end to end. With the first name in A2 (Léa) and the surname in B2 (Martin):

  • =A2&B2 gives "LéaMartin": nothing is added between the two.
  • =A2&" "&B2 gives "Léa Martin": the space in quotation marks is text like any other.
  • =UPPER(B2)&", "&A2 gives "MARTIN, Léa".

Example: creating the interns' email addresses

In C2: =LOWER(A2&"."&B2)&"@company.com"

ABC
1First nameSurnameEmail
2LéaMartinléa.martin@company.com
3HugoPetithugo.petit@company.com

Notice the accent in "léa": Excel doesn't remove it. In a real file, you'd need to replace it (with Find and Replace, for example), because accents cause problems in email addresses.

CONCAT: the function version

=CONCAT(A2," ",B2) gives the same result as =A2&" "&B2. Its advantage: it accepts a range, =CONCAT(A2:C2) joins the three cells. CONCAT has existed since Excel 2019 and is in Excel 365. In older versions, you'll find CONCATENATE, which does the same thing but doesn't accept ranges.

TEXTJOIN: joining with a separator

=TEXTJOIN(delimiter, ignore_empty, text1, text2, …)

With Excel, Word and PowerPoint in A2:A4: =TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,A2:A4) gives "Excel, Word, PowerPoint". The delimiter is added automatically between each item, never at the end. With TRUE, empty cells are ignored (no ", ,"). Available since Excel 2019 and in Excel 365, as well as in Google Sheets.

Numbers and dates in text: the TEXT function

If B2 contains 1250.5 formatted as "€1,250.50", the formula ="Total: "&B2 displays "Total: 1250.5". The formatting is lost, because & uses the raw value. The fix: ="Total: "&TEXT(B2,"€#,##0.00") displays "Total: €1,250.50". For a date: TEXT(C2,"dd/mm/yyyy").

Splitting with the Text to Columns tool

You receive a "Full name" column to split in two. Without a formula:

  1. Select the column to split (and check the columns to the right are empty, otherwise they'll be overwritten).
  2. Data tab, Text to Columns button.
  3. Choose Delimited, then the delimiter (space, semicolon, comma, tab or other).
  4. Choose the format of each column and click Finish.

It's the ideal tool for a CSV file where everything has landed in a single column. Careful: the result is fixed, it doesn't update if the data changes. In Excel 365, the TEXTSPLIT function does the same split with a formula, for example =TEXTSPLIT(A2," "); it doesn't exist in the 2019 and 2021 versions.

Flash Fill

This is the most impressive tool in the lesson. You type one or two examples of the result you want next to your data, and Excel works out the rule.

AB (you type)B after Ctrl+E
2Martin LéaLéaLéa
3Petit HugoHugo
4Durand PaulPaul

Type "Léa" in B2, move to B3 and press Ctrl+E (or Data tab, Flash Fill). It has existed since Excel 2013.

  • Advantage: no formula to write, and it works for extracting, swapping, reformatting (a phone number, initials…).
  • Limits: the result is fixed (no automatic update), and Excel can guess wrongly on irregular cases (a double-barrelled name, a middle name). Always check a few rows, especially the most unusual ones.

On a Mac, the shortcut is Cmd+E in recent versions; the button stays on the Data tab.

Exercise

  1. A2 contains "Nantes", B2 contains "44000". Write a formula with & that displays "44000 Nantes".
  2. A2:A5 contains Monday, (empty), Wednesday, Thursday. What does =TEXTJOIN(" / ",TRUE,A2:A5) give? And with FALSE?
  3. B2 contains 0.125 displayed as "12.5%". What does ="Rate: "&B2 give? How do you get "Rate: 12.5%"?
  4. Your colleague has 2,000 "First name Surname" rows to split, just once, for a mailing. Which tool do you recommend, and what precaution?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =B2&" "&A2: 44000 Nantes.
  2. With TRUE: Monday / Wednesday / Thursday. With FALSE, the empty cell keeps its place: Monday / / Wednesday / Thursday.
  3. It displays Rate: 0.125, because & takes the raw value. The fix: ="Rate: "&TEXT(B2,"0.0%").
  4. For a one-off need, Text to Columns (space delimiter) or Flash Fill. Precaution: check double-barrelled names or double first names, which may be split wrongly, and make sure the destination columns are empty.

Key takeaways

  • & joins text: =A2&" "&B2. Don't forget the space.
  • CONCAT (Excel 2019 and 365) accepts ranges; TEXTJOIN adds a delimiter and can ignore blanks.
  • TEXT(value,"format") keeps the formatting of a number or date inside text.
  • Text to Columns (Data tab) splits a column by a delimiter.
  • Ctrl+E: Flash Fill. Quick, but fixed: check the unusual cases.

Next lesson: how Excel stores dates, and the TODAY, DATE, YEAR, MONTH and DAY functions.

18.titre: Dates: how Excel stores them, TODAY, DATE, YEAR, MONTH, DAY
18.html:
Why it matters

Invoice due dates, the length of a placement, an employee's length of service, sales by month: dates are everywhere. And they cause a lot of confusion in Excel. The good news is that a single principle explains almost everything: to Excel, a date is a number. Once you've understood that, date calculations become simple additions and subtractions.

A date is a day number

Excel counts days from 1 January 1900, which is number 1. Each following day adds 1. This number is called the serial number. What you see (15/09/2025) is just a display format laid over this number.

Date displayedNumber stored
01/01/19001
01/01/202545658
15/09/202545915

Try it: type a date, then set the cell to General format (Home, Number group). You see the number. Switch back to Short Date and the date returns. Nothing changed in the cell, only its appearance. Times are fractions of a day: midday is 0.5.

What this lets you do

  • Add days: if A2 contains 15/09/2025, =A2+30 gives 15/10/2025.
  • Count days: =B2-A2 gives the number of days between two dates. From 15/09/2025 to 15/10/2025: 30 days.
  • Compare: =IF(A2<B2,"Late","OK") works, because you're comparing two numbers.

The classic trap: you subtract two dates and the result is displayed as a strange date (for example 30/01/1900). It's just the format: set the cell back to General and you'll see 30. Conversely, a date that aligns left is often text, not a real date: it can't be used in calculations.

TODAY: today's date

=TODAY() returns today's date, with no argument (the empty brackets are required). It updates every time the file is recalculated or reopened. Ideal for calculating a number of days remaining: =B2-TODAY(). Its cousin =NOW() returns the date and time.

If, on the contrary, you want to freeze today's date (to record when a row was entered), use the shortcut Ctrl+; (Ctrl and semicolon): it types the date as a value, which won't change again.

DATE: building a date

=DATE(year, month, day)

=DATE(2025,9,15) returns 15/09/2025. It's the safest way to write a date in a formula, because it doesn't depend on the country's format (is 09/10 the 9th of October or the 10th of September?). DATE also handles overflows: =DATE(2025,13,1) gives 01/01/2026.

YEAR, MONTH, DAY: breaking a date down

These three functions extract part of the date, as a number.

ABCDE
1Sale date=YEAR(A2)=MONTH(A2)=DAY(A2)=WEEKDAY(A2,2)
215/09/202520259151
301/01/20252025113

WEEKDAY(date,2) gives the day of the week, from 1 (Monday) to 7 (Sunday). 15/09/2025 is a Monday (1), 01/01/2025 a Wednesday (3).

A practical use: with a MONTH column next to your sales, you can use SUMIF (module 3) to total September's sales. Another tip: =DATE(YEAR(A2),MONTH(A2),1) returns the first day of the month of the date in A2.

Google Sheets works on the same principle (a date is a number) and uses the same function names.

Exercise

  1. A2 contains 15/09/2025. What does =A2+45 give?
  2. A placement runs from 01/09/2025 to 28/02/2026. Which formula gives the number of days between the two dates? What result?
  3. You want to record in a column the date each invoice was received, without it changing afterwards. Do you use TODAY() or Ctrl+;? Why?
  4. A2 contains 15/09/2025. Write the formula that returns 15/09/2026, using DATE, YEAR, MONTH and DAY.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 45915 + 45 = 45960, which is 30/10/2025 (15 days left in September, 30 in October).
  2. =B2-A2: 180 days. If a date is displayed, set the cell back to General format.
  3. Ctrl+;: it types a fixed value. TODAY() would change every day, and all your invoices would show today's date.
  4. =DATE(YEAR(A2)+1,MONTH(A2),DAY(A2)) returns 15/09/2026.

Key takeaways

  • A date is a number of days since 01/01/1900; what you see is just a format.
  • You add days with +, you count days with -.
  • TODAY() updates; Ctrl+; freezes the date.
  • DATE(year,month,day) builds a date safely.
  • YEAR, MONTH, DAY, WEEKDAY break a date down. A date aligned left is often text.

Next lesson: advanced date calculations with DATEDIF, NETWORKDAYS, WORKDAY and EOMONTH.

19.titre: Date calculations: DATEDIF, NETWORKDAYS, WORKDAY, EOMONTH
19.html:
Why it matters

Subtracting two dates gives a number of days. But in business, the questions are more precise: how many complete months of service?
