How many working days in the placement, excluding weekends and bank holidays? What's the due date of an invoice payable "30 days end of month"? Four functions answer these questions.

DATEDIF: the gap in years, months or days

=DATEDIF(start date, end date, "unit")

UnitReturns
"y"the number of complete years
"m"the number of complete months
"d"the number of days

A quirk: DATEDIF is a "hidden" function. It works, but Excel doesn't suggest it in AutoComplete and doesn't show help on its arguments. Type it out in full. The start date must be before the end date, otherwise it returns #NUM!.

Example: a placement and an age

A (start)B (end)FormulaResult
201/09/202528/02/2026=DATEDIF(A2,B2,"m")5
301/09/202528/02/2026=DATEDIF(A3,B3,"d")180
414/05/200301/09/2025=DATEDIF(A4,B4,"y")22

The placement lasts 5 complete months (the sixth isn't finished on 28/02). The intern born on 14/05/2003 is 22 on 01/09/2025. For age as of today: =DATEDIF(A4,TODAY(),"y").

NETWORKDAYS: counting working days

=NETWORKDAYS(start date, end date, [holidays])

It counts the days from Monday to Friday between two dates, both dates included. The third argument, optional, is a range containing the bank holidays to exclude.

For the placement from 01/09/2025 to 28/02/2026, without bank holidays: =NETWORKDAYS(A2,B2) returns 130. With the French bank holidays in the period in E2:E5 (01/11/2025, 11/11/2025, 25/12/2025, 01/01/2026): =NETWORKDAYS(A2,B2,E2:E5) returns 127. Why only 3 fewer? Because 01/11/2025 falls on a Saturday: it wasn't being counted anyway.

Excel doesn't know any country's bank holidays: it's up to you to list them. If your company doesn't work the same days (for example Tuesday to Saturday), there's a variant, NETWORKDAYS.INTL, which lets you choose the weekend days.

WORKDAY: moving forward n working days

=WORKDAY(start date, days, [holidays])

It's the reverse: from a date, it moves forward a number of working days and returns the resulting date. The start date isn't counted. Example: an order placed on Friday 19/12/2025, delivered in 10 working days. =WORKDAY(A2,10,E2:E5) returns 06/01/2026, skipping the weekends, 25/12 and 01/01. If the result is displayed as a number, apply the Date format.

EOMONTH: the last day of a month

=EOMONTH(date, months)

  • =EOMONTH(A2,0): last day of the month of A2. For 15/09/2025: 30/09/2025.
  • =EOMONTH(A2,1): last day of the following month: 31/10/2025.
  • =EOMONTH(A2,-1): last day of the previous month: 31/08/2025. Add 1 and you get the first day of the month of A2.

Example: "30 days end of month" due date

A common way to read this payment term: add 30 days to the invoice date, then go to the end of that month. In C2: =EOMONTH(A2+30,0).

A (invoice date)A2+30C (due date)
215/09/202515/10/202531/10/2025
320/01/202619/02/202628/02/2026

Always check the exact rule written in the terms and conditions of sale: there are several ways to calculate these due dates. A related function, EDATE(date,n), moves forward n months keeping the same day.

Exercise

  1. An employee joined on 01/03/2020. Which formula gives their length of service in complete years as at 01/09/2025? What result?
  2. How many working days in November 2025, excluding 11/11 (01/11 is a Saturday)? Write the formula, with the bank holidays in E2:E5.
  3. An invoice is dated 10/12/2025. What is its "30 days end of month" due date, using the method from the lesson?
  4. Nora writes =DATEDIF(B2,A2,"m") with A2 = start and B2 = end. What does she get?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =DATEDIF(A2,B2,"y"): from 01/03/2020 to 01/09/2025, 5 years complete (the sixth anniversary falls on 01/03/2026).
  2. =NETWORKDAYS(DATE(2025,11,1),DATE(2025,11,30),E2:E5). November 2025 has 20 days from Monday to Friday; minus 11/11 (a Tuesday): 19 working days.
  3. 10/12/2025 + 30 days = 09/01/2026, then end of month: 31/01/2026. Formula: =EOMONTH(A2+30,0).
  4. The dates are the wrong way round: the start date is after the end date, so DATEDIF returns #NUM!.

Key takeaways

  • DATEDIF(start,end,"y"/"m"/"d"): years, complete months or days. A hidden function, to type out in full.
  • NETWORKDAYS counts the days from Monday to Friday, both ends included, minus the holidays you supply.
  • WORKDAY moves forward n working days (start date not counted).
  • EOMONTH(date,n) returns the last day of the month, shifted by n months.
  • Excel doesn't know bank holidays: list them in a separate range.

Next lesson: cleaning an imported file, duplicates, spaces and formats.

20.titre: Cleaning an imported file: duplicates, spaces, formats
20.html:
Why it matters

First day of your placement. Your supervisor sends you an export from the company's management software, which is set up in French: "Can you do me the total per customer?" You run a SUMIF… and the total is wrong. Some customers appear twice, some amounts refuse to add up, some names have hidden spaces. That's the reality of imported files. Analysts often say it: cleaning data takes longer than analysing it. This lesson brings the whole module together to give you a method.

The starting file

A (Customer)B (Amount)C (Date)
2"Dupont SA"1250,50 (text)15/09/2025
3"dupont sa "8002025-09-16 (text)
4"Martin SARL"1.200,00 (text)17/09/2025
5"Dupont SA"1250,50 (text)15/09/2025

Four problems: an extra space and different case in A3, amounts stored as text (in the French format, with a decimal comma), a date in text format, and a duplicate row (row 5 is identical to row 2).

Step 1: work on a copy

Never touch the original file. Duplicate the sheet (right-click the tab, Move or Copy, tick Create a copy). Cleaning formulas go in columns alongside; once checked, you can turn them into values (copy, then Paste Special, Values).

Step 2: spaces and case

=PROPER(TRIM(A2)), seen in lesson 16, turns "dupont sa" followed by a space into "Dupont Sa". Note: PROPER gives "Sa", not "SA". For abbreviations, UPPER is sometimes a better fit. What matters is that all the rows for the same customer become identical.

The non-breaking space: some exports (copied from a web page, for example) contain a special space, character no. 160, which TRIM doesn't remove. If LEN shows you one character too many despite TRIM, try =TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(A2,CHAR(160)," ")): SUBSTITUTE replaces each non-breaking space with a normal space, which TRIM can then deal with.

Step 3: numbers stored as text

Symptoms: the number is aligned left, a small green triangle appears in the corner of the cell, and SUM ignores it (it returns 0 or a total that's too low). Three solutions:

  1. The green triangle: select the cells, click the warning diamond, then Convert to Number.
  2. VALUE: =VALUE(B2) turns text such as "1250.50" into the number 1,250.50.
  3. Find and Replace (Ctrl+H) or NUMBERVALUE for separators: a French export writes 1250,50 or 1.200,00. With UK English Excel, you need decimal points.

For "1250,50" (decimal comma): =VALUE(SUBSTITUTE(B2,",",".")). SUBSTITUTE replaces the comma with a point, leaving "1250.50", which VALUE converts to 1,250.50. For "1.200,00" (point as the thousands separator), the cleanest option is =NUMBERVALUE(B4,",","."): you tell Excel that the decimal separator is the comma and the group separator is the point, and it returns 1,200.

Step 4: dates as text

"2025-09-16" aligned left is text. Depending on the case, =DATEVALUE(C3) or =VALUE(C3) turns it into a real date (a serial number, to be formatted as a Date). If the format is too unusual, rebuild the date with the text functions and DATE: =DATE(LEFT(C3,4),MID(C3,6,2),RIGHT(C3,2)) gives 16/09/2025. The Text to Columns tool (lesson 17) also lets you specify, at its last step, that a column is a date in YMD format (year, month, day).

Step 5: duplicates

First spot them, to understand. In D2: =COUNTIF(A$2:A2,A2), copied down. The range grows with each row (only the start is locked): the formula counts how many times the customer has appeared so far. A result greater than 1 flags a repeat. Careful, the same customer can have several legitimate orders: a true duplicate is a row that is entirely identical (same customer, same amount, same date).

Then remove them: select the table, Data tab, Remove Duplicates, then tick the columns that must be identical for a row to count as a duplicate. Here, tick all three columns. Excel tells you how many rows were removed. This removal is permanent in the sheet (hence step 1).

The result

A (Customer)B (Amount)C (Date)
2Dupont SA1,250.5015/09/2025
3Dupont SA800.0016/09/2025
4Martin SARL1,200.0017/09/2025

Now, =SUMIF(A2:A4,"Dupont SA",B2:B4) returns 1,250.50 + 800 = €2,050.50. On the raw file, the same formula would have given 0: Dupont SA's amounts were text (ignored by the sum), and the €800 row was written "dupont sa" with a space, so it wasn't recognised. The grand total is €3,250.50.

Exercise

  1. A column of amounts shows values aligned left with a green triangle, and =SUM(B2:B50) returns 0. What's the problem? Give two ways to fix it.
  2. A2 contains "2.450,75" (text, French format with a point as the thousands separator). Write the formula that gives the number 2,450.75.
  3. After TRIM, LEN still shows one character too many. What's the likely cause and which formula should you try?
  4. Your list contains two rows "Martin SARL, 500, 02/10/2025" and one row "Martin SARL, 300, 05/10/2025". In Remove Duplicates, what happens if you only tick the Customer column? What should you tick?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. The amounts are stored as text. Solutions: the warning diamond then Convert to Number, or a column with =VALUE(B2).
  2. =NUMBERVALUE(A2,",","."): the comma is declared as the decimal separator and the point as the thousands separator, giving 2,450.75. (Alternative: =VALUE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(A2,".",""),",",".")).)
  3. Probably a non-breaking space (character 160). Try =TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(A2,CHAR(160)," ")).
  4. With only the Customer column, Excel keeps a single Martin SARL row and removes the other two, including the legitimate €300 order. You need to tick all three columns: only the truly repeated row (€500 on 02/10) is removed, leaving two rows totalling €800.

Key takeaways

  • Always work on a copy, with cleaning columns alongside.
  • Spaces and case: TRIM, PROPER/UPPER, and SUBSTITUTE(…,CHAR(160)," ") for the non-breaking space.
  • Numbers as text: aligned left, green triangle; VALUE, Convert to Number, SUBSTITUTE or NUMBERVALUE for separators.
  • Dates as text: DATEVALUE, or rebuild with DATE and the text functions.
  • Duplicates: spot them with COUNTIF, then Data, Remove Duplicates, ticking the right columns.

Next step: the module recap, to tie together text, dates and cleaning.

21.html:
Why it matters

In a real file, information is rarely all in one place. A product's price is in a catalogue, a customer's name in another sheet, the commission rate in a scale. Copying this data across by hand is slow and the best way to make mistakes. Lookup functions fetch the right information for you.

VLOOKUP is the oldest and best known. You'll come across it in almost every business file, even though there are better options today. So you need to be able to read it and write it, and know its traps.

The principle

VLOOKUP (the V stands for "vertical") looks for a value in the first column of a table, then returns the value on the same row, in the column of your choice.

=VLOOKUP(lookup_value,table_array,col_index_num,FALSE)

  • lookup_value: what you're looking for (a reference, a name...).
  • table_array: the range to search. The lookup value must be in its first column.
  • col_index_num: the column to return, counted from the left of the table (1 = first column).
  • FALSE: exact match. It's what you want in 95% of cases.

Example: your placement's catalogue

You're on a placement in a small computer shop. The catalogue is in A1:C5:

ABC
1RefProductPrice
2P01Keyboard€25
3P02Mouse€15
4P03Monitor€180
5P04Headset€60

In F2, you type the reference P03. To get its price:

FormulaWhat it doesResult
=VLOOKUP(F2,A2:C5,3,FALSE)Looks for P03 in column A, returns the 3rd column€180
=VLOOKUP(F2,A2:C5,2,FALSE)Same row, 2nd columnMonitor
=VLOOKUP("P09",A2:C5,3,FALSE)P09 doesn't exist#N/A

If you copy the formula down, remember to lock the table with $ signs (lesson 8): =VLOOKUP(F2,$A$2:$C$5,3,FALSE). Otherwise the range slides and the lookup ends up missing rows.

Approximate match: the case of rate scales

With TRUE as the last argument, VLOOKUP no longer looks for the exact value: it takes the largest value less than or equal to the one you're looking for. That's perfect for a banded scale, on one condition: the first column must be sorted in ascending order.

HI
1Revenue fromCommission
2€00%
3€1,0003%
4€5,0005%
5€10,0008%

A sales rep brings in €6,200 of revenue: =VLOOKUP(6200,$H$2:$I$5,2,TRUE) returns 5%, because 5,000 is the largest threshold less than or equal to 6,200. Their commission: 6,200 × 5% = €310.

The four traps of VLOOKUP

  1. Forgetting the last argument. If it's left out, Excel assumes TRUE (approximate match). On an unsorted list, you then get a wrong result with no error message at all. Always write FALSE (or 0) when you want an exact value.
  2. It only looks to the right. The lookup value must be in the first column. You can't find the reference (column A) from the product name (column B).
  3. The column number is hard-coded. If someone inserts a column in the middle of the table, the 3 now points to a different column and the formula returns the wrong information, again with no error.
  4. It returns the first match. If a reference appears twice, you'll only get the first row.

That's why Microsoft created XLOOKUP (next lesson). VLOOKUP is still worth knowing though: it works in every version of Excel, and thousands of files use it. In Google Sheets it has the same name, VLOOKUP. There's also HLOOKUP (H for horizontal), which searches the first row instead of the first column.

Exercise

  1. Using the catalogue above, write the formula that returns the name of the product whose reference is in F2. What does it give if F2 contains P01?
  2. What does =VLOOKUP(14000,$H$2:$I$5,2,TRUE) return? And =VLOOKUP(800,$H$2:$I$5,2,TRUE)?
  3. Your placement supervisor has a grade scale in K2:L6: 0 "Insufficient", 10 "Pass", 12 "Good", 14 "Very good", 16 "Excellent". Write the formula that gives the grade for a mark in M2. Which grade for 13.5?
  4. A colleague inserts a "Category" column between A and B in the catalogue. What happens to =VLOOKUP(F2,A2:D5,3,FALSE)?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =VLOOKUP(F2,$A$2:$C$5,2,FALSE). With P01, it returns Keyboard.
  2. 14,000: the largest threshold less than or equal is 10,000, so 8%. 800: the only threshold less than or equal is 0, so 0%.
  3. =VLOOKUP(M2,$K$2:$L$6,2,TRUE). For 13.5, the largest threshold less than or equal is 12: Good. It works because the thresholds are sorted in ascending order.
  4. The 3rd column is now "Product" (A = Ref, B = Category, C = Product, D = Price). So the formula returns the product name instead of the price, with no error message. You'd need to change the 3 to a 4: that's exactly the hard-coded column number trap.

Key takeaways

  • =VLOOKUP(value,table,col_num,FALSE) searches the first column and returns the requested column.
  • Always put FALSE for an exact lookup. TRUE is for rate scales, sorted in ascending order.
  • Lock the table with $ signs before copying.
  • Its limits: it only looks to the right, its column number breaks if a column is inserted, and it returns #N/A if nothing is found.

Next lesson: XLOOKUP, the modern version that fixes all these shortcomings.

22.html:
Why it matters

Yesterday, you saw that VLOOKUP has some annoying flaws: it only looks to the right, it breaks if a column is inserted, and its default mode is dangerous. XLOOKUP sorts all that out in one go. If your version of Excel offers it, it's the one you'll use day to day.

Availability: XLOOKUP exists in Excel 365, Excel 2021 and later versions, as well as Excel for the web. It does not exist in Excel 2019 or earlier: if you send your file to someone on an old version, they'll see an error. Google Sheets offers it under the same name, XLOOKUP.

The syntax

=XLOOKUP(lookup_value,lookup_array,return_array)

The big difference: instead of a table and a number, you give two separate columns. One to search, one for the result. No more counting column numbers, no more compulsory "first column".

Example: the same catalogue

ABC
1RefProductPrice
2P01Keyboard€25
3P02Mouse€15
4P03Monitor€180
5P04Headset€60
FormulaWhat it doesResult
=XLOOKUP("P03",A2:A5,C2:C5)Looks for P03 in column A, returns column C€180
=XLOOKUP("Headset",B2:B5,A2:A5)Searches in B, returns column A, to the leftP04
=XLOOKUP("P09",A2:A5,C2:C5,"Unknown")P09 doesn't existUnknown

The second row is impossible with VLOOKUP: XLOOKUP looks to the left with no problem. And if a column is inserted, the ranges A2:A5 and C2:C5 shift by themselves: the formula keeps returning the price.

The optional arguments

The full syntax has six arguments, but only the first three are required:

=XLOOKUP(lookup_value,lookup_array,return_array,[if_not_found],[match_mode],[search_mode])

ArgumentValuesEffect
if_not_founda text or a valueReplaces the #N/A with whatever you want
match_mode0 (default)Exact match
-1Exact, otherwise the next smaller value
1Exact, otherwise the next larger value
2Wildcards (* and ?)
search_mode1 (default)First to last
-1Last to first

Good news: by default, XLOOKUP does an exact search. VLOOKUP's forgotten-last-argument trap disappears.

The commission scale, XLOOKUP version

With the scale from the previous lesson (thresholds €0, €1,000, €5,000, €10,000 in H2:H5, rates 0%, 3%, 5%, 8% in I2:I5):

=XLOOKUP(6200,H2:H5,I2:I5,"Off scale",-1) returns 5%. Mode -1 takes the exact value or, failing that, the next smaller value: 5,000.

Finding the last occurrence

Here's the shop's sales log, from oldest to most recent:

ABC
1DateCustomerAmount
203/03Durand€360
305/03Martin€125
409/03Durand€60
512/03Petit€60

=XLOOKUP("Durand",B2:B5,C2:C5) returns €360 (first sale found). =XLOOKUP("Durand",B2:B5,C2:C5,,1,-1) searches from the bottom up and returns €60, his last sale. The two commas in a row leave the if_not_found argument empty.

Returning several columns at once

If the return array is a range of several columns, XLOOKUP returns the whole row. In the catalogue, =XLOOKUP("P03",A2:A5,B2:C5) writes Monitor in the formula's cell and €180 in the cell to its right. This result that "overflows" onto several cells is a spill: we'll come back to it in lesson 25.

Exercise

  1. Using the catalogue, write the formula that gives the price of the product "Mouse". Result?
  2. Write the formula that returns the reference of the product named in G2, with "Not in catalogue" if the name doesn't exist. What does it give if G2 contains "Tablet"?
  3. A sales rep brings in €999 of revenue. What does =XLOOKUP(999,H2:H5,I2:I5,"Off scale",-1) return? And with mode 1 instead of -1?
  4. In the sales log, what is Martin's last sale, and which formula gets it?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =XLOOKUP("Mouse",B2:B5,C2:C5) returns €15.
  2. =XLOOKUP(G2,B2:B5,A2:A5,"Not in catalogue"). With "Tablet", it displays Not in catalogue instead of #N/A.
  3. Mode -1: 999 doesn't exist, the next smaller value is 0, so 0%. Mode 1: the next larger value is 1,000, so 3%, which would be wrong for a "from" scale. Mode -1 is the right one here.
  4. =XLOOKUP("Martin",B2:B5,C2:C5,,1,-1) returns €125. Martin has only one sale, so the first and the last are the same.

Key takeaways

  • =XLOOKUP(value,lookup_array,return_array): two separate columns, no number.
  • It searches exactly by default, looks left as well as right, and copes with inserted columns.
  • The 4th argument replaces the #N/A with a clear message.
  • Match mode -1 for a scale, search mode -1 for the last occurrence.
  • Available in Excel 365 and Excel 2021 or later, not in Excel 2019.

Next lesson: INDEX + MATCH, the pair that works in every version and allows two-way lookups.

23.html:
Why it matters

Before XLOOKUP, advanced users had already got round VLOOKUP's flaws by combining two functions: INDEX and MATCH. This pair works in every version of Excel and in Google Sheets. You'll see it in lots of financial models. And it can do something very handy: look up both a row and a column in a two-way table.

INDEX: "give me cell number..."

INDEX returns the contents of a cell based on its position in a range.

=INDEX(array,row_num,[column_num])

ABC
1RefProductPrice
2P01Keyboard€25
3P02Mouse€15
4P03Monitor€180
5P04Headset€60
FormulaWhat it doesResult
=INDEX(B2:B5,3)3rd cell of B2:B5Monitor
=INDEX(A2:C5,4,3)4th row, 3rd column of A2:C5€60

MATCH: "what position is... in?"

MATCH does the reverse: it looks for a value and returns its position in a range.

=MATCH(lookup_value,lookup_array,0)

The final 0 asks for an exact match. As with VLOOKUP, don't forget it: by default, MATCH does an approximate search (type 1).

FormulaResult
=MATCH("P03",A2:A5,0)3
=MATCH("Headset",B2:B5,0)4
=MATCH("P09",A2:A5,0)#N/A

The pair: INDEX(MATCH)

The idea: MATCH finds the row, INDEX fetches the value on that row, in the column you want.

=INDEX(return_column,MATCH(value,lookup_column,0))

For the price of the reference in F2 (P03): =INDEX(C2:C5,MATCH(F2,A2:A5,0)).

  1. MATCH(F2,A2:A5,0) finds P03 in 3rd position.
  2. INDEX(C2:C5,3) returns the 3rd value of C2:C5: €180.

You'll recognise XLOOKUP's logic: one column to search, one column for the result. So it can look to the left (=INDEX(A2:A5,MATCH("Headset",B2:B5,0)) returns P04) and it copes with inserted columns.

The two-way lookup

This is where INDEX + MATCH shines. Here are the monthly sales of three sales reps, in A1:D4:

ABCD
1JanFebMar
2Alice€1,200€1,500€1,100
3Bruno€900€1,300€1,600
4Chloé€1,400€1,000€1,250

You want Bruno's sales in March. One MATCH for the row, another for the column:

=INDEX(B2:D4,MATCH("Bruno",A2:A4,0),MATCH("Mar",B1:D1,0))

  1. MATCH("Bruno",A2:A4,0) = 2 (2nd row).
  2. MATCH("Mar",B1:D1,0) = 3 (3rd column).
  3. INDEX(B2:D4,2,3) = €1,600.

In practice, you put the name and the month in two cells (for example G1 and G2): you just change them and the result follows. It's the basis of many dashboards.

So which one should you choose?

FunctionStrengthsLimits
VLOOKUPKnown by everyone, all versionsOnly looks right, fragile column number
XLOOKUPSimple, exact by default, message if not foundExcel 365 and 2021 or later only
INDEX + MATCHAll versions, two-way, robustLonger to write and to read back

If your colleagues all have Excel 365, XLOOKUP is enough for most lookups. If the file has to circulate on older versions, INDEX + MATCH is the safe choice. Note: Excel 365 also offers XMATCH, a modernised version of MATCH, exact by default.

Exercise

  1. What does =INDEX(A2:C5,2,2) return in the catalogue?
  2. Using INDEX + MATCH, write the formula that returns the name of the product whose price is €60. Result?
  3. In the sales reps' table, write the formula that gives Chloé's sales in February. Result?
  4. Your colleague wrote =MATCH("Bruno",A2:A4) without the 0. Why is that risky?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 2nd row (P02), 2nd column: Mouse.
  2. =INDEX(B2:B5,MATCH(60,C2:C5,0)). MATCH finds 60 in 4th position, INDEX returns Headset.
  3. =INDEX(B2:D4,MATCH("Chloé",A2:A4,0),MATCH("Feb",B1:D1,0)): row 3, column 2, which is €1,000.
  4. Without the 0, MATCH does an approximate search that assumes a list sorted in ascending order. Here the names happen to be sorted, so it works by luck. But if "Adam" is added at the bottom of the list, the result can become wrong with no visible error. Always include the 0.

Key takeaways

  • INDEX(array,row,column) returns a value from its position.
  • MATCH(value,array,0) returns the position of a value. The 0 is essential.
  • =INDEX(return_column,MATCH(value,lookup_column,0)) replaces VLOOKUP, and looks to the left.
  • With two MATCHes, you do a two-way lookup (row and column).
  • The pair works in every version of Excel.

Next lesson: structured tables (Ctrl+T), for ranges that grow by themselves and readable formulas.

24.html:
Why it matters

Until now, your formulas have pointed at fixed ranges like A2:C5. The problem: when you add a row at the bottom, the range doesn't move, and your totals miss the new data. Structured tables (often just called "tables") fix that: the range grows by itself, and formulas become as readable as a sentence.

It's probably the habit that most improves the quality of a file. Many professionals turn every data list into a table as soon as they create it.

Creating a table

  1. Click in any cell of your list (with a header row, and no blank row or column in the middle).
  2. Press Ctrl+T (or Insert > Table).
  3. Check the suggested range and tick "My table has headers". Confirm.
  4. In the Table Design tab that appears, give it a clear name in the "Table Name" box, for example Sales (no spaces).

Here's the Sales table from your placement shop:

SellerProductQuantityPriceAmount
AliceKeyboard4€25€100
BrunoMonitor2€180€360
AliceMouse10€15€150
ChloéHeadset3€60€180
BrunoKeyboard8€25€200

What the table does for you

  • It grows by itself: type a new sale just below the last row and it becomes part of the table. Every formula that uses the table takes it into account.
  • Formulas fill down by themselves: a formula typed in a column is applied to the whole column (this is called a calculated column).
  • Filters and formatting: filter buttons on the headers, banded rows, headers that stay visible as you scroll.
  • Total row: tick "Total Row" in the Table Design tab (or Ctrl+Shift+T). A drop-down list lets you choose sum, average, count...

Structured references

In a table, Excel replaces cell addresses with column names. When you click on cells in the table while writing a formula, it writes them for you.

Written asMeaning
Sales[Amount]The whole Amount column (without the header)
[@Quantity]The quantity on the row where the formula is
Sales[#All]The whole table, headers included
Sales[#Headers]The header row

The Amount column

In the first cell of the Amount column, type =, click on the quantity, type *, click on the price. Excel writes:

=[@Quantity]*[@Price]

Confirm: the whole column fills in. For Bruno and his monitors: 2 × 180 = €360. For Bruno and his keyboards: 8 × 25 = €200.

Calculations on the whole table

FormulaCalculationResult
=SUM(Sales[Amount])100 + 360 + 150 + 180 + 200€990
=SUMIF(Sales[Seller],"Bruno",Sales[Amount])360 + 200€560
=COUNTIF(Sales[Product],"Keyboard")Rows with Keyboard2
=XLOOKUP("Headset",Sales[Product],Sales[Seller])Who sold the headset?Chloé

Compare =SUMIF(Sales[Seller],"Bruno",Sales[Amount]) with =SUMIF(A2:A6,"Bruno",E2:E6): the first can be read without looking at the sheet. And if you add a 6th sale (Chloé, Mouse, 4, €15), the total goes up to 990 + 60 = €1,050 without touching the formula.

Good practice

  • One table = one list: one row per record, one column per piece of information, no subtotal row in the middle.
  • Short, clear names for the table and the columns: they'll appear in all your formulas.
  • Leave at least one empty row and column around the table, otherwise it may swallow neighbouring data.
  • To go back to a normal range: Table Design tab, Convert to Range.

Structured tables are also the foundation of PivotTables (module 6) and Power Query (module 8): the source grows, the analysis follows.

Exercise

  1. Write the formula that calculates Alice's total sales in the Sales table. Result?
  2. Which formula gives the total quantity sold? Result?
  3. You add a "VAT" column to the table. What formula do you write to calculate 20% of each row's amount? How much for Chloé's row?
  4. Your supervisor has a formula =SUM(E2:E6) under his list and complains that the total "forgets" new sales. What do you advise?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =SUMIF(Sales[Seller],"Alice",Sales[Amount]): 100 + 150 = €250.
  2. =SUM(Sales[Quantity]): 4 + 2 + 10 + 3 + 8 = 27.
  3. =[@Amount]*20% (or =[@Amount]*0.2). For Chloé: 180 × 20% = €36. The column fills in by itself.
  4. Turn the list into a table with Ctrl+T, name it, then write =SUM(TableName[Amount]). New rows will be included automatically.

Key takeaways

  • Ctrl+T turns a list into a table; give it a name straight away.
  • The table grows by itself and column formulas fill down by themselves.
  • Sales[Amount] = the whole column; [@Price] = the value on the current row.
  • Formulas become readable and no longer miss new rows.
  • A clean list: one row per record, no subtotal in the middle.

Next lesson: dynamic arrays, with FILTER, SORT and UNIQUE.

25.html:
Why it matters

Until now, a formula returned a single value in a single cell. Excel 365 can now return a whole list from a single formula: these are called dynamic arrays. With three functions, FILTER, SORT and UNIQUE, you can extract, sort and de-duplicate data without copy-pasting, and the result updates by itself.

Availability: these functions exist in Excel 365, Excel 2021 and later, and Excel for the web. Not in Excel 2019 or earlier. Google Sheets offers FILTER, SORT and UNIQUE.

Spilling

When a formula returns several values, the result spills into the neighbouring cells, downwards and to the right. Only the first cell contains the formula; the others show the result greyed out in the formula bar.

  • If a cell in the spill range isn't empty, Excel shows the #SPILL! error. Clear the range and the result appears.
  • To refer to the whole spilled result, add # after the first cell: H2#.

Let's go back to the Sales table from the previous lesson:

SellerProductQuantityPriceAmount
AliceKeyboard4€25€100
BrunoMonitor2€180€360
AliceMouse10€15€150
ChloéHeadset3€60€180
BrunoKeyboard8€25€200

UNIQUE: the list without duplicates

=UNIQUE(Sales[Seller]) returns Alice, Bruno, Chloé, on three rows. If a new seller appears in the table, they're added to the list automatically.

With its 3rd argument set to TRUE, UNIQUE keeps only the values that appear exactly once: =UNIQUE(Sales[Seller],,TRUE) returns only Chloé.

SORT: sorting without touching the data

=SORT(array,[sort_index],[sort_order]) with order 1 = ascending (default), -1 = descending.

=SORT(Sales,5,-1) sorts the whole table by its 5th column (Amount), from largest to smallest:

SellerProductQuantityPriceAmount
BrunoMonitor2€180€360
BrunoKeyboard8€25€200
ChloéHeadset3€60€180
AliceMouse10€15€150
AliceKeyboard4€25€100

The original data doesn't move: it's a sorted copy, always up to date. There's also SORTBY, which sorts by a column you point to directly: =SORTBY(Sales,Sales[Amount],-1) gives the same result.

FILTER: extracting the rows you're interested in

=FILTER(array,include,[if_empty])

FormulaRows returned
=FILTER(Sales,Sales[Seller]="Alice")Alice Keyboard €100; Alice Mouse €150
=FILTER(Sales,Sales[Amount]>=180)Bruno Monitor €360; Chloé Headset €180; Bruno Keyboard €200
=FILTER(Sales,Sales[Seller]="David","No sales")No sales

Without the 3rd argument, a filter that finds nothing returns the #CALC! error. So remember to provide a message.

Several conditions

FILTER doesn't use AND and OR. You write each condition in brackets, then:

  • * for "and": =FILTER(Sales,(Sales[Seller]="Bruno")*(Sales[Amount]>200)) returns a single row, Bruno Monitor €360 (200 isn't strictly greater than 200).
  • + for "or": =FILTER(Sales,(Sales[Product]="Monitor")+(Sales[Product]="Headset")) returns Bruno Monitor and Chloé Headset.

Combining them

These functions nest:

  • =SORT(UNIQUE(Sales[Product])): the list of products, without duplicates, in alphabetical order: Headset, Keyboard, Monitor, Mouse.
  • =SORT(FILTER(Sales,Sales[Amount]>=180),5,-1): sales of at least €180, from biggest to smallest (360, 200, 180).

A mini summary by seller

In H2, type =UNIQUE(Sales[Seller]). In I2, type =SUMIF(Sales[Seller],H2#,Sales[Amount]). Thanks to H2#, the sum is calculated for each seller and spills too:

H (UNIQUE)I (SUMIF)
Alice€250
Bruno€560
Chloé€180

Total: 250 + 560 + 180 = €990, the same as the table total. Add a seller to Sales: a row appears in this summary by itself.

Exercise

  1. What does =UNIQUE(Sales[Product]) return? How many rows?
  2. Write the formula that extracts keyboard sales, with the message "None" if there aren't any. Which rows do you get?
  3. Write the formula that extracts Alice's sales of at least €120. Result?
  4. Your formula =UNIQUE(Sales[Seller]) shows #SPILL!. What do you check?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Keyboard, Monitor, Mouse, Headset (in order of appearance): 4 rows.
  2. =FILTER(Sales,Sales[Product]="Keyboard","None") returns Alice Keyboard 4 × €25 = €100 and Bruno Keyboard 8 × €25 = €200.
  3. =FILTER(Sales,(Sales[Seller]="Alice")*(Sales[Amount]>=120)): a single row, Alice Mouse €150 (the €100 sale is excluded).
  4. That the cells below the formula (at least two more, since there are three sellers) are empty. Any value, even a space, blocks the spill.

Key takeaways

  • A formula can return a list that spills; H2# refers to the whole result.
  • #SPILL!: the destination range isn't empty.
  • UNIQUE de-duplicates, SORT sorts (1 ascending, -1 descending), FILTER extracts.
  • In FILTER: * for "and", + for "or", and a 3rd argument to avoid #CALC!.
  • Available in Excel 365 and Excel 2021 or later.

Next step: the module recap, with a summary exercise on all the lookup functions.

26.html:
Why it matters

In the previous module, you learnt to fetch data. Now you need to read it. Faced with a 500-row list, nobody spots anything with the naked eye. Three simple tools change everything: sorting to rank, filtering to show only what matters, and conditional formatting to make the important figures jump out.

Here are the first-quarter sales of your placement company, in A1:D6:

ABCD
1Sales repRegionMonthRevenue
2AliceNorthJan€1,200
3BrunoSouthJan€900
4ChloéNorthFeb€1,500
5DavidEastFeb€700
6EmmaSouthMar€1,300

Sorting

Click in the list, then Data > Sort. Choose the Revenue column and the order "Largest to Smallest". Result: Chloé (€1,500), Emma (€1,300), Alice (€1,200), Bruno (€900), David (€700).

  • Multi-level sort: in the same window, "Add Level". For example, sort by Region (A to Z), then by Revenue descending within each region: East (David), North (Chloé, Alice), South (Emma, Bruno).
  • The trap: if you select a single column before sorting, Excel may sort only that column and scramble your rows (Chloé's revenue credited to Alice...). Just click in the list without selecting anything: Excel detects the whole range. In a structured table (Ctrl+T), this risk disappears.

Filtering

Turn on filters with Data > Filter or Ctrl+Shift+L. An arrow appears on each header (they're already there in a structured table).

  • Click the Region arrow and keep only North: only Alice and Chloé remain visible. The other rows aren't deleted, just hidden.
  • On a column of numbers, Number Filters offers "Greater Than", "Top 10"...
  • To show everything again: Data > Clear.

The total that follows the filter: SUBTOTAL

SUM also adds up the rows hidden by the filter. For a total that only counts visible rows, use SUBTOTAL with code 109 (sum):

FormulaNo filterFilter Region = North
=SUM(D2:D6)€5,600€5,600
=SUBTOTAL(109,D2:D6)€5,600€2,700

With the North filter: 1,200 + 1,500 = €2,700. In fact, SUBTOTAL is what a structured table's Total row uses.

Conditional formatting

It changes the appearance of a cell depending on its value, and updates by itself. Select D2:D6, then Home > Conditional Formatting.

Rule typeExampleUse
Highlight Cells RulesGreater Than 1,000: green fillSpot what exceeds a threshold
Top/Bottom RulesTop 2 valuesSpot the top or bottom of the ranking
Data BarsA bar proportional to revenueCompare at a glance
Colour ScalesFrom red (low) to green (high)See a distribution
Icon SetsArrows or traffic lightsFlag a status

With "Greater Than 1,000", three cells turn green: Alice (€1,200), Chloé (€1,500) and Emma (€1,300).

Colouring the whole row with a formula

Select A2:D6, then New Rule > Use a formula to determine which cells to format, and type:

=$D2>1000

The $ in front of D locks the column (mixed reference, lesson 8): each cell in the row looks at its row's revenue. Alice's, Chloé's and Emma's rows are coloured in full. Without the $, cell A2 would look at D2, but B2 would look at E2, which is empty: only part of the row would be coloured.

To review or delete your rules: Conditional Formatting > Manage Rules. Avoid piling up too many: three well-chosen colours are better than a Christmas tree.

Exercise

  1. Sort the list by Month, then by Revenue ascending within each month. What is the order of the sales reps? (Excel sorts text months alphabetically: Feb, Jan, Mar.)
  2. You filter on Region = South. What do =SUM(D2:D6) and =SUBTOTAL(109,D2:D6) return?
  3. Which formula rule colours the whole row for sales reps in the East region? Who is affected?
  4. With the rule "Less Than 1,000", which revenue cells are formatted?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Feb: David (€700), Chloé (€1,500). Jan: Bruno (€900), Alice (€1,200). Mar: Emma (€1,300). Order: David, Chloé, Bruno, Alice, Emma. For chronological order, you'd need real dates or a custom list (Order > Custom List).
  2. SUM: €5,600 (it ignores the filter). SUBTOTAL: 900 + 1,300 = €2,200.
  3. On A2:D6: =$B2="East". Only David's row is coloured.
  4. Bruno (€900) and David (€700): 2 cells.

Key takeaways

  • Sort: click in the list (without selecting a single column), Data > Sort, several levels possible.
  • Filter: Ctrl+Shift+L; rows are hidden, not deleted.
  • =SUBTOTAL(109,range) only counts visible rows; SUM counts everything.
  • Conditional formatting makes important values stand out and updates by itself.
  • To colour a whole row: a formula rule with $ in front of the column, for example =$D2>1000.

Next lesson: PivotTables, to summarise thousands of rows in a few clicks.

27.html:
Why it matters

Your manager asks: "How much did we sell per region? And per product within each region?" You could write SUMIFS everywhere. Or you could build a PivotTable in thirty seconds. It's the most used analysis tool in business: on a placement, being able to make a clean PivotTable is often what makes people say "they really know Excel".

A PivotTable summarises a list: it groups rows by category and calculates totals, without a single formula, and you can rearrange the result by drag and drop.

The starting data

A PivotTable starts from a clean list: one header row, one row per sale, no blank rows or subtotals. Ideally, a structured table (lesson 24). Here's the Sales table:

RegionProductRevenue
NorthKeyboard€200
NorthMonitor€540
SouthKeyboard€150
SouthMonitor€360
EastMouse€90
NorthMouse€60
SouthMouse€120
EastMonitor€180

Creating the PivotTable

  1. Click in the table, then Insert > PivotTable.
  2. Choose "New Worksheet" and confirm. An empty area appears, with the PivotTable Fields pane on the right.
  3. The pane lists your columns (the "fields") and four areas: Filters, Columns, Rows, Values.

Drag Region into Rows and Revenue into Values:

Row LabelsSum of Revenue
East€270
North€800
South€630
Grand Total€1,700

Let's check: North = 200 + 540 + 60 = €800; South = 150 + 360 + 120 = €630; East = 90 + 180 = €270. Regions are sorted alphabetically by default.

Crossing two criteria

Now drag Product into Columns:

Sum of RevenueKeyboardMonitorMouseGrand Total
East€180€90€270
North€200€540€60€800
South€150€360€120€630
Grand Total€350€1,080€270€1,700

The empty cell means no keyboards were sold in the East. A field placed in Filters lets you analyse only part of the data (for example a single product) above the PivotTable.

Changing the calculation

By default, a number field is summed, a text field is counted. To change it: right-click a value in the PivotTable, Summarize Values By (Sum, Count, Average, Max, Min...).

  • Count of sales per region: East 2, North 3, South 3.
  • Average per region: North 800 / 3 ≈ €266.67; South 630 / 3 = €210; East 270 / 2 = €135.

Right-click, Show Values As > % of Grand Total turns the amounts into shares:

Region% of totalCalculation
East15.88%270 / 1,700
North47.06%800 / 1,700
South37.06%630 / 1,700

Tip: drag Revenue into Values twice to get both the amount and the percentage.

Habits to get into

  • Refresh: a PivotTable does not update by itself when the data changes. Right-click > Refresh, or Alt+F5 (Ctrl+Alt+F5 to refresh all).
  • Source as a structured table: new rows will be included at the next refresh. With a fixed range, they'd be missed.
  • Double-click an amount: Excel creates a new sheet with the rows that make up that figure. Handy for checking.
  • Number format: right-click > Value Field Settings > Number Format, so the format holds even after refreshing.

Google Sheets also offers pivot tables (Insert > Pivot table), with the same logic of rows, columns and values.

Exercise

  1. Build the PivotTable with Product in Rows and Revenue in Values. Which totals do you get?
  2. What share of total revenue do monitors represent? Round to 0.1%.
  3. You switch the calculation to "Count". How many mouse sales?
  4. Your colleague adds a sale (East, Keyboard, €100) to the Sales table, but the PivotTable still shows €1,700. Why, and what should they do? What will the new East total be?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. There's no Headset here: Keyboard €350 (200 + 150), Monitor €1,080 (540 + 360 + 180), Mouse €270 (90 + 60 + 120). Total: €1,700.
  2. 1,080 / 1,700 ≈ 63.5%.
  3. 3 mouse sales (East, North, South).
  4. The PivotTable doesn't refresh by itself. They need to right-click > Refresh (or Alt+F5). As the source is a structured table, the new row is included: East goes up to 270 + 100 = €370 and the total to €1,800.

Key takeaways

  • A PivotTable summarises a list without formulas: Insert > PivotTable.
  • Four areas: Rows, Columns, Values, Filters.
  • Summarise by Sum, Count, Average...; Show Values As % of total.
  • A PivotTable doesn't update by itself: Refresh (Alt+F5).
  • A clean structured table as the source, with no blank rows.

Next lesson: advanced PivotTables, with grouping by month, calculated fields and slicers.

28.titre: Advanced PivotTables: grouping, calculated fields, slicers
28.html:
Why it matters

Yesterday, you built your first PivotTable. But in real life, data arrives with dates (and your manager wants totals by month), you're asked for margins that aren't in the source, and the table needs to be easy to explore for someone who doesn't know Excel. Three tools handle this: grouping, the calculated field and slicers.

Here's the quarter's Sales table, with the purchase cost of each sale:

DateProductRevenueCost
05/01/2026Keyboard€200€120
18/01/2026Monitor€540€400
03/02/2026Keyboard€150€90
21/02/2026Monitor€360€270
14/03/2026Mouse€120€50
27/03/2026Monitor€180€130

Grouping dates by month

Drag Date into Rows. In recent versions, Excel often groups dates automatically (by years, quarters and months). If not: right-click a date in the PivotTable, Group, select Months (and Years if your data covers several years, otherwise January 2025 and January 2026 would be added together). With Revenue and Cost in Values:

MonthSum of RevenueSum of Cost
Jan€740€520
Feb€510€360
Mar€300€180
Grand Total€1,550€1,060

January: 200 + 540 = €740 of revenue and 120 + 400 = €520 of cost. To go back to the detailed dates: right-click, Ungroup.

Grouping numbers into bands

Grouping works on numbers too. Put Revenue in Rows, right-click, Group, with Starting at 0, Ending at 599 and By 200: you get the bands 0-199, 200-399 and 400-599. Here: 3 sales between €0 and €199 (150, 120, 180), 2 between €200 and €399 (200, 360), 1 between €400 and €599 (540). Useful for seeing the spread of basket sizes or salaries.

The calculated field

The margin isn't in the source? No need to add a column: create a calculated field. Click in the PivotTable, then PivotTable Analyze > Fields, Items & Sets > Calculated Field. Give it a name and a formula that uses the fields (double-click a field to insert it):

  • Name: Margin, formula: =Revenue-Cost
  • Name: Margin rate, formula: =(Revenue-Cost)/Revenue (percentage format)
MonthRevenueCostMarginMargin rate
Jan€740€520€22029.7%
Feb€510€360€15029.4%
Mar€300€180€12040.0%
Total€1,550€1,060€49031.6%

Key point: a calculated field works on the sums, not row by row. So the total rate is 490 / 1,550 ≈ 31.6%, which is correct. The average of the three monthly rates, (29.7 + 29.4 + 40.0) / 3 ≈ 33.0%, would be wrong, because March carries much less weight than January. Another limit: a calculated field can't use cell references (no B2), only fields and constants.

Slicers and the timeline

A slicer is a panel of clickable buttons that filters the PivotTable. Click in the PivotTable, then PivotTable Analyze > Insert Slicer and tick Product. Click "Monitor": the PivotTable now shows only monitors, i.e. €540 in January, €360 in February and €180 in March, €1,080 in total. Ctrl+click to select several buttons, and the crossed-out filter icon to show everything again.

  • The timeline (Insert Timeline) is a special slicer for dates: a strip where you pick a month, a quarter or a period.
  • The same slicer can drive several PivotTables built on the same source: right-click the slicer, Report Connections. That's the basis of a dashboard.
  • Slicers also work on structured tables (Table Design tab).

Exercise

  1. With the Product slicer on "Keyboard", which monthly revenues does the PivotTable show? What total margin?
  2. Calculate the margin rate for monitors over the quarter.
  3. Your colleague calculates the quarterly margin rate by averaging the rates of each sale. The rates are: 40%, 25.9%, 40%, 25%, 58.3% and 27.8%. What does she get (rounded to 0.1%)? Why is it different from 31.6%?
  4. Your data covers January 2025 to March 2026. You group by Months only. What's the problem?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. January €200, February €150, March nothing. Margin: (200 − 120) + (150 − 90) = 80 + 60 = €140.
  2. Monitor revenue: 540 + 360 + 180 = €1,080. Cost: 400 + 270 + 130 = €800. Rate: (1,080 − 800) / 1,080 = 280 / 1,080 ≈ 25.9%.
  3. (40 + 25.9 + 40 + 25 + 58.3 + 27.8) / 6 = 217 / 6 ≈ 36.2%. It's wrong, because each sale counts equally, whereas the €120 mouse (58.3%) carries far less weight than the €540 monitor. The right rate divides total margin by total revenue: 490 / 1,550 ≈ 31.6%. That's what the calculated field does.
  4. January 2025 and January 2026 would be added together in the same "Jan" row. You need to group by Months and Years.

Key takeaways

  • Group: dates by months, quarters, years; numbers into bands. Remember to add the years.
  • The calculated field creates a measure (margin, rate) from existing fields.
  • It calculates on the sums: a correct overall rate, not an average of rates.
  • Slicers and the timeline filter in one click and can drive several PivotTables.

Next lesson: choosing and building the right chart.

29.titre: Choosing and building the right chart
29.html:
Why it matters

A table of figures takes effort from the reader. A good chart gets the message across in three seconds. A bad chart confuses or even misleads. In a placement presentation, the chart is often what your manager will remember. The good news: choosing a chart follows a few simple rules.

Start from the message, not the chart

Before clicking Insert, ask yourself one question: what do I want to show? Each message has its chart:

You want to show...ChartExample
A comparison between categoriesColumn chart (vertical bars)Revenue by region
A ranking with long namesBar chart (horizontal)Sales by product, sorted
A change over timeLine chartRevenue month by month over a year
How a whole is split (few parts)Pie or doughnut chartShare of each item in a budget
The link between two measuresScatter chartAd budget and sales per shop
The distribution of valuesHistogramSpread of a class's marks

The pie chart is the most misused: it only works with few slices (about 5 at most) that make up a real total. To compare close values, the eye is bad at judging angles: bars are almost always easier to read.

Building the chart

Let's take the sales by region from the PivotTable in lesson 27:

RegionRevenue
North€800
South€630
East€270
  1. Select the data with its headers (Region and Revenue).
  2. Insert > Recommended Charts: Excel suggests several types suited to your data. Or choose Clustered Column directly.
  3. Shortcuts: Alt+F1 creates a default chart on the same sheet, F11 creates it on a new sheet.
  4. The + button next to the chart (on Windows) adds or removes elements: title, data labels, legend, gridlines.

The Chart Design and Format tabs let you change the type, the colours, or swap rows and columns (Switch Row/Column) if Excel has misread your series.

A title that states the message

A title like "Revenue by region" describes. A title like "The North brings in almost half of revenue" informs: the reader knows immediately what to look at. Let's check: 800 / 1,700 ≈ 47%, which is indeed almost half. Get into the habit of message titles, especially in a presentation.

The settings that make the difference

  • Sort the bars from largest to smallest (sort the source data): the ranking becomes obvious. Here: North, South, East.
  • Data labels rather than gridlines: €800, €630, €270 right on the bars.
  • Delete the legend when there's only one series: it adds nothing.
  • A single colour, and a bright colour only for what you want people to notice.
  • No 3D: it distorts proportions and makes nothing clearer.

If your data is in a PivotTable, you can create a PivotChart (PivotTable Analyze > PivotChart): it follows the PivotTable's filters and slicers.

Exercise

  1. Which chart do you choose for each case: a) revenue from January to December; b) the share of rent, groceries, transport and leisure in a student's budget; c) the sales of 12 products with long names; d) the link between revision hours and the mark obtained for 30 pupils?
  2. Léo's monthly budget: rent €450, groceries €200, transport €50, leisure €100. What share does rent represent? Suggest a message title.
  3. Your colleague presents the three regions' revenue in a 3D pie chart with a legend. What improvements do you suggest?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. a) Line chart (change over time). b) Pie or doughnut (4 parts of a whole), or bars. c) Sorted horizontal bar chart (long names, 12 items). d) Scatter chart (link between two measures).
  2. Total: 450 + 200 + 50 + 100 = €800. Rent: 450 / 800 = 56.25%. Possible title: "Rent takes up more than half of Léo's budget".
  3. Switch to a column (or bar) chart sorted from largest to smallest, remove the 3D, replace the legend with data labels, and add a message title such as "The North brings in almost half of revenue".

Key takeaways

  • Start from the message: comparison (column, bar), change over time (line), split of a whole (pie, few slices), link (scatter).
  • Insert > Recommended Charts, or Alt+F1 / F11.
  • A message title that says what to take away.
  • Sorted bars, data labels, one accent colour, no 3D.

Next lesson: professional charts, with combo charts, the secondary axis and sparklines.

30.titre: Professional charts: combo, secondary axes, sparklines, good practice
30.html:
Why it matters

Yesterday, you chose the right chart for a simple message. But in business, you often want to show two things at once: revenue and margin rate, sales and target. And in a dashboard, you want to see the trend of dozens of rows without drawing ten charts. Here are the tools for "pro" charts.

The combo chart and the secondary axis

Let's take the quarter's figures again (lesson 28):

MonthRevenueMargin rate
Jan€74029.7%
Feb€51029.4%
Mar€30040.0%

If you put these two series in a simple column chart, the rate (0.4 at most) is squashed next to the revenue (740): it's invisible. The solution: a combo chart with a secondary axis.

  1. Select the table, then Insert > Combo Chart (or, on an existing chart, Change Chart Type > Combo).
  2. For the Revenue series: Clustered Column.
  3. For the Margin rate series: Line, and tick Secondary Axis.

Revenue is read on the left axis (in euros), the rate on the right axis (in %). The message appears: revenue falls every month, but March's margin climbs clearly to 40%. Remember to title both axes (+ button > Axis Titles) so the reader knows which one to read.

Another classic use: actual sales as columns and the target as a line, this time on the same axis, since both are in euros.

Sparklines

A sparkline is a mini chart that fits in a single cell. Ideal for showing the trend of each row in a table.

Sales repJanFebMarAprTrend
Alice1,2001,5001,1001,600(sparkline)
Bruno9001,3001,6001,800(sparkline)
Chloé1,4001,0001,250950(sparkline)
  1. Select the cells where you want the sparklines (the Trend column).
  2. Insert > Sparklines, choose Line, Column or Win/Loss.
  3. Enter the data range (the four months).
  4. In the Sparkline tab, tick High Point and Low Point to mark the best and worst month.

At a glance: Bruno improves every month, Chloé declines over the period, Alice is up and down. Careful: by default, each sparkline has its own scale. To compare levels between rows, set the axis (Sparkline tab > Axis) to "Same for All Sparklines". Google Sheets has a SPARKLINE function that does the same job.

The pros' good practice

  • A column chart starts at 0. If the axis starts at €500, a €600 bar looks twice as tall as a €550 bar, when the gap is only 9%. A line chart, on the other hand, can have an axis that doesn't start at 0 if this is flagged.
  • One message per chart, announced in the title.
  • Few colours: grey for context, an accent colour for what matters.
  • Less ink: remove unnecessary gridlines, borders, shadow effects, 3D.
  • State the source and the unit ("in thousands of euros", "source: CRM extract, March 2026").
  • Use the secondary axis sparingly: two axes already demand a lot of the reader. Never three series on two different axes without clear titles.
  • Chart linked to the data: if the source is a structured table, the chart extends when you add a row.

Exercise

  1. You want to show the number of customers per month (between 80 and 120) and the average basket (between €45 and €60). Which chart do you build?
  2. In the sparklines table, what is each sales rep's high point and low point?
  3. A chart compares two shops: €600 and €550 of revenue, with an axis starting at €500. What does the reader see, and what is the real gap in %?
  4. Calculate Bruno's growth between January and April, in %.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. A combo chart: number of customers as columns, average basket as a line on a secondary axis (different units: customers and euros). With axis titles.
  2. Alice: high 1,600 (April), low 1,100 (March). Bruno: high 1,800 (April), low 900 (January). Chloé: high 1,400 (January), low 950 (April).
  3. The €600 bar rises 100 above the axis, the €550 bar 50: the reader thinks one is double the other. Real gap: (600 − 550) / 550 ≈ 9.1%. The axis should start at 0.
  4. (1,800 − 900) / 900 = 100%: Bruno doubled his sales.

Key takeaways

  • Combo chart: two chart types; secondary axis when units or orders of magnitude differ.
  • Title both axes.
  • Sparklines: one mini chart per cell, Insert > Sparklines, with high and low points.
  • A column chart starts at 0.
  • One message per chart, few colours, no 3D, source and unit stated.

Next step: the module recap, with a summary exercise that goes from the raw list to the chart.

31.titre: Modelling cleanly: assumptions, calculations, results, colour coding
31.html:
Why it matters

Welcome to the finance module! Before talking about loans, NPV or scenarios, you need to know how to build a model: a file that starts from a few input figures and derives results from them. On a placement, you'll often be asked to "put together a little model". A good model can be read in two minutes, changed in ten seconds and hides no errors. A bad model is a plate of spaghetti where nobody dares touch a cell.

The golden rule: split into three blocks

Assumptions → Calculations → Results. Every figure typed in by hand lives in the assumptions, and nowhere else.

  • Assumptions (the inputs): selling price, volumes, rates, durations. These are the only cells you type on the keyboard.
  • Calculations: only formulas that point to the assumptions. No hard-coded numbers in a formula.
  • Results (the outputs): the few figures your manager wants to see, at the top or on a separate sheet.

For a small model, three areas on one sheet are enough. For a big model, you make one sheet per block: Assumptions, Calculations, Summary.

Example: Léa's online shop

Léa, on a placement with a small handbag brand, has to estimate the monthly profit of a new model. Here's her sheet:

CellLabel (column A)Contents (column B)Value displayed
B2Unit selling price25€25
B3Monthly volume400400
B4Unit variable cost10€10
B5Monthly fixed costs3000€3,000
B8Revenue=B2*B3€10,000
B9Variable costs=B4*B3€4,000
B10Contribution margin=B8-B9€6,000
B12Monthly profit=B10-B5€3,000
B13Break-even point (units)=B5/(B2-B4)200

Rows 2 to 5: the assumptions. Rows 8 to 10: the calculations. Rows 12 and 13: the results. If the supplier raises the cost to €12, Léa changes a single cell (B4) and everything updates: profit €2,200, break-even about 231 units.

The hard-coded number trap

Writing =B3*25 instead of =B3*B2 gives the same result today. But the day the price goes up to €28, someone changes B2... and revenue doesn't move. This kind of error is invisible and can skew an entire decision. One constant = one assumption cell.

Colour coding

In banks and audit firms, a very widespread convention lets you see at a glance what each cell is:

Font colourMeaningExample
BlueManual input (assumption)25, 400, 4%
BlackFormula calculated on the same sheet=B2*B3
GreenLink to another sheet or another file=Assumptions!B2

Many teams add a pale yellow fill to assumption cells. It's not an official rule: what matters is to choose one, write it in a small key at the top of the file, and stick to it.

Good modelling habits

  1. One row = one logic. The formula in column B should be the same as in columns C, D, E (just shifted). You can then drag the fill handle without surprises.
  2. Use absolute references (lesson 8) to point to a single assumption: =C3*$B$2.
  3. Name the key cells: select B2, then Formulas > Define Name, and call it Price. The formula becomes =Price*Volume, readable by everyone.
  4. Add checks: a cell that checks two totals are equal, for example =IF(ABS(B20-B21)<0.01,"OK","ERROR").
  5. State the units in the labels: "in €", "in € thousands", "in %". Mixing euros and thousands of euros is a classic mistake.
  6. Don't merge cells in the calculation area: it gets in the way of filling and sorting.

This advice also applies in Google Sheets and on a Mac: a model's logic doesn't depend on the software.

Exercise

  1. In Léa's model, the price goes up to €28 (cost still €10). Calculate revenue, contribution margin, profit and the break-even point.
  2. A colleague wrote in B9: =10*B3. What's the problem?
  3. What font colour should cells B3, B10 and a cell =Assumptions!B3 on another sheet be?
  4. Write a check formula that displays "OK" if the profit in B12 really equals B8-B9-B5.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Revenue: 28 × 400 = €11,200. Variable costs: 10 × 400 = €4,000. Margin: 11,200 − 4,000 = €7,200. Profit: 7,200 − 3,000 = €4,200. Break-even: 3,000 / (28 − 10) ≈ 166.7, so 167 units.
  2. The €10 cost is hard-coded. If assumption B4 changes, B9 doesn't follow. It should be =B4*B3.
  3. B3: blue (input). B10: black (formula). The cell linked to another sheet: green.
  4. =IF(ABS(B12-(B8-B9-B5))<0.01,"OK","ERROR"). You compare with a small tolerance to avoid rounding differences.

Key takeaways

  • A model splits into assumptions, calculations, results.
  • Every constant lives in a single assumption cell: never a hard-coded number in a formula.
  • Common colour code: blue for inputs, black for formulas, green for links to other sheets.
  • Absolute references, defined names and check cells make the model reliable.

Next lesson: the financial functions PMT, PV, FV, RATE and NPER, to calculate a monthly payment or savings in one formula.

32.titre: Financial functions: PMT, PV, FV, RATE, NPER
32.html:
Why it matters

How much will I pay each month for this loan? How much will I have in 10 years if I put €100 aside every month? What's the real rate on this credit deal? These questions come up all the time, in corporate finance as in personal life. Excel answers them with five functions that all work together. Once you've understood their shared logic, you can use them all.

The five shared parameters

ArgumentMeaningFunction that calculates it
rateInterest rate per periodRATE
nperNumber of periods (payments)NPER
pmtPayment made each periodPMT
pvPresent value (the amount at the start)PV
fvFuture value (the amount at the end)FV

Each function calculates one of the five from the others. There's also a final optional argument, type: 0 (or omitted) if payments are made at the end of the period, which is the case for standard loans; 1 if they're made at the start of the period.

Two traps you absolutely must know

  • The rate and the duration must be in the same unit. For monthly payments, divide the annual rate by 12 and count the duration in months: 4%/12 and 60, not 4% and 5.
  • The sign matters. Excel thinks in cash flows: money you receive is positive, money you pay out is negative. That's why you often put a minus sign in front of the amount, to get a positive result.

PMT: a loan's monthly payment

Syntax: =PMT(rate,nper,pv,[fv],[type]). Tom borrows €15,000 for his car, at 4% a year over 5 years, repaid monthly:

AB
1Amount borrowed€15,000
2Annual rate4%
3Duration (months)60
4Monthly payment=PMT(B2/12,B3,-B1) → €276.25
5Total repaid=B4*B3 → €16,574.87
6Cost of interest=B5-B1 → €1,574.87

Without the minus sign in front of B1, Excel displays -€276.25: the amount is right, it's only the direction of the flow that changes.

FV: how much I'll have at the end

Syntax: =FV(rate,nper,pmt,[pv],[type]). Sarah pays €100 a month into an investment at 3% a year for 10 years:

=FV(3%/12,120,-100) → €13,974.14. She paid in 120 × 100 = €12,000: compound interest earned her almost €1,974.

PV: how much I can borrow

Syntax: =PV(rate,nper,pmt,[fv],[type]). PV does the reverse of PMT. Nadia can repay at most €250 a month for 5 years, at 4%:

=PV(4%/12,60,-250) → €13,574.77. That's the maximum amount she can borrow.

RATE: the real rate of a credit deal

Syntax: =RATE(nper,pmt,pv,[fv],[type],[guess]). A seller offers €10,000 repaid in 48 monthly instalments of €230. What's the rate?

=RATE(48,-230,10000) → about 0.41% per month. To get it per year: =RATE(48,-230,10000)*12 → about 4.94%. Don't forget the ×12: it's the most common mistake with RATE.

NPER: how long

Syntax: =NPER(rate,pmt,pv,[fv],[type]). Hugo owes €8,000 at 3% a year and repays €200 a month. How long until he's finished?

=NPER(3%/12,-200,8000) → about 42.2 months, so 43 monthly payments (the last one smaller).

Summary

QuestionFormulaResult
Monthly payment for €15,000 at 4% over 60 months=PMT(4%/12,60,-15000)€276.25
Saving €100/month at 3% over 10 years=FV(3%/12,120,-100)€13,974.14
Amount you can borrow with €250/month=PV(4%/12,60,-250)€13,574.77
Annual rate of 48 × €230 for €10,000=RATE(48,-230,10000)*124.94%
Duration for €8,000 at €200/month=NPER(3%/12,-200,8000)42.2 months

Good to know: these functions also exist in Google Sheets and in Excel for Mac, with the same arguments. Excel's results don't include borrower insurance or arrangement fees: the real cost of a loan is therefore a little higher.

Exercise

  1. Calculate the monthly payment on an €8,000 loan at 5% a year over 48 months, and the total cost of interest.
  2. Inès pays €150 a month for 5 years into a savings account at 2% a year. How much will she have at the end?
  3. Someone writes =PMT(5%,4,-8000) for question 1. What does that actually calculate, and why is it wrong?
  4. Hugo owes €5,000 at 5% a year and repays €150 a month. How many monthly payments does he need?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =PMT(5%/12,48,-8000) → €184.23. Total: 184.23 × 48 ≈ €8,843.25. Interest: about €843.25.
  2. =FV(2%/12,60,-150) → €9,457.10, for €9,000 paid in.
  3. It calculates an annual instalment: 4 yearly payments at 5%. It's not a monthly payment. The rate and the duration must both be monthly: 5%/12 and 48.
  4. =NPER(5%/12,-150,5000) → about 35.96, so 36 monthly payments.

Key takeaways

  • Five linked functions: PMT (payment), PV (start), FV (end), RATE, NPER (duration).
  • Rate and duration in the same unit: annual rate / 12 for months.
  • Sign convention: what you pay out is negative, what you receive is positive.
  • A RATE calculated on months is multiplied by 12 to get an annual rate.

Next lesson: NPV and IRR, to decide whether an investment is worth it.

33.titre: NPV and IRR in Excel (NPV, IRR, XNPV, XIRR)
33.html:
Why it matters

A company is weighing up buying a machine, launching a product, opening a shop. It spends money today to get more back later. But €1,000 in three years is worth less than €1,000 today. NPV and IRR are the two basic tools for comparing these flows over time. Here, we focus on how to calculate them correctly in Excel, because a very common syntax mistake skews the result.

The two concepts in brief

  • NPV (net present value): you bring each future cash flow back to its value today using a discount rate, then add them up, investment included. If NPV is positive, the project earns more than the required rate.
  • IRR (internal rate of return): the rate at which NPV is exactly zero. If IRR is higher than the required rate, the project is worthwhile.

The present value of a cash flow F received in n years, at rate t, is calculated like this: F / (1 + t)^n.

Example: Malik's project

Malik, on a placement at a small business, is studying the purchase of a €20,000 machine. It should generate the following cash flows. The company requires 8% a year.

A (Year)B (Cash flow)
20-€20,000
31€6,000
42€7,000
53€8,000
64€6,000

The NPV function and its trap

Syntax: =NPV(rate,value1,[value2],...). Careful: Excel assumes the first cash flow in the list arrives in one year. So it discounts everything, even the first one.

FormulaResultComment
=NPV(8%,B3:B6)+B2€2,317.76Correct: the year-0 investment is added separately, without discounting
=NPV(8%,B2:B6)€2,146.08Wrong: the investment is treated as if it happened in one year

NPV is positive: at the required rate of 8%, the project creates about €2,318 of value. The wrong version underestimates the project at 2,317.76 / 1.08 ≈ €2,146.08: everything is shifted by a year.

The IRR function

Syntax: =IRR(values,[guess]). Here, there's no shifting trap: you take the whole range, year 0 included.

=IRR(B2:B6) → about 13.0%. That's more than 8%: the project passes this test too. For IRR to work, the range must contain at least one negative and one positive cash flow.

When dates are irregular: XNPV and XIRR

NPV and IRR assume cash flows spaced at equal periods. In real life, cash flows often fall on specific dates: one payment in March, another in November... Then you use:

  • =XNPV(rate,values,dates): NPV with real dates. The first cash flow is the starting point and isn't discounted: no need to add it separately.
  • =XIRR(values,dates,[guess]): the annual IRR with real dates.

If you put the dates from 01/01/2026 to 01/01/2030 in column C (one per year):

FormulaResult
=XNPV(8%,B2:B6,C2:C6)€2,315.50
=XIRR(B2:B6,C2:C6)13.0%

The result is very close to NPV, but not identical: these functions count the actual days on a 365-day basis, and 2028 is a leap year. With truly irregular dates, the difference becomes significant. In business, XNPV and XIRR are often preferred for this reason.

Classic mistakes

  1. Including year 0 in NPV: that's mistake number one. Add the investment separately.
  2. Forgetting the minus sign on the investment: with only positive cash flows, IRR returns #NUM!.
  3. Mixing periods: monthly cash flows with an annual rate. You need a monthly rate, or use XNPV.
  4. Comparing only the IRRs of two projects of very different sizes: NPV tells you how much value is created in euros, IRR doesn't.

These functions exist in Excel for Mac. In Google Sheets, they have the same names: NPV, IRR, XNPV and XIRR.

Exercise

  1. A project costs €5,000 today and brings in €2,000 a year for 3 years. Write the NPV formula at 6% (cash flows in B2:B5, year 0 in B2) and give the result.
  2. What is this project's IRR? Is the project worthwhile if 6% is required?
  3. What would =NPV(6%,B2:B5) give, and why is it wrong?
  4. The final year's cash flow goes up to €2,500. Does NPV go up or down?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =NPV(6%,B3:B5)+B2 → about €346.02.
  2. =IRR(B2:B5) → about 9.7%. That's more than 6% (and NPV is positive): the project is worthwhile.
  3. About 346.02 / 1.06 ≈ €326.44: Excel also discounts the €5,000 by one year, as if it were paid in a year's time. The result is too low.
  4. It goes up: a higher cash flow adds value. It rises to about €765.83 and IRR to about 13.8%.

Key takeaways

  • NPV > 0 or IRR > required rate: the project creates value.
  • In Excel, =NPV(rate,future cash flows)+investment: year 0 is added separately.
  • =IRR(full range), year 0 included.
  • With specific dates: XNPV and XIRR, which count actual days.

Next lesson: building a loan amortisation schedule row by row.

34.html:
Why it matters

PMT gave you a loan's monthly payment. But within that payment, how much goes on interest, and how much actually repays the capital? How much is left to repay after a year? The amortisation schedule answers all of this, month by month. It's a classic in banking interviews and placements, and an excellent exercise for revising absolute references.

The logic of one row

For a loan with fixed monthly payments, each month follows the same mechanism:

  1. Interest for the month = outstanding capital at the start of the month × monthly rate.
  2. Capital repaid = monthly payment − interest.
  3. Capital outstanding at the end of the month = opening capital − capital repaid.

At the start, the outstanding capital is high: interest weighs heavily. As the months go by, it decreases and the share of capital repaid increases. The monthly payment itself doesn't change.

Example: Chloé's student loan

Chloé borrows €12,000 at 3.6% a year over 12 months (a short example so that everything fits on screen). She puts her assumptions separately, in column H:

CellAssumptionValue
H1Amount€12,000
H2Annual rate3.6%
H3Duration (months)12

The formulas in the first row (row 2)

ColumnContentsFormula in row 2
AMonth1
BOpening capital=$H$1
CMonthly payment=PMT($H$2/12,$H$3,-$H$1)
DInterest=B2*$H$2/12
ECapital repaid=C2-D2
FClosing capital=B2-E2

In row 3, only one formula changes: the opening capital is the previous month's closing capital, =F2. In A3, you write =A2+1. Then you select A3:F3 and drag the fill handle down to row 13. The $ signs keep the assumptions fixed; the relative references move down one row.

The result

MonthOpening capitalMonthly paymentInterestCapital repaidClosing capital
112,000.001,019.6136.00983.6111,016.39
211,016.391,019.6133.05986.5610,029.84
310,029.841,019.6130.09989.529,040.32
..................
112,030.071,019.616.091,013.521,016.56
121,016.561,019.613.051,016.560.00

First month: 12,000 × 3.6% / 12 = €36 of interest, so 1,019.61 − 36 = €983.61 of capital repaid. The closing capital in month 12 falls to 0.00: that's the best check that your schedule is right.

Checks to add

CheckFormulaResult
Total interest=SUM(D2:D13)€235.29
Same thing, another method=C2*$H$3-$H$1€235.29
Total capital repaid=SUM(E2:E13)€12,000.00
Final capital zero?=IF(ABS(F13)<0.01,"OK","ERROR")OK

The shortcuts: IPMT and PPMT

Excel can also give you directly the interest or capital part of a specific payment, without building the whole schedule:

  • =IPMT(3.6%/12,1,12,-12000) → €36.00 of interest in month 1.
  • =PPMT(3.6%/12,1,12,-12000) → €983.61 of capital in month 1.

The second argument is the period number. These functions are handy for checking a row of the schedule.

Excel 365 variant

In Excel 365, =SEQUENCE($H$3) in A2 generates the numbers 1 to 12 in one go. If the duration changes, the column adapts. In older versions, you stick with =A2+1.

In real life, a mortgage lasts 20 or 25 years: 240 or 300 rows, but exactly the same formulas. Also remember View > Freeze Panes to keep the headings visible.

Exercise

  1. A €6,000 loan at 6% a year over 6 months. Calculate the monthly payment with PMT.
  2. Fill in the first row: interest, capital repaid, closing capital.
  3. What is the total cost of interest?
  4. Your closing capital in the last month shows €152.30. Give two possible causes.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =PMT(6%/12,6,-6000) → €1,017.57.
  2. Interest: 6,000 × 6% / 12 = €30.00. Capital repaid: 1,017.57 − 30 = €987.57. Closing capital: 6,000 − 987.57 = €5,012.43.
  3. 1,017.57 × 6 − 6,000 ≈ €105.44.
  4. For example: a forgotten $ on the rate (the reference slides to an empty cell), an annual rate not divided by 12, or a monthly payment typed in by hand and rounded instead of being calculated with PMT.

Key takeaways

  • Interest = opening capital × rate / 12; capital repaid = monthly payment − interest.
  • A month's opening capital = the previous month's closing capital.
  • The $ signs fix the assumptions: write the row once, then copy it down.
  • Check: the final capital must be 0. IPMT and PPMT check a specific row.

Next lesson: scenario analysis with Goal Seek, the data table and Scenario Manager.

35.titre: Scenario analysis: Goal Seek, data tables, Scenario Manager
35.html:
Why it matters

A model never gives "the" answer: it depends on the assumptions. What happens if sales fall by 25%? How much can I borrow if I don't want to pay more than €300 a month? Excel offers three tools to make your model talk, all found under Data > What-If Analysis. They work all the better when your model clearly separates assumptions and calculations (lesson 31).

1. Goal Seek: starting from the result you want

Usually, you change an assumption and look at the result. Goal Seek does the reverse: you set the result you want, and Excel looks for the input value that gets there.

Let's go back to Tom's loan (lesson 32). In B1 the amount, in B2 the rate (4%), in B3 the duration (60), in B4 =PMT(B2/12,B3,-B1). Tom doesn't want to pay more than €300 a month. How much can he borrow?

  1. Data > What-If Analysis > Goal Seek.
  2. Set cell: B4 (it must contain a formula).
  3. To value: 300.
  4. By changing cell: B1 (it must contain a value, not a formula).
  5. OK: Excel replaces B1 with €16,289.72.
CellBeforeAfter Goal Seek
B1 Amount€15,000.00€16,289.72
B4 Monthly payment€276.25€300.00

You can check with =PV(4%/12,60,-300), which also gives €16,289.72. Careful: Goal Seek overwrites the value in B1. Note the old value if you want to go back (or undo with Ctrl+Z straight afterwards).

2. The data table: testing lots of values at once

The data table calculates your result for a whole grid of assumptions. Example: the monthly payment on €15,000 depending on the rate (in rows) and the duration (in columns).

  1. In the top-left corner of the grid (say E2), write a formula that returns the result: =B4.
  2. To the right of E2 (F2:H2), the durations: 48, 60, 72. Below E2 (E3:E5), the rates: 3%, 4%, 5%.
  3. Select E2:H5, then Data > What-If Analysis > Data Table.
  4. Row input cell: B3 (the duration, because the durations are along the top row). Column input cell: B2 (the rate).
Rate \ Duration48 months60 months72 months
3%€332.01€269.53€227.91
4%€338.69€276.25€234.68
5%€345.44€283.07€241.57

You can see straight away that 4% over 60 months does give €276.25. The table cells contain a special formula, {=TABLE(B3,B2)}: you can't edit them one by one. If your workbook becomes slow, data tables are often the cause; in Formulas > Calculation Options, the "Automatic Except for Data Tables" mode helps (then press F9 to recalculate).

3. Scenario Manager: named sets of assumptions

Back to Léa's model (lesson 31): price €25, variable cost €10, fixed costs €3,000, volume in B3. Her manager wants three cases: cautious, central, optimistic.

  1. Data > What-If Analysis > Scenario Manager > Add.
  2. Name: "Cautious", changing cells: B3. Value: 300.
  3. Repeat for "Central" (400) and "Optimistic" (500).
  4. Show applies a scenario to the model; Summary creates a new summary sheet, with B12 (profit) as the result cell.
ScenarioVolume (B3)Profit =(B2-B4)*B3-B5
Cautious300€1,500
Central400€3,000
Optimistic500€4,500

A scenario can change up to 32 cells at once (volume, price and cost together, for example).

Which one should you choose?

ToolQuestionNumber of assumptions that vary
Goal Seek"Which input gives me this result?"1
Data table"What does the result look like across a whole grid?"1 or 2
Scenario Manager"What do a few consistent cases give?"Several at once

All three tools exist in Excel for Mac. Google Sheets has no equally complete built-in equivalent: people often use add-ons or a hand-made grid of formulas.

Exercise

  1. Maximum monthly payment €250, rate 3%, duration 48 months. What amount will Goal Seek find? Check it with a function from lesson 32.
  2. In the data table above, which row and column input cells would you choose if you put the rates along the top and the durations down the left?
  3. In Léa's model, which volume gives a profit of €0? Which tool would you use to find it?
  4. A "Crisis" scenario sets volume to 250 and variable cost to €12. What profit do you get?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. About €11,294.67. Check: =PV(3%/12,48,-250).
  2. The values along the top are then rates: row input cell = B2 (rate), column input cell = B3 (duration).
  3. 200 units (the break-even point: 3,000 / 15). Tool: Goal Seek, set cell B12, to value 0, by changing cell B3.
  4. (25 − 12) × 250 − 3,000 = 3,250 − 3,000 = €250.

Key takeaways

  • It's all under Data > What-If Analysis.
  • Goal Seek: you set the result, Excel finds the input (and overwrites its value).
  • Data table: a grid of results for 1 or 2 assumptions; be careful not to swap the row and column input cells.
  • Scenario Manager: named cases that change several cells, with an automatic summary.

To finish this module: the recap sheet, linking models, financial functions, NPV, amortisation and scenarios.

36.html:
Why it matters

Welcome to the final module! You can calculate, analyse and model. What's left is making your files robust when other people use them. The number one enemy of a shared table is data entry: "Transport", "transport", "Transports", "travel"... and your SUMIF can't find anything any more. Data validation stops these mistakes at the source, and the drop-down list makes data entry faster.

Where to find it

Select the cells to control, then Data > Data Validation. The window has three tabs:

  • Settings: what is allowed (list, whole number, decimal, date, text length, custom formula).
  • Input Message: a help bubble that appears when you click in the cell.
  • Error Alert: what happens if the entry is rejected. The Stop style blocks it, Warning and Information let it through after confirmation.

Example: Yanis's expense claims
