Yanis, on a placement, has to keep his team's expense claims. He prepares the list of categories in F2:F5 (Transport, Meals, Hotel, Other), then applies two rules:

  1. On B2:B50 (Category): Allow: List, Source: =$F$2:$F$5. An arrow appears in each cell.
  2. On C2:C50 (Amount): Allow: Decimal, between 0 and 500. An amount of €5,000 typed by mistake is rejected.
A (Date)B (Category)C (Amount)
206/10Transport€45.00
306/10Meals€18.50
407/10Hotel€89.00
507/10Meals€22.00
608/10Transport€12.40

Thanks to the list, categories are always written the same way, and the formulas from module 3 are guaranteed to work:

FormulaResult
=SUMIF(B2:B6,"Meals",C2:C6)€40.50
=COUNTIF(B2:B6,"Transport")2
=SUM(C2:C6)€186.90

Typing the list directly

For a small list that never changes, you can type the values in the Source box, separated by commas in the English version: Yes,No. For a list that evolves, a range of cells is better.

A list that grows by itself

If Yanis adds "Parking" in F6, the source =$F$2:$F$5 doesn't see it. Two solutions:

  • Structured table + name (lesson 24): put the categories in a table (Ctrl+T) called Categories, create a name CatList that refers to =Categories[Category] (Formulas > Name Manager), then use =CatList as the source. The table grows, the list follows.
  • Excel 365: if the list comes from a dynamic formula such as =SORT(UNIQUE(...)) in H2 (lesson 25), the source =$H$2# follows the spilled range.

Custom validation

With Allow: Custom, you write a formula that must return TRUE. Example: rejecting duplicates in a column of invoice numbers (A2:A100):

=COUNTIF($A$2:$A$100,A2)=1

If the number already exists elsewhere in the column, COUNTIF returns 2 and the entry is rejected.

Limits to be aware of

  • Validation doesn't check data that's already there. To spot it: Data > Data Validation > Circle Invalid Data.
  • A copy-paste over a validated cell can wipe out the rule. For a shared file, combine it with protection (next lesson).
  • To remove a rule: same window, Clear All button.

On a Mac, the menu is the same. In Google Sheets, it's Data > Data validation, with lists shown as coloured chips.

Exercise

  1. Which rule would you put on an "Expense date" column to accept only the year 2026?
  2. Yanis adds a row: Hotel, €95. What do =SUM(C2:C7) and =COUNTIF(B2:B7,"Hotel") become?
  3. Someone types €650 in the Amount column with the Warning alert style. What happens?
  4. Write a custom rule that only accepts in D2 a text of exactly 6 characters (an employee code).
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Allow: Date, between 01/01/2026 and 31/12/2026, with the Stop style.
  2. 186.90 + 95 = €281.90, and 2 hotel nights.
  3. Excel shows a message and asks whether to continue. If the person answers Yes, the value is accepted. Only the Stop style really blocks it.
  4. Allow: Custom, formula =LEN(D2)=6. (You can also use Allow: Text length, equal to 6.)

Key takeaways

  • Data > Data Validation: list, numbers, dates, length, custom formula.
  • A drop-down list guarantees identical labels, and so reliable SUMIFs.
  • For a list that grows: structured table + name, or a dynamic # range in Excel 365.
  • Validation doesn't check existing data and can be bypassed by copy-paste: Circle Invalid Data.

Next lesson: protecting, sharing, commenting and recovering older versions of a file.

37.html:
Why it matters

An Excel file in business rarely lives on its own. Your manager reviews it, a colleague adds to it, accounts pick up the figures. Anyone can overwrite a formula without meaning to. This lesson teaches you to protect what needs protecting, to work together on the same file, to comment properly and to go back if something goes wrong.

Protecting a sheet: the two-step logic

This is the point that surprises everyone: by default, all cells are already "locked". But this lock does nothing until the sheet is protected. The method:

  1. Unlock the input cells: select them, Ctrl+1 (Format Cells), Protection tab, untick Locked.
  2. Protect the sheet: Review > Protect Sheet. Choose what remains allowed (select cells, sort, filter...) and, if you like, a password.

Result: people can type in the input cells, but can't touch the formulas.

Example: Clara's team budget

Item (A)Budget (B)Actual (C)Variance (D) =B2-C2
Office rent€700€700€0
Supplies€300€342-€42
Travel€150€120€30
Total€1,150€1,162-€12

Clara unlocks only C2:C4 (the actuals, entered by her colleagues), then protects the sheet. The budget, the variances and the totals (=SUM(B2:B4)...) can no longer be changed by mistake.

The three levels of protection

ProtectionWhereWhat it prevents
SheetReview > Protect SheetChanging locked cells
Workbook structureReview > Protect WorkbookAdding, deleting, renaming or hiding sheets
Opening the fileFile > Info > Protect Workbook > Encrypt with PasswordOpening the file without the password

Sheet protection prevents mistakes, not snooping. It's fairly easy to get round. For confidential data, only encryption on opening really protects it. And if you lose that password, Microsoft can't recover it.

Sharing and working together

In Excel 365, working together goes through the cloud:

  1. Save the file on OneDrive or SharePoint (often the case in companies, via Teams).
  2. Click Share (top right), choose the people and the permission: can edit or view only.
  3. Several people can then edit at the same time: this is co-authoring. You see their coloured cursors, and AutoSave saves as you go.

Avoid the old method of "I'll email you the file, you email it back": you soon end up with Budget_v3_final_REALLY.xlsx and lost changes.

Comments and notes

Excel 365 offers two different tools:

  • Comments (Review > New Comment): a real conversation. You can reply, mention a colleague with @ (they get an email notification), and mark the thread as resolved.
  • Notes (Review > Notes > New Note): a simple yellow sticky note, with no replies. Handy for explaining an assumption: "Rate provided by the bank on 12/09".

In Clara's budget, a comment on C3: "@Julien, why €342 of supplies this month?". Julien replies, Clara resolves the thread.

Going back: version history

When the file is on OneDrive or SharePoint, Excel keeps the old versions: File > Info > Version History. You can open an old version, copy what was lost, or restore it entirely. It's the safety net when someone deleted a column yesterday.

In Google Sheets, the equivalents are Data > Protect sheets and ranges and File > Version history. On a Mac, Excel's menus are the same.

Exercise

  1. You protect a sheet without unlocking anything first. What can your colleagues do?
  2. In Clara's budget, actual travel goes up to €190. What do this row's variance and the total variance become?
  3. You want a colleague to explain a figure to you and to be notified. Note or comment?
  4. A colleague accidentally deleted the "Assumptions" sheet from a file shared on OneDrive, and closed the file. What do you do, and which protection would have prevented it?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. No input is possible: all cells are locked by default. You need to unlock the input cells first.
  2. Variance: 150 − 190 = -€40. Total actual: 700 + 342 + 190 = €1,232; total variance: 1,150 − 1,232 = -€82.
  3. A comment with an @ mention: they get a notification and can reply.
  4. File > Info > Version History, open the earlier version and restore it (or copy the sheet across). Protecting the workbook structure would have prevented the sheet from being deleted.

Key takeaways

  • Protecting a sheet = unlock the inputs (Ctrl+1 > Protection), then Review > Protect Sheet.
  • Sheet, structure, opening: three levels. Only encryption protects confidentiality.
  • Sharing on OneDrive or SharePoint: co-authoring and AutoSave.
  • Comments for discussion (@mention, resolve), notes for explanation.
  • Version history lets you restore a file.

Next lesson: Power Query, to automatically import and clean data that comes back every month.

38.titre: Power Query: importing and transforming automatically
38.html:
Why it matters

At the start of every month, Emma receives the sales export from the shop's till software: a CSV file with extra spaces, amounts recognised as text, blank rows. In lesson 20, you learnt to clean that by hand. That's fine once. Twelve times a year, it's a waste of time and a risk of error. Power Query records your cleaning steps once and for all and replays them in one click.

Where to find it

Power Query is built into Excel 365 (and into Excel since 2016), on the Data tab, Get & Transform Data group. The most common entry points:

  • Data > Get Data > From File > From Text/CSV: an export.
  • From File > From Excel Workbook: another Excel file.
  • From File > From Folder: all the files in a folder, stacked into a single table.
  • Data > From Table/Range: data already in your workbook.

On a Mac, Power Query exists in Excel 365 but with fewer sources available. Google Sheets has no direct equivalent.

Example: Emma's sales export

Here's what Emma receives (the till software is set up in French, so amounts use a decimal comma):

DateRegionAmount
02/10/2026␣North␣1 250,00 (text)
03/10/2026South980,00 (text)
05/10/2026North␣␣430,00 (text)
06/10/2026East760,00 (text)

(The ␣ symbol represents an invisible extra space.)

The steps in the Power Query Editor

After choosing the file, Emma clicks Transform Data (not Load): the Power Query Editor opens.

  1. If needed, Home > Use First Row as Headers.
  2. Home > Remove Rows > Remove Blank Rows.
  3. Right-click the Region column: Transform > Trim.
  4. Click the type icon to the left of the column name: Date for Date, Decimal Number for Amount. As the amounts are in French format, use Change Type > Using Locale and choose French (France) so that the comma is read as the decimal separator.
  5. Home > Close & Load: the result arrives in a new sheet, as a structured table.

On the right of the editor, the Applied Steps pane keeps a list of everything you've done. You can click a step to see the data at that point, delete it or edit it. Behind the scenes, Power Query writes these steps in a language called M, but you don't need to know it to get started.

The loaded result

DateRegionAmount
02/10/2026North1,250.00
03/10/2026South980.00
05/10/2026North430.00
06/10/2026East760.00

If the loaded table is called Sales, the formulas finally work:

FormulaResult
=SUM(Sales[Amount])3,420.00
=SUMIFS(Sales[Amount],Sales[Region],"North")1,680.00

Before Power Query, the sum would have given 0 (amounts as text) and "North" would only have found one row out of two because of the spaces.

The magic moment: refreshing

The following month, Emma replaces the CSV with the new one (same name, same location), then clicks Data > Refresh All (shortcut Ctrl+Alt+F5). All the steps are replayed, the table updates, and so do the formulas and PivotTables built on it. Zero manual cleaning.

Even better with From Folder: Emma drops each new export into a "Sales" folder, and Power Query stacks all the months into a single table at each refresh.

Other useful transformations

  • Split Column (by delimiter): separating "Dupont;Marie" into two columns.
  • Remove Duplicates: right-click the column.
  • Filter: the column arrow, like a normal filter, but the step is recorded.
  • Merge Queries: the equivalent of an XLOOKUP between two tables.
  • Add Custom Column: a row-by-row calculation.

Power Query never changes the source file. It reads, transforms and loads a clean copy. If you make a mistake, delete the step: the original is untouched.

Exercise

  1. In which order will you do these steps: change the Amount type to number, remove blank rows, use the first row as headers?
  2. The following month, the export also contains a South row at 540,00. After refreshing, what do =SUM(Sales[Amount]) and the South total give?
  3. Emma changed a cell in the loaded table by hand. What will happen at the next refresh?
  4. Why did the amounts stored as text make SUM fail?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Headers first, then removing blank rows, then the type. Changing the type before having the right headers would make the conversion fail on the heading row.
  2. 3,420 + 540 = 3,960.00. South: 980 + 540 = 1,520.00.
  3. Her change will be overwritten: the table is completely reloaded from the source and the steps. Corrections must be made in Power Query.
  4. SUM ignores cells containing text, even if that text looks like a number. The type has to be converted.

Key takeaways

  • Power Query: Data > Get Data, then Transform Data.
  • Each action becomes an applied step, replayed at each refresh.
  • Refresh All (Ctrl+Alt+F5) replaces hours of manual cleaning.
  • The source is never changed; don't fix the loaded table by hand.

Next lesson: LET, LAMBDA and first steps towards automation.

39.titre: LET, LAMBDA and first steps towards automation (macros in a nutshell)
39.html:
Why it matters

The further you go, the longer your formulas get. A formula that repeats the same calculation three times is hard to read, slow, and a trap: if you change one part, you have to remember the other two. LET lets you name the steps of a formula. LAMBDA goes further: it lets you create your own functions. Finally, we'll say a word about macros for automating repetitive actions.

LET: naming the steps

Syntax: =LET(name1,value1,[name2,value2,...],calculation). The names only exist inside the formula. Available in Excel 365 and Excel 2021 (and later).

Example: Sofia's quotes

Sofia, on a placement at an agency, calculates quotes. The rule: the amount excl. VAT = quantity × price; a 10% discount if the amount excl. VAT reaches €500; then 20% VAT. Without LET:

=IF(B2*C2>=500,B2*C2*0.9,B2*C2)*1.2

The calculation B2*C2 appears three times. With LET:

=LET(net,B2*C2,discount,IF(net>=500,10%,0),net*(1-discount)*1.2)

RowQuantity (B)Price excl. VAT (C)Excl. VATDiscountIncl. VAT (LET formula)
220€30€60010%€648.00
35€40€2000%€240.00
410€50€50010%€540.00

Check on row 2: 600 × 0.9 = 540, then 540 × 1.2 = €648. Row 4: 500 hits the threshold exactly, so the discount applies (>=).

Good practice (lesson 31): in reality, the threshold, the discount rate and VAT would go in assumption cells. LET makes the formula readable; a clean model makes it easy to change.

LAMBDA: creating your own function

Syntax: =LAMBDA([parameter1,parameter2,...],calculation). Available in Excel 365 (and Excel 2024). A LAMBDA on its own in a cell returns an error: you need to give it a name.

  1. Formulas > Name Manager > New.
  2. Name: PriceInclVAT.
  3. Refers to: =LAMBDA(net,rate,net*(1+rate)).
  4. OK. From now on, throughout the workbook: =PriceInclVAT(100,20%) → 120.

To test a LAMBDA before naming it, you can pass it its values straight afterwards, in brackets: =LAMBDA(x,x*2)(5) → 10.

FormulaResult
=PriceInclVAT(100,20%)120
=PriceInclVAT(540,20%)648
=PriceInclVAT(50,5.5%)52.75

The benefit: a business rule written only once. If it changes, you edit the name, and every cell follows. Google Sheets also offers LET, LAMBDA and "named functions".

Macros, in a nutshell

LET and LAMBDA automate calculations. To automate actions (formatting a report, copying sheets, exporting to PDF), you use macros:

  • The macro recorder (View > Macros > Record Macro) records your clicks and translates them into code. You can then replay the macro in one click.
  • This code is written in VBA (Visual Basic for Applications), visible on the Developer tab (to be switched on in the options, under Customize Ribbon).
  • A workbook with macros is saved as .xlsm: an .xlsx doesn't keep them.
  • Security: a macro can do a lot of things on your computer. Never enable macros in a file you've received unless you're sure of it. In fact, Excel blocks macros in files from the internet by default.

In some business versions of Excel 365 and in Excel for the web, an Automate tab also offers Office Scripts, a more modern alternative. Before diving into macros, ask yourself whether Power Query (lesson 38) or a formula would do the job: it often will.

Exercise

  1. Using Sofia's LET formula, calculate the price incl. VAT for 12 items at €45 excl. VAT.
  2. Same question for 8 items at €60 excl. VAT.
  3. Rewrite with LET: =IF(AVERAGE(B2:B10)>=10,AVERAGE(B2:B10),"Resit").
  4. Create a LAMBDA called Margin that takes a selling price and a cost and returns the margin rate (price − cost) / price. What does =Margin(25,10) give?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Excl. VAT: 12 × 45 = €540 ≥ 500, so a discount. 540 × 0.9 = 486; × 1.2 = €583.20.
  2. Excl. VAT: 8 × 60 = €480 < 500, no discount. 480 × 1.2 = €576.00. Note: 12 items cost barely more than 8 thanks to the discount.
  3. =LET(avg,AVERAGE(B2:B10),IF(avg>=10,avg,"Resit")). The average is only calculated once.
  4. Name Margin, refers to =LAMBDA(price,cost,(price-cost)/price). =Margin(25,10) → 15 / 25 = 0.6, i.e. 60%.

Key takeaways

  • LET names the steps of a formula: more readable, calculated only once (Excel 365 and 2021).
  • LAMBDA creates your own functions, to be named in the Name Manager (Excel 365 and 2024).
  • Macros (VBA, .xlsm files) automate actions; be careful with files you receive.
  • Before reaching for a macro, think formula or Power Query.

Next lesson: the final project, a budget-tracking dashboard from A to Z.

40.titre: Final project: building a budget-tracking dashboard from A to Z
40.html:
Why it matters

This is the last lesson of the course. We won't discover any new functions: we'll put together everything you've learnt to build a real tool, the kind you'll be asked for on a placement or in your first job. The subject: tracking the monthly budget of Lucas, a work-study student who earns €1,200 a month. Follow the steps in your own file: it's the best way to consolidate everything.

The workbook plan

SheetRoleLessons used
SettingsIncome, categories and budget per category (the assumptions)24, 31
TransactionsOne row per expense24, 36, 38
DashboardResults for the chosen month, chart, alerts14, 19, 26, 29

Step 1: the settings

In Settings, create a structured table (Ctrl+T) called T_Budget, with the income in B1 above it (named Income, blue font):

CategoryMonthly budget
Housing€450
Groceries€200
Transport€50
Going out€120
Other€80

Total budgeted: =SUM(T_Budget[Monthly budget]) → €900.

Step 2: the transactions

In Transactions, a table T_Trans with the columns Date, Description, Category, Amount. On the Category column, a drop-down list (lesson 36) whose source is a name CatList that refers to =T_Budget[Category]. On Amount: decimal greater than 0. If the bank provides a CSV export, Power Query (lesson 38) can feed this table automatically.

An extract of Lucas's groceries:

DateDescriptionCategoryAmount
03/10/2026SupermarketGroceries€62.40
10/10/2026MarketGroceries€48.90
17/10/2026SupermarketGroceries€71.20
26/10/2026SupermarketGroceries€53.50
02/11/2026SupermarketGroceries€40.00

Step 3: calculating actuals per month

In Dashboard, the month being studied is chosen in B1 (a date, for example 01/10/2026, with Date-type validation). The categories are in A4:A8. In C4, the category's actual spending for the month:

=SUMIFS(T_Trans[Amount],T_Trans[Category],A4,T_Trans[Date],">="&$B$1,T_Trans[Date],"<="&EOMONTH($B$1,0))

For October groceries: 62.40 + 48.90 + 71.20 + 53.50 = €236.00. The 02/11 row is excluded thanks to the two date criteria. EOMONTH($B$1,0) returns 31/10/2026 (lesson 19).

A more readable version with LET (Excel 365):

=LET(start,$B$1,end,EOMONTH(start,0),SUMIFS(T_Trans[Amount],T_Trans[Category],A4,T_Trans[Date],">="&start,T_Trans[Date],"<="&end))

Step 4: the dashboard

Category (A)Budget (B)Actual (C)Variance (D) =B4-C4% used (E) =IFERROR(C4/B4,0)
Housing€450€450€0100%
Groceries€200€236-€36118%
Transport€50€38€1276%
Going out€120€150-€30125%
Other€80€64€1680%
Total€900€938-€38104.2%

In B4: =XLOOKUP(A4,T_Budget[Category],T_Budget[Monthly budget]) (lesson 22). Add three key indicators at the top of the sheet:

IndicatorFormulaOctober
Spending for the month=SUM(C4:C8)€938
Savings for the month=Income-SUM(C4:C8)€262
Savings rate=(Income-SUM(C4:C8))/Income21.8%

Step 5: making the dashboard clear and robust

  1. Conditional formatting (lesson 26) on E4:E8: Home > Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules > Greater Than 100%, in red. Groceries and Going out stand out immediately.
  2. Chart (lesson 29): a clustered column chart of Budget against Actual, on A3:C8. A title that states the message: "October: groceries and going out over budget".
  3. Protection (lesson 37): unlock B1 (the month), then protect the Dashboard sheet so nobody overwrites a formula.
  4. Check (lesson 31): verify that the dashboard total equals the month's transactions total, with an "OK" cell.

The following month, Lucas adds his expenses (or refreshes the Power Query query), changes B1 to 01/11/2026, and everything recalculates.

Questions to ask yourself before handing in a dashboard

  • Can the message be understood in 10 seconds?
  • Does every figure have a clear unit and period?
  • Are the assumptions separate and easy to spot (colour)?
  • What happens if a category or a transaction is added? (The structured tables should absorb everything.)
  • Is there a check that warns you of any inconsistency?

Exercise

In November, Lucas's actual spending is: Housing €450, Groceries €185, Transport €62, Going out €95, Other €80.

  1. Calculate the variance and the % used for each category. Which ones turn red?
  2. Calculate the month's spending, savings and savings rate.
  3. Lucas adds the category "Subscriptions" (budget €30) to T_Budget. What does he need to do in the dashboard for it to appear? And the drop-down list in the transactions?
  4. Why do we use IFERROR in the % used?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Housing: €0, 100%. Groceries: 200 − 185 = €15, 92.5%. Transport: 50 − 62 = -€12, 124%. Going out: 120 − 95 = €25, 79.2%. Other: €0, 100%. Only Transport turns red (100% is not "greater than" 100%).
  2. Spending: 450 + 185 + 62 + 95 + 80 = €872. Savings: 1,200 − 872 = €328. Rate: 328 / 1,200 ≈ 27.3%.
  3. In the dashboard, add a "Subscriptions" row and copy the formulas down (and extend the chart's range and the conditional formatting if necessary). The drop-down list, on the other hand, adapts by itself, because CatList points to a structured table column. In Excel 365, you could even generate the dashboard's categories with =T_Budget[Category] to automate everything.
  4. If a budget is 0 or empty, C4/B4 returns #DIV/0! (lesson 10). IFERROR displays 0 instead (lesson 15).

Key takeaways

  • A good tool separates settings, data and dashboard.
  • Structured tables + drop-down lists = clean data that grows without breaking formulas.
  • SUMIFS with two date criteria and EOMONTH calculates the actuals for any month.
  • Conditional formatting, a chart with a title that speaks, protection and checks make the difference.
  • Well done: you've completed the whole Excel course!

All that's left is this module's recap sheet, to review everything at a glance.

1.html:
What this first module taught you

In five lessons, you've gone from "I open Excel and don't know where to start" to a solid foundation: you know the vocabulary, you enter clean data, you present it clearly, you get around with the keyboard and you know how to organise, print and save a workbook. These are the moves used in 100% of files.

This recap goes over each lesson in a few lines, then ends with an exercise that brings them all together. Try it without looking at the answers: it's the best test before tackling formulas.

Lesson 1: the layout of Excel

Excel is a spreadsheet: it stores data, calculates and presents results.

  • A workbook contains sheets, made up of cells identified by column then row: B3. A range is written B2:B5.
  • The ribbon groups the commands, the Name Box shows the address, the formula bar shows the real contents.
  • A formula starts with = and recalculates by itself.

One piece of information per cell, headings in row 1, no blank rows in the middle.

Lesson 2: entering data

  • Enter, Tab, F2, Esc. Text on the left, numbers and dates on the right: a number aligned left is suspicious.
  • Decimal point (12.5), dates in the format 15/09/2026, an apostrophe to keep a leading zero ('07).
  • Fill handle: a single number is copied, two numbers create a series, days and months extend. Double-click the handle or use Ctrl+D to go fast.

Lesson 3: formatting

Formatting changes what is displayed, never the stored value.

  • Ctrl+1: Format Cells. Number, Currency, Accounting, Percentage, Date.
  • 15.5% is stored as 0.155: type 15.5% directly.
  • Avoid merging; ######## just means the column is too narrow.

Lesson 4: shortcuts

NeedShortcut
Jump to the edge of the dataCtrl+arrow
Select up to the edgeCtrl+Shift+arrow
AutoSumAlt+=
Fill several cells at onceCtrl+Enter
Find and replaceCtrl+H
Show the ribbon lettersAlt

Lesson 5: organising your workbook

  • Well-named sheets: Data, Calculations, Summary.
  • Freeze Panes: everything above and to the left of the chosen cell stays visible.
  • Ctrl+P for the preview, fit to one page, print titles.
  • .xlsx for working, .csv for exchanging (active sheet, values only), .pdf for sharing.

How it all fits together

Well-entered data (lesson 2) is the condition for correct calculations. Clear formatting (lesson 3) makes it readable. Shortcuts (lesson 4) save you time at every step, and good organisation (lesson 5) makes the file usable by others. In module 2, all this will be the foundation for formulas.

Summary exercise

Malo (fictional), on a placement at a travel agency, has to track a week's bookings. He enters this:

ABCD
1DayBookingsAverage basket (€)Revenue (€)
2Monday4850=B2*C2
3Tuesday6720
4Wednesday31100
5Thursday5640
6Friday7780,5
  1. Malo only typed "Monday" in A2. How did he get the other days?
  2. How do you copy the formula in D2 down to D6 as fast as possible? What are D2, D3, D4 and D5?
  3. Cell C6 aligns left. Why, and how do you fix it? What is D6 then?
  4. Malo puts a total in D7 with Alt+=. Which formula and what result?
  5. He wants to display the amounts with the € symbol and 2 decimal places, and keep row 1 visible while scrolling. What does he do?
  6. His supervisor asks for the file "to import into the management software", then a version "to print for the meeting". Which formats?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. With the fill handle: he dragged A2 down to A6, and Excel extended Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday.
  2. Double-click the handle in D2 (or select D2:D6 then Ctrl+D). D2 = 4 × 850 = 3,400; D3 = 6 × 720 = 4,320; D4 = 3 × 1,100 = 3,300; D5 = 5 × 640 = 3,200.
  3. "780,5" was typed with a comma: UK English Excel sees it as text. You need to type 780.5. D6 = 7 × 780.5 = 5,463.5.
  4. =SUM(D2:D6) → 3,400 + 4,320 + 3,300 + 3,200 + 5,463.5 = 19,683.5.
  5. He selects C2:D7, presses Ctrl+1 and chooses Currency with 2 decimal places (D7 displays €19,683.50). Then View tab, Freeze Top Row.
  6. For the software: .csv (values only, keeping the .xlsx alongside). For the meeting: .pdf, after a Ctrl+P preview and fitting to one page.

Next module: basic formulas, operators, SUM, AVERAGE, absolute references and percentages.

2.html:
What this module taught you

In module 1, you learnt to store and present data. This module taught you to calculate with it: write correct formulas, use the basic functions, copy without breaking anything thanks to $, handle percentages and round cleanly, then diagnose errors. With these five lessons, you can already build most of the tables you'll be asked for on a placement.

This recap goes over each lesson in a few lines, shows how they link together, and ends with an exercise that brings them all together.

Lesson 6: writing a formula

  • A formula starts with = and uses references rather than hard-coded numbers.
  • Operators: + - * / ^, and & to join text.

Precedence: brackets, powers, multiplication and division, addition and subtraction, then left to right.

A forgotten bracket gives a wrong result with no error message: =B4*1+B3 is not =B4*(1+B3).

Lesson 7: the basic functions

FunctionReturns
SUM, AVERAGETotal, average of the numbers
MIN, MAXSmallest, largest number
COUNTNumber of cells containing a number
COUNTANumber of non-empty cells

Arguments separated by ,. AVERAGE ignores blanks and text, but counts zeros.

Lesson 8: references

  • B1 relative, $B$1 absolute, B$1 and $B1 mixed. F4 cycles through the forms.
  • Always lock a parameter (rate, price, total) before copying: =B3*$B$1, =B2/$B$6.
  • Mixed references are for copying in both directions: =$A2*B$1.

Lesson 9: percentages and rounding

Change = (new − old) / old

  • Increase of t: =value*(1+t); decrease: =value*(1-t). Successive percentages multiply: +20% then −20% gives −4%.
  • Difference between two percentages: in points.
  • ROUND to the nearest, ROUNDUP upwards (tables, minibuses), ROUNDDOWN downwards (whole units).

Lesson 10: errors

  • #DIV/0! zero or empty divisor, #VALUE! text instead of a number, #REF! deleted cell, #N/A lookup with no result, #NAME? unknown name.
  • Errors spread: trace back to the first one with Trace Precedents and Evaluate Formula.
  • No error displayed doesn't mean the result is right.

How it all fits together

A good formula (lesson 6) uses the right functions (lesson 7) and the right references (lesson 8) so it can be copied. Percentages and rounding (lesson 9) turn results into useful information. And when things go wrong, reading the errors (lesson 10) tells you where to look. In module 3, we'll add logic: doing a different calculation depending on a condition.

Summary exercise

Rayan (fictional), an intern in the management control team of a chain of 4 cafés, receives this table. The bonus rate is in B1:

ABCDE
1Bonus rate2%
2CaféRevenue 2025 (€)Revenue 2026 (€)ChangeBonus (€)
3Station80,00092,000
4Centre120,000114,000
5Campus50,00061,000
6Harbour70,00073,500
7Total
  1. Which formulas go in B7 and C7? What results?
  2. Which formula goes in D3, to copy down to D7? Give the five changes (1 decimal place).
  3. Each café's bonus is the rate in B1 applied to 2026 revenue. Rayan writes =C3*B1 in E3 and copies it down. What does E4 show, and why? Correct the formula and give the bonuses, rounded to the euro with a function.
  4. Which café has the highest 2026 revenue? Write the formula that gives this amount, and the one that gives the average 2026 revenue.
  5. The Centre café fell by 5% in 2026. If it rises by 5% in 2027, does it get back to its €120,000?
  6. Rayan accidentally deletes column B. Which error appears in the change column, and what should he do?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =SUM(B3:B6) → 80,000 + 120,000 + 50,000 + 70,000 = €320,000. =SUM(C3:C6) → 92,000 + 114,000 + 61,000 + 73,500 = €340,500.
  2. =(C3-B3)/B3. Station: 12,000 / 80,000 = 15.0%. Centre: −6,000 / 120,000 = −5.0%. Campus: 11,000 / 50,000 = 22.0%. Harbour: 3,500 / 70,000 = 5.0%. Total: 20,500 / 320,000 ≈ 6.4% (and not the average of the four changes).
  3. In E4, copying gives =C4*B2: B2 contains the text "Revenue 2025 (€)", hence #VALUE!. The rate should have been locked: =ROUND(C3*$B$1,0). Bonuses: Station 92,000 × 2% = €1,840; Centre €2,280; Campus €1,220; Harbour 73,500 × 2% = €1,470.
  4. The Centre café: =MAX(C3:C6) → €114,000. Average: =AVERAGE(C3:C6) → 340,500 / 4 = €85,125.
  5. No: 114,000 × 1.05 = €119,700. Percentages multiply: it would need a rise of 6,000 / 114,000 ≈ 5.3%.
  6. The formulas that used column B show #REF! (and so do the totals that depend on them, by spreading). The reflex: Ctrl+Z immediately.

Next module: logic, with IF, AND, OR, COUNTIF, SUMIF and IFERROR.

3.html:
What this module taught you

In five lessons, you've learnt to make Excel reason. You can get it to make a decision with IF, combine conditions, choose between several results, count and add up with conditions, and make your formulas robust against missing data. It's the step from "I can do a sum" to "I can build a real tracking tool".

This recap goes over each lesson in a few lines, shows how they link together, and ends with an exercise that brings them all together. Try it without looking at the answers.

Lesson 11: the IF function

=IF(test, value if true, value if false)

  • The test compares with =, <>, >, <, >=, <=. "At least 10" is written >=10.
  • Text in quotation marks, numbers without; "" displays an empty cell. Forgetting the quotation marks gives #NAME?.
  • Results can be calculations: =IF(B2>=20000,B2*5%,0) gives a €1,250 bonus for €25,000 of sales.

Lesson 12: AND, OR, NOT, nested IFs, IFS

  • AND: all the conditions; OR: at least one; NOT: the opposite.
  • For more than two results, you nest IFs; Excel stops at the first true test, so you arrange the thresholds in order.
  • IFS (Excel 2019 and 365) is more readable; you end with TRUE,"…" to avoid #N/A.

Lesson 13: COUNTIF, SUMIF, AVERAGEIF

  • =COUNTIF(range,criteria), =SUMIF(range,criteria,sum_range), =AVERAGEIF(range,criteria,average_range).
  • Criteria: "North", ">1000", "<>North", "B*", and ">"&F1 to compare with a cell.
  • In the lesson's sales, the North accounted for 3 sales, €2,700, so €900 on average.

Lesson 14: COUNTIFS, SUMIFS

  • Several criteria, all required (an AND).
  • =SUMIFS(sum_range,range1,criteria1,range2,criteria2): the sum range comes first, the opposite of SUMIF.
  • Ranges of the same size, otherwise #VALUE!. A range of values uses two criteria on the same range; an OR uses two SUMIFs added together.

Lesson 15: IFERROR and robust formulas

  • =IFERROR(value,value if error) replaces any error with a fallback value.
  • Prefer "" or "n/a" to 0: a 0 distorts averages.
  • IFERROR can hide real bugs; a targeted test like =IF(C2=0,"n/a",B2/C2) is often safer. IFNA only handles #N/A.

The module's common thread

Everything rests on the same building block: a test that is TRUE or FALSE. IF uses it to choose a result, AND and OR combine several, COUNTIF and SUMIF apply it to every row of a range, and IFERROR tests one special case: "is there an error?".

NeedFunctionExample
Choose between two resultsIF=IF(B2>=10,"Pass","Fail")
Combine conditionsAND, OR, NOT=IF(AND(B2>=12,C2="Yes"),…,…)
More than two resultsNested IFs, IFS=IFS(B2>=16,"Excellent",…,TRUE,"Fail")
Count with a conditionCOUNTIF, COUNTIFS=COUNTIF(B2:B6,"North")
Add up with a conditionSUMIF, SUMIFS=SUMIFS(D2:D7,B2:B7,"Groceries",C2:C7,"Card")
Average with a conditionAVERAGEIF, AVERAGEIFS=AVERAGEIF(B2:B6,"North",C2:C6)
Handle an errorIFERROR, IFNA=IFERROR(B2/C2,"n/a")

Classic mistakes

  • Mixing up > and >=: the person right on the threshold switches sides.
  • Forgetting the quotation marks around text (#NAME?), or putting them around a number.
  • Ordering nested IFs badly: test 10 before 16, and everyone gets "Pass".
  • Writing ">F1" instead of ">"&F1 in a criterion.
  • Reversing the argument order between SUMIF and SUMIFS.
  • Putting IFERROR everywhere, right from the start, and hiding a #REF! that revealed a real problem.

Key takeaways

  • A test is TRUE or FALSE: it's the basis of all of Excel's logic.
  • IF chooses, AND/OR combine, nested IFs and IFS classify.
  • The IF and IFS functions count, add up and average without a helper column.
  • Thresholds and criteria in separate cells, ranges locked with $.
  • Check that your subtotals add back up to the total.
  • IFERROR last, with a fallback value that doesn't mislead the reader.

Summary exercise

You're on a placement at a travel agency. Your supervisor gives you the week's sales:

ABCD
1AgentDestinationAmountNo. of travellers
2InèsEurope€1,8002
3KarimAsia€4,2003
4InèsAsia€2,500(empty)
5KarimEurope€9001
6InèsEurope€3,0004
  1. In E2, display "Big booking" if the amount is at least €2,500, otherwise nothing. How many rows are big bookings?
  2. In F2, grade the amounts: €3,000 and over "A", from €1,500 to under €3,000 "B", under €1,500 "C". Write the formula with nested IFs and give the five results.
  3. Write the formula that counts Inès's sales, then the one for the total sold by Inès.
  4. Write the formula for the total of Inès's Europe sales, then the one for the average amount of sales to Asia.
  5. In G2, calculate the amount per traveller (C2/D2). What happens on row 4? Suggest a targeted robust formula.
  6. Something to think about: a colleague suggests =IFERROR(C2/D2,0) and then averages column G. Why is that a bad idea?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =IF(C2>=2500,"Big booking",""). Big bookings: €4,200, €2,500 (right on the threshold, counted thanks to >=) and €3,000, so 3 rows.
  2. =IF(C2>=3000,"A",IF(C2>=1500,"B","C")). Results: €1,800 B, €4,200 A, €2,500 B, €900 C, €3,000 A.
  3. =COUNTIF(A2:A6,"Inès"): 3. =SUMIF(A2:A6,"Inès",C2:C6): 1,800 + 2,500 + 3,000 = €7,300.
  4. =SUMIFS(C2:C6,A2:A6,"Inès",B2:B6,"Europe"): 1,800 + 3,000 = €4,800. =AVERAGEIF(B2:B6,"Asia",C2:C6): (4,200 + 2,500) / 2 = €3,350.
  5. Row 4: D4 is empty, so it counts as 0, and 2,500 / 0 gives #DIV/0!. Targeted formula: =IF(D2=0,"n/a",C2/D2). Results: €900, €1,400, n/a, €900, €750.
  6. With 0, the average amount per traveller becomes (900 + 1,400 + 0 + 900 + 750) / 5 = €790, whereas the true average of the four known rows is (900 + 1,400 + 900 + 750) / 4 = €987.50. The 0 suggests a free trip. Better to use "n/a" or "", which AVERAGE ignores, and above all to ask for the missing number of travellers.

Next module: text and dates, to split, join and clean data like a pro.

4.html:
What this module taught you

In five lessons, you've learnt to handle everything that isn't a simple number: text (splitting it, joining it, cleaning it) and dates (understanding how Excel stores them, and calculating durations and due dates). The last lesson brought it all together into a method for cleaning an imported file, a task you'll do very often on placements.

This recap goes over each lesson in a few lines, shows how they link together, and ends with an exercise that brings them all together. Try it without looking at the answers.

Lesson 16: text functions

  • LEFT(text,num), RIGHT(text,num), MID(text,start,num) extract; LEN counts characters, spaces included. For FR-2025-0153: FR, 0153, 2025 and 12 characters.
  • Their result is text: VALUE turns it into a number. FIND gives the position of a character.
  • UPPER, LOWER, PROPER standardise the case; TRIM removes extra spaces.

Lesson 17: joining and splitting

  • =A2&" "&B2 joins text; CONCAT (Excel 2019 and 365) accepts ranges.
  • =TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,A2:A4) adds a delimiter and ignores blanks (Excel 2019 and 365).
  • TEXT(B2,"€#,##0.00") keeps the formatting inside joined text.
  • Text to Columns (Data tab) splits by a delimiter; Ctrl+E (Flash Fill) works out the rule from an example. Both give a fixed result.

Lesson 18: dates

A date is a number of days since 01/01/1900. What you see is just a format.

  • You add days with +, you count days with -.
  • TODAY() updates; Ctrl+; freezes today's date.
  • DATE(year,month,day) builds a date; YEAR, MONTH, DAY, WEEKDAY break it down.

Lesson 19: date calculations

  • DATEDIF(start,end,"y"), "m" or "d": years, complete months or days. A hidden function; start before end.
  • NETWORKDAYS(start,end,holidays): days from Monday to Friday, both ends included. The placement from 01/09/2025 to 28/02/2026 has 130, and 127 with the bank holidays.
  • WORKDAY(start,n,holidays) moves forward n working days; EOMONTH(date,n) gives the last day of the month.

Lesson 20: cleaning an imported file

  • Work on a copy, with cleaning columns alongside.
  • Spaces and case; non-breaking spaces with SUBSTITUTE(A2,CHAR(160)," ").
  • Numbers as text (aligned left, green triangle): VALUE, Convert to Number, SUBSTITUTE or NUMBERVALUE for separators.
  • Duplicates: spot them with COUNTIF(A$2:A2,A2), then Data, Remove Duplicates, ticking all the columns that define a true duplicate.

The module's common thread

Two ideas run through the whole module. First, what you see isn't necessarily what's stored: an extracted "2025" is text, a date is a number, an imported amount can be text, a space can be invisible. Second, functions nest: PROPER(TRIM(A2)), NUMBERVALUE(B2,",","."), EOMONTH(A2+30,0).

NeedToolExample
Extract a pieceLEFT, RIGHT, MID=MID(A2,4,4)
Clean textTRIM, PROPER=PROPER(TRIM(A2))
Join&, CONCAT, TEXTJOIN=A2&" "&B2
Split without a formulaText to Columns, Ctrl+EData tab
Text to numberVALUE, NUMBERVALUE=NUMBERVALUE(B2,",",".")
Today's dateTODAY(), Ctrl+;=B2-TODAY()
DurationDATEDIF, NETWORKDAYS=DATEDIF(A2,B2,"m")
Due dateWORKDAY, EOMONTH=EOMONTH(A2+30,0)
DuplicatesRemove DuplicatesData tab

Classic mistakes

  • Adding up numbers extracted with LEFT or MID without VALUE: they're text.
  • Forgetting the space in =A2&B2.
  • Thinking a date subtraction is wrong because it's displayed as a date: it's the format.
  • Using TODAY() to record an entry date that should stay fixed.
  • Forgetting bank holidays in NETWORKDAYS, or thinking Excel knows them.
  • Removing duplicates on a single column and wiping out legitimate orders.
  • Cleaning the original file directly, without a copy.

Key takeaways

  • Text functions extract, join and clean; their result is text.
  • TRIM and VALUE fix most problems with imported files.
  • A date is a number: addition and subtraction work directly.
  • DATEDIF, NETWORKDAYS, WORKDAY and EOMONTH cover the usual duration and due-date calculations.
  • Flash Fill and Text to Columns are quick but fixed: check the unusual cases.
  • Clean before analysing: otherwise, your SUMIFs will give wrong totals without warning.

Summary exercise

You're preparing the intern tracker for a company. The HR export looks like this:

A (Name)B (Code)C (Start)D (End)
2" martin LÉA"MKT-2025-01401/09/202528/02/2026
3"petit hugo"FIN-2025-00715/09/202515/12/2025

The bank holidays in the period (01/11/2025, 11/11/2025, 25/12/2025, 01/01/2026) are in H2:H5.

  1. Write the formula that gives the proper name in E2. How many characters does A2 have before and after cleaning (one space at the start)?
  2. Extract the department (the first three letters of the code) and the intern's number as a number.
  3. Build the ID "MKT-Martin Léa" with &, from B2 and E2.
  4. Calculate the length of Hugo's placement in complete months and in days.
  5. How many working days does Léa's placement have, excluding bank holidays? Write the formula.
  6. Léa's September allowance is paid on the last day of the following month. Which formula gives the payment date from C2, and what result?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. =PROPER(TRIM(A2)) gives "Martin Léa". Before: 1 space + "martin" (6) + 1 space + "LÉA" (3) = 11 characters. After: 10.
  2. Department: =LEFT(B2,3), i.e. MKT. Number: =VALUE(RIGHT(B2,3)), i.e. the number 14 (the text "014" becomes 14).
  3. =LEFT(B2,3)&"-"&E2 gives MKT-Martin Léa.
  4. =DATEDIF(C3,D3,"m"): 3 months complete (from 15/09 to 15/12). =D3-C3 or =DATEDIF(C3,D3,"d"): 15 + 31 + 30 + 15 = 91 days.
  5. =NETWORKDAYS(C2,D2,H2:H5): 130 days from Monday to Friday, minus 3 bank holidays falling on weekdays (01/11/2025 is a Saturday), so 127 working days.
  6. =EOMONTH(C2,1): the last day of the month after September, i.e. 31/10/2025.

Next module: looking up data, from VLOOKUP to XLOOKUP, INDEX and MATCH, and dynamic arrays.

5.html:
What this module taught you

In five lessons, you've learnt to make Excel work for you: instead of copying information from one table to another, you look it up with a formula. You discovered the old method (VLOOKUP), the modern one (XLOOKUP), the most versatile one (INDEX + MATCH), then two tools that change the way you work: structured tables and dynamic arrays.

This recap goes over each lesson in a few lines, shows how they link together, and ends with an exercise that brings them all together. Try it without looking at the answers.

Lesson 21: VLOOKUP

=VLOOKUP(value,table,col_num,FALSE)

  • Searches the first column of the table and returns the requested column.
  • FALSE for an exact lookup. Without the last argument, Excel does an approximate lookup.
  • TRUE for a rate scale (thresholds sorted in ascending order): €6,200 of revenue gives 5% commission.
  • Its limits: only looks to the right, fragile column number, #N/A if nothing is found.

Lesson 22: XLOOKUP

=XLOOKUP(value,lookup_array,return_array,[if_not_found])

  • Exact by default, looks left as well as right, copes with inserted columns.
  • Match mode -1 for a scale, search mode -1 for the last occurrence.
  • Excel 365 and Excel 2021 or later only.

Lesson 23: INDEX + MATCH

=INDEX(return_column,MATCH(value,lookup_column,0))

  • MATCH finds the position, INDEX returns the value at that position. MATCH's 0 is essential.
  • With two MATCHes: a two-way lookup (Bruno in March: €1,600).
  • Works in every version.

Lesson 24: structured tables

  • Ctrl+T, then a clear name (Sales).
  • The table grows by itself, calculated columns fill down by themselves.
  • Sales[Amount] = the whole column, [@Price] = the value on the current row.

Lesson 25: FILTER, SORT, UNIQUE

  • A formula returns a list that spills; H2# refers to the whole result; #SPILL! if the range isn't empty.
  • UNIQUE de-duplicates, SORT sorts, FILTER extracts (* for "and", + for "or").
  • Excel 365 and Excel 2021 or later only.

The module's common thread

All these functions answer the same question: where is the information, and how do I bring it here without copying it? Structured tables make sources reliable (they grow by themselves), lookup functions bring back a value, and dynamic arrays bring back whole lists. Together, they let you build files that update themselves.

NeedToolExample
A value from a keyXLOOKUP=XLOOKUP(F2,A2:A5,C2:C5)
Same, all versionsINDEX + MATCH=INDEX(C2:C5,MATCH(F2,A2:A5,0))
A rate in a scaleVLOOKUP TRUE or XLOOKUP -1=XLOOKUP(6200,H2:H5,I2:I5,,-1)
Cross a row and a columnINDEX + 2 MATCHes=INDEX(B2:D4,MATCH(...,0),MATCH(...,0))
A source that growsTable (Ctrl+T)=SUM(Sales[Amount])
A list without duplicatesUNIQUE=UNIQUE(Sales[Seller])
The rows that meet a criterionFILTER=FILTER(Sales,Sales[Amount]>=180)

Classic mistakes

  • Forgetting FALSE in VLOOKUP (or the 0 in MATCH): a wrong result, with no error message.
  • Not locking the table with $ signs before copying a VLOOKUP.
  • A hard-coded column number that no longer points to the right column after an insertion.
  • Using XLOOKUP or FILTER in a file meant for someone on Excel 2019 or older.
  • Fixed ranges (A2:E6) that miss new rows: switch to a structured table.
  • Leaving cells occupied under a formula that spills (#SPILL!).

Key takeaways

  • Don't copy: look up the information with a formula.
  • XLOOKUP by default on Excel 365; INDEX + MATCH if the file has to circulate on older versions.
  • VLOOKUP is still worth knowing to read existing files, with FALSE.
  • Always plan for the "not found" case (if_not_found, if_empty).
  • Turn your lists into structured tables from the start.
  • FILTER, SORT, UNIQUE build lists that update by themselves.

Summary exercise

During your placement, you manage two tables. The Products table:

RefProductPrice
P01Keyboard€25
P02Mouse€15
P03Monitor€180
P04Headset€60

And the Orders table, which is missing the Price and Amount columns:

CustomerRefQuantity
DurandP032
MartinP015
DurandP041
PetitP024
MartinP031
  1. Both lists are normal ranges. What do you do first, and why?
  2. In Orders, write the formula for the Price column with XLOOKUP, then the one for the Amount column. Calculate each amount and the total.
  3. Your manager has Excel 2016. Rewrite the Price formula so it works for him, in two ways.
  4. Write the formula that returns the name of product P02 with INDEX + MATCH.
  5. Build a summary by customer with UNIQUE and SUMIF. What amounts do you get?
  6. Write the formula that lists orders of at least €150, from biggest to smallest. How many rows?
  7. Something to think about: a customer orders reference P09, which doesn't exist yet. What happens, and how do you plan for it?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Turn them into structured tables with Ctrl+T and name them Products and Orders. New orders and new products will be included automatically, and the formulas will be readable.
  2. Price: =XLOOKUP([@Ref],Products[Ref],Products[Price]). Amount: =[@Quantity]*[@Price]. Durand P03: 2 × 180 = €360; Martin P01: 5 × 25 = €125; Durand P04: 1 × 60 = €60; Petit P02: 4 × 15 = €60; Martin P03: 1 × 180 = €180. Total: =SUM(Orders[Amount]) = €785.
  3. =VLOOKUP([@Ref],Products,3,FALSE) or =INDEX(Products[Price],MATCH([@Ref],Products[Ref],0)). Structured tables exist in Excel 2016; it's XLOOKUP and dynamic arrays that are missing.
  4. =INDEX(Products[Product],MATCH("P02",Products[Ref],0)) returns Mouse.
  5. In H2: =UNIQUE(Orders[Customer]) gives Durand, Martin, Petit. In I2: =SUMIF(Orders[Customer],H2#,Orders[Amount]) gives Durand 360 + 60 = €420, Martin 125 + 180 = €305, Petit €60. Check: 420 + 305 + 60 = €785.
  6. =SORT(FILTER(Orders,Orders[Amount]>=150,"None"),5,-1) (Amount is the 5th column). 2 rows: Durand P03 €360, then Martin P03 €180.
  7. XLOOKUP can't find P09: the Price shows #N/A, so does the Amount, and the total in turn becomes #N/A. To plan for it, add a 4th argument, for example =XLOOKUP([@Ref],Products[Ref],Products[Price],0): the price is 0 and the total stays correct, but a message like "Unknown ref" is better for spotting the problem. The Amount formula will then need to handle this text (with IFERROR, seen in module 3). The real fix is still to add P09 to the Products table.

6.html:
What this module taught you

In five lessons, you've gone from the raw list to analysis. You can make a list talk with sorting, filters and conditional formatting, summarise it with a PivotTable, enrich it with grouping, calculated fields and slicers, then present the result with the right chart.

This recap goes over each lesson in a few lines, shows how they link together, and ends with an exercise that brings them all together. Try it without looking at the answers.

Lesson 26: sorting, filtering, conditional formatting

  • Sort: click in the list, Data > Sort, several levels possible. Never select a single column.
  • Filter: Ctrl+Shift+L; rows are hidden, not deleted.
  • =SUBTOTAL(109,range) only counts visible rows; SUM counts everything.
  • Conditional formatting: highlights, data bars, colour scales, icons; for a whole row, a formula rule such as =$D2>1000.

Lesson 27: PivotTables, the basics

  • Insert > PivotTable, from a clean list (ideally a structured table).
  • Four areas: Rows, Columns, Values, Filters.
  • Summarise by Sum, Count, Average; show as % of total (North: 800 / 1,700 ≈ 47.06%).
  • A PivotTable doesn't update by itself: Refresh (Alt+F5).

Lesson 28: advanced PivotTables

  • Group dates by month (and year), numbers into bands.
  • Calculated field: Margin =Revenue-Cost, Rate =(Revenue-Cost)/Revenue. It calculates on the sums: 490 / 1,550 ≈ 31.6%, not the average of the rates.
  • Slicers and the timeline to filter in one click, possibly several PivotTables at once.

Lesson 29: choosing the right chart

  • Comparison: column or bar. Change over time: line. Split of a whole (few slices): pie. Link between two measures: scatter.
  • Insert > Recommended Charts, Alt+F1 or F11.
  • A message title, sorted bars, data labels, no 3D.

Lesson 30: professional charts

  • Combo chart with a secondary axis for two units (revenue in euros, rate in %).
  • Sparklines: a mini chart per cell to see trends.
  • A column chart starts at 0; few colours; source and unit stated.

The module's common thread

These lessons follow the path of an analysis: explore the list (sorting, filters, colours), summarise it (PivotTable), dig deeper (grouping, margins, slicers), then present it (charts). The structured table from module 5 is the foundation of everything: the source grows, and both the PivotTable and the chart follow after a refresh.

QuestionToolReflex
Who's on top?SortClick in the list, not on a column
How much for one category?Filter + SUBTOTALCode 109
Where are the unusual values?Conditional formatting$ in front of the column for the whole row
How much per region, per product?PivotTableRefresh after every change
What margin per month?Grouped PivotTable + calculated fieldAn overall rate, not an average of rates
How do I show it?ChartOne message, a message title
Two different units?Combo chartSecondary axis, titled axes
Trend of each row?SparklinesHigh point, low point

Classic mistakes

  • Sorting a single column and scrambling the rows.
  • Using SUM under a filtered list and presenting a total that includes the hidden rows.
  • Forgetting to refresh a PivotTable after the data changes.
  • Averaging rates instead of dividing a total by a total.
  • Grouping by month without the years on data covering several years.
  • A 10-slice pie chart, 3D, or a column chart whose axis doesn't start at 0.

Key takeaways

  • Explore, summarise, dig deeper, present: that's the path of any analysis.
  • Filtered rows are hidden: SUBTOTAL(109,...) for visible totals.
  • The PivotTable summarises without formulas; remember to refresh it.
  • The calculated field gives correct rates, calculated on the totals.
  • A chart is chosen according to the message and carries a message title.
  • Secondary axis for two units, sparklines for trends, column charts from 0.

Summary exercise

Your placement manager sends you the quarter's Sales table:

MonthRegionRevenueCost
JanNorth€400€250
JanSouth€300€210
FebNorth€500€320
FebSouth€200€150
MarNorth€450€300
MarSouth€350€220
  1. Sort the list by Revenue descending. What are the first three rows?
  2. You filter on Region = South. What do =SUM(Sales[Revenue]) and a SUBTOTAL with code 109 on the same column return?
  3. You apply the rule "Less Than 300" to the Revenue column. Which cells are formatted?
  4. Build a PivotTable with Region in Rows and Revenue in Values. What totals, and what share of the total for the North (rounded to 0.1%)?
  5. Add the calculated fields Margin and Margin rate. What results for the North, the South and the total?
  6. Your manager wants a chart showing, month by month, total revenue and the margin rate. Which one do you build? Calculate the three monthly rates.
  7. Something to think about: a colleague announces an average margin rate of 33.7% by averaging the rates of the two regions. What do you think?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Feb North €500, Mar North €450, Jan North €400. Then Mar South €350, Jan South €300, Feb South €200.
  2. SUM: 400 + 300 + 500 + 200 + 450 + 350 = €2,200 (it ignores the filter). =SUBTOTAL(109,Sales[Revenue]): 300 + 200 + 350 = €850.
  3. Only Feb South (€200). Jan South is exactly €300, which isn't strictly less.
  4. North: 400 + 500 + 450 = €1,350. South: €850. Total: €2,200. North's share: 1,350 / 2,200 ≈ 61.4%.
  5. Costs: North 250 + 320 + 300 = €870; South 210 + 150 + 220 = €580; total €1,450. Margins: North 1,350 − 870 = €480, South 850 − 580 = €270, total €750. Rates: North 480 / 1,350 ≈ 35.6%, South 270 / 850 ≈ 31.8%, total 750 / 2,200 ≈ 34.1%.
  6. A combo chart: revenue as columns, margin rate as a line on a secondary axis, with titled axes. January: revenue €700, margin 150 + 90 = €240, rate ≈ 34.3%. February: revenue €700, margin 180 + 50 = €230, rate ≈ 32.9%. March: revenue €800, margin 150 + 130 = €280, rate = 35.0%. Possible message title: "Revenue picks up in March, and margin with it".
  7. (35.6 + 31.8) / 2 = 33.7%: it's an average of rates that gives the same weight to both regions, whereas the North makes up 61% of revenue. The true overall rate is 750 / 2,200 ≈ 34.1%. That's exactly what the PivotTable's calculated field calculates.
